entries.term: Unit of analysis: the collaborative arrangement
entries.plain: The unit of analysis is the thing a study's findings are about, its 'case'. It decides what is counted and compared.
in_this_thesis: 'The collaborative arrangement: each observed or attempted collaboration, described by whether the parties' markets overlapped, what was shared, and what bound it' (1.4).
It is 'the case in Yin's (2018) sense, the thing the research question is about' (3.1).

Each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration a participant described is one row of Appendix H, coded for overlap, what was pooled and withheld, what bound it, who began it, its status at interview and whether it used time; in October 2026 each row was coded again for the meeting point, its holder, whether the holder sells delivery to the parties' customers and whether its co-users are rivals (3.1).
Operators and documents are the sources; the survey is read by organisation and for scale only (1.4).

Each case is limited 'to what the participant described, and no further', the discipline Miles, Huberman and Saldaña (2014) ask for, which lets the 117 rows be read beside the 241 papers (unit: the paper) and Ghent's permit categories (unit: the class of operator) (3.1).
entries.why: 'Because a finding about willingness concerns a pair of markets and a finding about binding concerns an arrangement, and neither is a property of a firm' (1.4).
entries.not_this: The firm: 'neither is a property of a firm' (1.4).
entries.analogy: Studying marriages rather than spouses: whether a marriage lasts is a property of the pair and what holds it, not of either person alone.

viva_questions.q: If the unit is the arrangement, why do you count transcripts at all?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because there are two units of counting and I keep them apart. Stances are counted by transcript, one participant's testimony each; arrangements by row of Appendix H. A count of transcripts is a count of accounts; a count of rows is a count of accounts of arrangements (3.1; 3.4).

viva_questions.q: How did you bound the case?
viva_questions.model_answer: By what the participant described and no further, as Miles, Huberman and Saldaña ask. Each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration a participant described is one row. That is what lets the 117 rows sit beside the 241 papers and Ghent's permit categories, each with its own unit (3.1).

quiz.q: What is the thesis's unit of analysis?
quiz.explanation: 1.4; a finding about willingness concerns a pair of markets, not a firm.

quiz.q: Which collaborations count as a row of Appendix H?
options: Operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed ones a participant described

entries.term: Finding versus proposition
entries.plain: A finding is something the evidence shows. A proposition is a claim the evidence points to and partly supports, offered for testing.
in_this_thesis: Four links are found; the fifth is proposed: 'Link 5, the holder, is different. The thesis proposes it rather than finding it (6.3)' (1.5); 'Four of the five were there to be read in the evidence; the fifth, the holder, is where that evidence points' (2.7).
The holder's evidence is graded: the interviews support it 'only under' rule 1a; the locker difference 'fits the link but does not test it'; and no rule found looks again when control changes (1.5).
Ghent's 2016 expectation that suppliers' traffic would not fall in the open window was not counted in either plan, so 'Chapter 6 treats it as expected and not as found' (5.2).
The one sentence is tested clause by clause and 'stands as a finding up to ‘the street’ and as a proposition after it' (6.5, Figure 6.7).
Because the design is theory-building, even the found links are offered as propositions P1 to P5 for others to test (7.2).
entries.why: For the holder, three reasons the thesis gives: the interviews support it only under a rule added after the results were seen; the locker test shows a difference by owner class, 'consistent with the clause and not a test of it'; and 'no city has yet done what the clause says' (6.5).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A weather service reports yesterday's rainfall as a finding; tomorrow's forecast, however well grounded, is a proposition until tomorrow comes.

viva_questions.q: Which parts of your one sentence are findings, and which are propositions?
viva_questions.model_answer: Up to 'the street' it is a finding: competition for the same customers, not a shortage of trust, stops carriers collaborating, and where they cannot share the street the line falls at the customer relationship. After it, that what they would share must be held by someone who does not want their customers and that a city can see it stays that way, it is a proposition: no city has yet done what the last clause says (6.5).

viva_questions.q: You have p = .008 on the lockers. Why not claim the holder as a finding?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because that is a difference by owner class at one time, consistent with the link and not a test of it; the interviews support the holder only under a coding rule added after the results were seen; and no rule found looks again when control changes. So I propose it, with its objections and its tests (1.5; 5.2; 6.5; 7.4).

entries.term: Systematic review
entries.plain: A literature review run to a written protocol: a stated search, stated criteria and a logged decision for each record, so others can repeat it and see what was left out and why.
in_this_thesis: The 2023 review: one search string to six databases on 1 September 2022; 860 records reduced in five stages to forty-nine studies; screened by the author; logged in the 2023 screening log (2.1; Table 3.3; Appendix E).
The 2026 update: six strings in OpenAlex on 16 September 2026; 1,535 records to 241 papers (2.2; Table 3.3).
'Like the 2023 review, the update followed Tranfield, Denyer and Smart (2003) and reports to the PRISMA 2020 standard (Page et al., 2021)' (3.2).

The update was screened and carded in three steps: written inclusion criteria applied at title and abstract; a second pass on every doubtful record with its abstract fetched; a reading card for every included paper, quotations located to the page wherever the full text was carded (3.2).
Who screened: in 2023 'the author'; in 2026 'the author's written criteria applied to every record, each decision logged with its reason; the included set verified by the author' (Table 3.3).
Every screening decision and card is logged with its reason and source in Appendix E, and both runs can be repeated from the strings (3.7).
entries.why: Tranfield, Denyer and Smart's requirement 'that a review be transparent and reproducible' (3.2), and the criterion the update 'could not do without', 'that a reader be able to run the search again' (3.2).
entries.not_this: For the rules and the locker networks the thesis uses a systematised review instead (Grant and Booth, 2009), a lighter form (3.5).
entries.analogy: An audited stocktake: every item counted in or out is logged with its reason, so anyone can run the count again.

viva_questions.q: Who screened the records?
viva_questions.model_answer: In 2023, I did. In 2026 my written criteria were applied to every record, each decision logged with its reason, and I verified the included set. The cards, the re-run of the 2023 full-text stage and the codings were likewise made to my written criteria, with every decision logged and checked by me (Table 3.3; 3.2).

viva_questions.q: What standard does the review report to?
viva_questions.model_answer: Both runs followed Tranfield, Denyer and Smart and report to PRISMA 2020. The flows are Figures 2.1 and 2.2, the logs are in Appendix E, and re-running the 2023 full-text stage answers PRISMA 2020's item 16b (3.2).

quiz.q: Which methodological source do both runs of the review follow?
quiz.explanation: And both report to PRISMA 2020 (3.2).

quiz.q: Where are the full logs of both runs?
quiz.explanation: Appendix H holds the arrangements, L the codebook for the 117, M the locker networks (3.2).

entries.term: The search string and the review's blind spot
entries.plain: A search string is the exact combination of words and logic (AND, OR) fed to a database. It decides what the review can see; work phrased outside it is invisible.
in_this_thesis: The 2022 string: ("collaborative" OR "multimodal") AND ("last mile") AND ("urban" OR "city") AND ("logistics" OR "delivery") (2.1).
Its forty-nine described 'a set of strategies for a small group of parcel carriers. That was not what the string had asked for. It was what the string could see' (2.1).

Its reach was tested before any new search: twelve papers sit inside the field's own citation trail on horizontal collaboration (Appendix F); run again in OpenAlex, the 2022 string returns none of them; the 2023 review held one, added by hand (2.2).
Three of the twelve come from outside freight, so 'the case that the 2022 string missed the collaboration literature rests on the other nine' (2.2).

Five corrected strings were added in September 2026: horizontal collaboration and cooperation, the noun collaboration, carrier and shipper terms, consolidation and micro-hub terms, and time-window terms (Table 3.3).

Of the 231 update papers not among the forty-nine, the 2022 string returns only 39, and 192 fall outside its terms; 33 of the 39 are dated before 2018 or from 2023; four of the remaining six, and two others, reached the 238 that passed the 2023 journal stage. So, 'with at most eight exceptions', the 2023 review did not weigh these papers and reject them (2.2).
Both strings are reported side by side and both trails kept (2.2; Appendix E). The 2023 string is the first object of reflexivity (3.7).
entries.why: The corrected strings 'name the subject the original could not see' (3.2), 'in the collaboration literature's own terms' (2.2). Both are kept because 'the two searches map two bodies of work that barely meet, the last-mile literature and the collaboration literature, and the thesis needs both' (2.2).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A fishing net cut for one species: it lands plenty, but a whole shoal of another kind swims through, and the catch looks complete.

viva_questions.q: How did you show the 2022 string missed the literature, rather than just assert it?
viva_questions.model_answer: I tested its reach before running a new search. Twelve papers sit in the field's own citation trail on horizontal collaboration, and run again in OpenAlex the 2022 string returns none of them. Then, of the 231 update papers not in the forty-nine, it returns only 39; 192 fall outside its terms. With at most eight exceptions, the 2023 review didn't weigh those papers and reject them; it couldn't find them (2.2).

viva_questions.q: Three of your twelve test papers aren't about freight. Doesn't that inflate the case?
viva_questions.model_answer: They are not about freight, so a last-mile string could not be expected to find them, and I say the case rests on the other nine. The three are read because each tests, outside freight, a condition the freight papers raise (2.2).

quiz.q: Of the 231 update papers not among the forty-nine, how many does the 2022 string return?
quiz.explanation: 192 fall outside its terms; 0 is how many of the twelve citation-trail papers it returns (2.2).

quiz.q: Which of these did the corrected strings add?
options: The noun collaboration, carrier and shipper terms, and time-window terms
quiz.explanation: Also horizontal collaboration and cooperation, and consolidation and micro-hub terms (Table 3.3).

entries.term: PRISMA 2020 and the flow diagram
entries.plain: PRISMA is a reporting standard for systematic reviews. Its flow diagram shows how many records were found and how many left at each screening stage, like a funnel.
in_this_thesis: 2023 flow (Figure 2.1; Table 3.3): 860 identified, a total that counts the eight hand-added papers twice.
662 after the date rule (the 198 published before 2018 set aside, except the eight kept by hand, which are among the 662).
596 downloaded once unsuitable records, duplicates and unobtainable files were out.

263 relevant on title and abstract; 238 after journal refining (25 removed, from fourteen journals, thirteen with a written reason); 72 judged relevant on reading the 238 and read in full; 49 included.

2026 flow (Figure 2.2; Table 3.3): 1,535 identified; 1,023 of eligible type; 254 relevant on title and abstract (208 at first pass, 46 of 150 doubtful records at a second pass with abstracts); 242 records after the citation rule, 241 papers once one article under two DOIs is counted once.
The 241 were carded: 170 from full text, 63 from abstracts, 8 from bibliographic records (Table 3.3).
PRISMA 2020 item 16b, which asks a review to cite studies that might appear to meet its criteria and say why each was excluded, is the reason the 2023 full-text stage was re-run (3.2).
entries.why: The thesis reports to PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021) and does not argue for it as such; its one use of a specific item is 16b, the reason for re-running the 2023 full-text stage (3.2).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative reporting standard.
entries.analogy: A stack of quarry sieves: each finer mesh holds back a known amount, and the log records what each layer removed.

viva_questions.q: Walk me through your 2023 flow.
viva_questions.model_answer: 860 records, a total that counts eight hand-added papers twice; 662 after the date rule; 596 once unsuitable records, duplicates and unobtainable files were out; 263 on title and abstract; 238 after journals whose field lay elsewhere were removed; 72 judged relevant on reading; 49 included after the full texts were read (2.1; Table 3.3).

viva_questions.q: Your 860 counts eight papers twice. Why report it that way?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because 860 is the total the 2023 review reported: 662 published from 2018 or kept by hand and 198 from before, with the eight hand-added papers in both. I give its make-up so the reader can see it, and Appendix E sets out the flow as the files support it (2.1; Table 3.3).

in_this_thesis: In the 2023 review, 'the quality appraisal followed the standard quality assessment criteria for primary research papers issued by the Alberta Heritage Foundation for Medical Research's HTA Initiative (Kmet, Lee and Cook, 2004), applied at the full-text stage' (2.1).
At the journal stage, 25 articles from fourteen journals were removed, thirteen of the journals with a written reason (2.1).

The synthesis reads the evidence by kind: of the forty-nine, 12 reviews, 8 frameworks, 16 models, 10 empirical studies, 3 reports; eighteen carry a numerical result of their own, almost all from a model, a simulation or a questionnaire (2.1).

In the update, the cards record what kind each result is: of 116 numerical results, seventy-seven computed from model instances, five carried from elsewhere, thirty-four from empirical studies, and eleven cards measure a running collaboration, seven with an operating figure (2.2).
entries.why: The thesis does not say why it chose Kmet, Lee and Cook's criteria, and it does not describe a separate quality appraisal for the 2026 update.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative appraisal tool.
entries.analogy: An MOT for papers: each gets the same checklist before it is allowed to carry weight in the argument.

viva_questions.q: How did you appraise the quality of the studies?
viva_questions.model_answer: In the 2023 review, at the full-text stage, against the standard quality assessment criteria for primary research papers from the Alberta Heritage Foundation's HTA Initiative, Kmet, Lee and Cook (2004). And the synthesis reads quality by kind: of the forty-nine, eighteen carry a numerical result of their own, and almost every one comes from a model, a simulation or a questionnaire (2.1).

viva_questions.q: Did the 2026 update appraise quality?
viva_questions.model_answer: The update's steps were written inclusion criteria at title and abstract, a second pass with abstracts for doubtful records, and a reading card for every included paper. The cards record what kind of result each paper carries, modelled, carried from elsewhere, empirical or measured on a running collaboration. The thesis doesn't describe a separate appraisal checklist for the update (3.2; 2.2).

quiz.q: Whose criteria did the 2023 quality appraisal follow?
quiz.explanation: The Alberta Heritage Foundation for Medical Research's HTA Initiative criteria (2.1).

quiz.q: At which stage of the 2023 review was the quality appraisal applied?

entries.gap: Why Kmet, Lee and Cook, and whether the update appraised quality, are not stated.

entries.term: The 2026 update (and the thirty-citation rule)
entries.plain: An update runs a review again later, here with corrected search terms, to reach work the first search could not see.
in_this_thesis: Run 16 September 2026 in OpenAlex's title-and-abstract field, through its public interface; six strings, the original plus five corrected (Table 3.3).

Document types: the written types of 2023, applied to the type the index records, so conference papers, dissertations and preprints were removed; two items recorded as articles, a capstone project and a peer-reviewed conference abstract, remain (Table 3.3).
Dates: 2018 onwards; earlier papers kept only if cited thirty times or more (Table 3.3).
1,535 identified; 1,023 of eligible type; 254 relevant on title and abstract (208 first pass; 46 of 150 doubtful records at a second pass with abstracts fetched); 242 records, 241 papers (Table 3.3).
Nine of the 241 were among the forty-nine; a tenth had reached the 2023 full-text stage and been set aside (2.2).
Recorded as change 3 in Table 3.8.
entries.why: The 2022 string 'was written for the last mile, and its reach could be tested before any new search was run'; the update 'was built to reach the literature the twelve belong to' (2.2). Three deliberate differences (3.2): the corrected strings name the subject; one index replaced four; and earlier papers were kept by a stated rule. On the rule: 'Tranfield, Denyer and Smart's (2003) requirement that a review be transparent and reproducible is better met by a threshold anyone can apply than by selection by judgement' (3.2). The second pass exists because OpenAlex carries fewer abstracts per article (3.2). The thesis does not say why the threshold is thirty rather than another number.
entries.not_this: The 2023 review kept earlier papers by judgement (eight added by hand as prominent) (3.2).
entries.analogy: Dredging a harbour again with a wider net after learning the first dredge missed a channel.

viva_questions.q: Why thirty citations?
viva_questions.model_answer: The rule was set for this review so that earlier papers were kept by a threshold anyone can apply rather than by judgement, as they had been in 2023; that's Tranfield, Denyer and Smart's requirement of transparency and reproducibility. The thesis doesn't argue for thirty over another number (3.2).

viva_questions.q: How did you handle records with little information?
viva_questions.model_answer: OpenAlex carries fewer abstracts per article than Web of Science or Scopus, so every doubtful record got a second pass with its abstract fetched: 46 of 150 doubtful records were kept at that pass, on top of 208 at the first (3.2; Table 3.3).

quiz.q: In the update, a paper published before 2018 was kept only if...
options: it named shippers in its title
it had been cited thirty times or more
quiz.explanation: The citation rule (3.2; Table 3.3).

quiz.q: How many of the 241 were among the 2023 forty-nine?
quiz.explanation: A tenth, Coenegrachts and colleagues (2021), had reached the 2023 full-text stage and been set aside (2.2).

entries.gap: Why the threshold is thirty citations is not argued.

entries.term: One open index: OpenAlex
entries.plain: OpenAlex is a free, open index of scholarly papers. Using it means anyone can re-run the same search without a library subscription.
in_this_thesis: 'One index replaced four databases, because OpenAlex's title-and-abstract field is the nearest single equivalent of the four and can be re-run by anyone with the strings in Appendix E' (3.2).

Grounds (3.2): Gusenbauer and Haddaway (2020) separate criteria that 'should always be met by search systems' from those a review may add; the one this review could not do without was that a reader be able to run the search again, which a public index through a public interface meets for any reader and four databases behind institutional logins meet only for subscribers.

OpenAlex replaced the Microsoft Academic Graph on its retirement in 2022, 'a fully-open (100% open data, open API, open-source code) source of scholarly metadata' (Priem, Piwowar and Orr, 2022, p. 1) (3.2).

On 16.8 million recent publications common to the three, it 'has average source reference numbers and internal coverage rates comparable to both Web of Science and Scopus' (Culbert et al., 2025, p. 2475), while carrying fewer abstracts per article, so every doubtful record was given a second pass with its abstract fetched (3.2).
The cost: counts are 'comparable in kind only as far as the title-and-abstract stage' (3.2).
entries.why: As above: reproducibility for any reader (Gusenbauer and Haddaway, 2020), openness (Priem et al., 2022) and comparable coverage (Culbert et al., 2025) (3.2).
entries.not_this: The four subscription databases of 2023: ScienceDirect, Scopus, Web of Science and TRID (Table 3.3).
entries.analogy: Publishing a recipe that uses supermarket ingredients rather than a private supplier's: anyone can cook it again and check the result.

viva_questions.q: Isn't one index a weaker search than four databases?
viva_questions.model_answer: The criterion I couldn't do without was that a reader be able to run the search again, which Gusenbauer and Haddaway class among the criteria any search system for a systematic review must meet. A public index through a public interface meets it for any reader; four databases behind logins meet it only for subscribers. On coverage, Culbert and colleagues found OpenAlex comparable to Web of Science and Scopus; its weakness is fewer abstracts, so every doubtful record got a second pass with its abstract fetched (3.2).

viva_questions.q: What did you lose by switching?
viva_questions.model_answer: Comparability beyond title and abstract. The forty-nine are papers included after full reading; the 241 were retained after title-and-abstract screening and the citation rule, 170 of them read in full. Wherever the two figures stand together I say which kind each is (3.2).

quiz.q: What criterion did 3.2 say this review's search could not do without?
options: That a reader be able to run it again
quiz.explanation: Gusenbauer and Haddaway (2020) (3.2).

quiz.q: What weakness of OpenAlex does 3.2 name?
options: It carries fewer abstracts per article
quiz.explanation: Hence the second pass with abstracts fetched (3.2).

entries.term: Re-running the 2023 full-text stage
entries.plain: Going back to a past screening stage and making a fresh, recorded decision on each paper that could have been excluded there, because the original record gave only general reasons.
in_this_thesis: The 2023 record gives its exclusion reasons at the full-text stage by topic, among them 'crowd-shipping, travelling salesman problems, bicycle deliveries, and public transport sharing', not paper by paper (2.1).
In 2026, 'the thirty-one papers that could have left at that stage were each assessed again against the 2023 criteria and coded twice, with every disagreement settled' (3.2).

Twenty-nine exclusions were upheld; two papers meet the criteria, and the forty-nine already include studies of the same kinds, 'so leaving those two out does not change the kinds of study the review covers' (3.2).

On subject the two codings agreed on thirty of thirty-one (alpha = .91); six further codes differed on publication type alone, all papers in conference proceedings, a kind the forty-nine include, and were settled by that precedent (3.2).
Appendix E gives each candidate with its settled code and reason, dated to the re-run (3.2). Recorded as change 4 in Table 3.8.

Why thirty-one: no list of the seventy-two survives; the candidates are the thirty records in the 2023 full-text export that are not among the forty-nine, plus Kanter (1994), the one hand-added paper not among them (Appendix E, E.2.7 and E.2.10).
entries.why: It answers PRISMA 2020 item 16b, which asks a review 'to cite the studies that might appear to meet its criteria and to say why each was excluded' (Page et al., 2021) (3.2); and 'the 2023 record gave its exclusion reasons by topic and did not name the papers it excluded at that stage' (Table 3.8).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Re-marking a batch of exam scripts where the original marker left only a general comment, so each script now carries its own mark and reason.

viva_questions.q: Seventy-two read in full and forty-nine included is twenty-three dropped. Why did you reassess thirty-one?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because no list of the seventy-two survives. The closest record is the 2023 full-text export, which holds the forty-nine plus thirty others, so I reassessed all thirty and Kanter (1994), the one hand-added paper not among the forty-nine. That way every paper that could have been among the twenty-three has a recorded decision and reason (Appendix E, E.2.7, E.2.10).

viva_questions.q: What did the re-run change?
viva_questions.model_answer: Twenty-nine exclusions stand. Two papers meet the 2023 criteria, but the forty-nine already include studies of the same kinds, so leaving them out does not change the kinds of study the review covers. Agreement on subject was thirty of thirty-one, alpha .91 (3.2).

quiz.q: Why was the 2023 full-text stage re-run?
options: The 2023 record gave its exclusion reasons by topic, not paper by paper
The original papers had been lost
A supervisor asked for a larger set
quiz.explanation: And to answer PRISMA 2020 item 16b (3.2; Table 3.8).

quiz.q: How many exclusions did the re-run uphold?
quiz.explanation: Thirty of thirty-one is the agreement on subject between the two codings (3.2).

quiz.q: What agreement did the two codings of the re-run reach on subject?
quiz.explanation: 112 of 130 is the transcripts; 98 of 117 the initiator re-check; kappa 1.00 the survey's open answers (3.2, 3.4, 3.6).

entries.gap: The main text does not reconcile thirty-one candidates with the twenty-three papers dropped between seventy-two and forty-nine; only Appendix E does. Know the appendix answer.

entries.term: Reading cards, the second reading, and counts of silence
entries.plain: A reading card is a structured note made for each paper, recording what it says on each point the review cares about. 'Silent' means the reading found nothing on that point, not that the paper denies it.
in_this_thesis: A card was made for every included paper; the 241 were carded 170 from full text, 63 from abstracts and 8 from bibliographic records, with quotations located to the page wherever the full text was carded (3.2; Table 3.3).

The cards were read a second time in September 2026, when full texts obtained that month were read and those cards set again; the counts of 2.2 are from the second reading, with the first reading's counts of silence beside them (3.2).
Silence fell on the second reading: on the boundary of sharing from 36 to 26, on overlap from 128 to 108, on time from 138 to 133 (2.2).
A card marked 'not in text' was counted as silent (2.2).

'A card counts as silent if its reading found nothing on the point. A reading can miss things, so the real counts of silence in 2.2 may be lower than those given there' (3.7; the same caution in 2.2 and 7.4).
On every link, papers supporting the chain outnumber those against by more than three to one (2.2).
entries.why: 'Not in text' counts as silent 'because a paper written for another purpose may simply not cover that concept, and this must not be read as a finding against it' (2.2). The second reading took in full texts obtained in September 2026 (3.2).
entries.not_this: Counting 'not in text' as evidence against (rejected, 2.2).
entries.analogy: A library catalogue card per book: a blank line means the cataloguer found nothing, not that the book has nothing.

viva_questions.q: Sixty-three of your cards come from abstracts. Doesn't that understate what the papers say?
viva_questions.model_answer: It can, and I say so: a card counts as silent if its reading found nothing on the point, and a reading can miss things, so the real counts of silence may be lower. The second reading already lowered them, overlap from 128 to 108, without changing which way the field points (2.2; 3.7).

viva_questions.q: Why count 'not in text' as silent rather than as against?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because a paper written for another purpose may simply not cover that concept, and that must not be read as a finding against it (2.2).

quiz.q: After the second reading, how many of the 241 cards were silent on overlap?
quiz.explanation: 128 at the first reading; 26 is silence on the boundary, 133 on time (2.2).

quiz.q: How were the 241 papers carded?
options: 170 from full text, 63 from abstracts, 8 from bibliographic records
quiz.explanation: Table 3.3.

entries.term: Stance: supports, contradicts, mixed, silent
entries.plain: A stance is the verdict a reading gives one source on one concept: it supports it, contradicts it, carries both (mixed), or says nothing on it (silent).
in_this_thesis: Used for the review's cards, 'a stance being whether a paper supports a link, contradicts it, is mixed or is silent' (2.2).
Used for transcripts: each of the twenty-six given a stance on each of the five concepts (3.1).
Table 3.5 states, for each concept, when a transcript SUPPORTS and when it CONTRADICTS, with an example quotation (3.4).
The second coding recorded, for every clause and every transcript, a stance, the exact words, their place in the transcript, and the evidence against as well as for (3.4).
Counts are written supports/contradicts/mixed/silent of twenty-six, for example overlap 15/1/5/5 (1.5; Table 7.1).
Qualifiers such as 'weak' or 'qualified' do not count as disagreement between readings (Table 3.6).
entries.why: The thesis defines the four values but does not say why four.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative scheme.
entries.analogy: A referee with four flags for each claim: for, against, both, or nothing seen.

viva_questions.q: What does 'mixed' mean in your counts?
viva_questions.model_answer: That one transcript carries evidence both ways on that concept. For overlap, five transcripts are mixed in the third coding; they are reported separately rather than folded into support (1.5; Table 3.5).

viva_questions.q: Give the counts for the binder.
viva_questions.model_answer: Twenty-four for, none against, one mixed, one silent in the third coding; twenty-five, none, one and none in the second reading (1.5; Table 7.1).

quiz.q: In '15/1/5/5' for overlap, what is the '1'?
quiz.explanation: Supports / contradicts / mixed / silent, of twenty-six (1.5).

quiz.q: Under Table 3.5, when does a transcript CONTRADICT the binder concept?
options: When a trustee holds the data
When peer trust alone sustains a working arrangement
When the participant says nothing about it
quiz.explanation: Table 3.5, concept 3; the last option is 'silent'.

entries.gap: Why four values is not argued.

entries.term: The decision rule on power in the update
entries.plain: A decision rule is a stated rule for turning what a source says into a count. If the rule assumes the claim being tested, that count cannot test the claim.
in_this_thesis: Two rules turned card stances into counts, each for a stated reason (2.2).
First: a card marked 'not in text' counts as silent.

Second, on power: the cards name who a paper treats as deciding and do not state a stance, so a paper naming shippers, receivers, cities or a neutral orchestrator was counted as support, and one naming carriers as against (2.2).
A neutral orchestrator is 'a party that sells neither delivery nor the parties' kind of goods to their customers' (2.2).
Thirty-eight of the 241 verdicts on power rest on that rule (2.2).

'That rule assumes the thesis's own claim, so this count cannot test it. It shows only whom the field assumes decides.' Power is tested in 4.5, on the interviews and on who began the 117 arrangements (2.2).
entries.why: Because the cards 'name who a paper treats as deciding and do not state a stance' (2.2).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative rule.
entries.analogy: Judging a cookery contest by counting how often the judges mention your recipe: it tells you what they talk about, not whether you won.

viva_questions.q: How many power verdicts rest on the rule, and what follows?
viva_questions.model_answer: Thirty-eight of the 241. So that count shows only whom the field assumes decides. Whether power sits with shippers, receivers and cities is tested in 4.5, on the interviews, 18 for, none against, 5 mixed, 3 silent, and on who began the 117 arrangements (2.2; 4.5).

viva_questions.q: Why did you need a rule at all?
viva_questions.model_answer: The cards name who a paper treats as deciding but don't state a stance on power, so a rule had to turn that into support or against: shippers, receivers, cities or a neutral orchestrator as support, carriers as against. I state that the rule assumes my claim (2.2).

quiz.q: How many of the 241 verdicts on power rest on the decision rule?
quiz.explanation: 113 papers name an initiator, 128 name none, 13 have a shipper or receiver beginning (2.2).

quiz.q: Where is the power link actually tested?
options: In 4.5, on the interviews and who began the 117 arrangements
quiz.explanation: 2.2 says its own count cannot test it.

story_refs: EQ ch2: Your count of power in the update assumes your own claim, doesn't it?

entries.term: Comparing the forty-nine and the 241: different kinds of count
entries.plain: Two sets of papers that passed different tests cannot be compared as if they were equal; every comparison has to say which test each set passed.
in_this_thesis: 'The forty-nine of 2023 are papers included after full-text reading, while the 241 of 2026 are papers retained after title-and-abstract screening and the citation rule, of which a hundred and seventy were read in full; wherever the two figures stand together in this thesis the text says which kind each is' (3.2).
'The comparisons that follow set a stricter set beside a looser one' (2.2).

By type: over half the 241 (124) are models or simulations, against a third of the forty-nine; reviews fall from a quarter to an eighth; empirical studies (56 in the 241) hold at about a fifth in both (2.2).
No initiator named: 128 of the 241 (53 per cent), against 23 of the forty-nine (47 per cent) counted the same way (2.2).

'At least thirty-two' of the forty-nine (65 per cent) is a separate count, of papers that observe no real arrangement: it takes in ten that name a type of actor in general and leaves out Allen and colleagues (2018), who name no one but track real vans (Table 2.1 note; 2.2).
entries.why: Because the two sets passed different tests (3.2).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Comparing pass rates when one school counts pupils who sat the exam and another counts every pupil who registered.

viva_questions.q: 'At least thirty-two' and 'twenty-three' both describe the forty-nine and the initiator. Which is right?
viva_questions.model_answer: Both; they are different counts. Twenty-three cards name no one as beginning the collaboration, 47 per cent, counted the same way as the 128 of 241. 'At least thirty-two', 65 per cent, counts papers that observe no real arrangement: it includes ten that name a type of actor in general and leaves out Allen and colleagues, who name no one but track real vans (Table 2.1 note; 2.2).

viva_questions.q: How do the 241 differ in kind from the forty-nine?
viva_questions.model_answer: Over half the 241 are models or simulations, against a third of the forty-nine; reviews fall from a quarter to an eighth; empirical studies hold at about a fifth. But the 241 passed a looser test, so it's a stricter set beside a looser one, and I say so each time (2.2; 3.2).

quiz.q: What test had the 241 update papers passed?
options: Title-and-abstract screening and the citation rule
quiz.explanation: 170 of them were read in full (3.2).

quiz.q: How many of the 241 name no initiator?
quiz.explanation: 23 is the forty-nine counted the same way; 113 name one; 'at least 32' is a separate count of the forty-nine (2.2).

entries.term: Emergent (not imposed) conceptual framework
entries.plain: A framework drawn from the data during the research, rather than fixed beforehand and imposed on it.
in_this_thesis: The fieldwork was designed under four pillars from the field as it stood in 2021: trust, efficiency, innovation, sustainability; the 2024 guide was built on them (2.7).

The data replaced them (Figure 2.5): trust survived chiefly as something supplied from outside the parties (95 of 117 accounts bound from outside, six by their own trust); efficiency moved firms but could not on its own make rivals collaborate; innovation was a facilitator; sustainability was demoted to a by-product (2.7).

Five concepts emerged. 'The first four concepts came out of the data before any theory named them.' The fifth, the holder, was drawn from the interviews read again beside the author's notes of 2022 and 2023, the locker networks, the rules and Chen's (1996) two kinds of overlap, and 'is a link the thesis proposes, not one it found' (2.7).

'The framework is emergent in the sense the methodology literature allows (Trafford and Leshem, 2008, pp. 84-87; Miles and Huberman, 1994): it was not imposed on the fieldwork, it was drawn from it, and Chapter 3 says how' (2.7).
The sequence that shows it emerged is the three codings (1.6; 3.4).
entries.why: 'A framework that came out of the data is a stronger claim to conceptualisation than one fixed before the data arrived, as long as the thesis shows how it came about' (1.6); 'a framework that emerged in that order can be shown to have emerged, and one that had been imposed could not' (1.6). Critical realism is why 'Chapter 2 presents the framework as coming out of the evidence rather than being laid over it' (3.1).
entries.not_this: An imposed framework, which is what the four pillars were for the 2024 guide (2.7).
entries.analogy: Paths across a park worn by people walking, rather than paved in advance: the map is drawn from where feet actually went.

viva_questions.q: Your framework is in Chapter 2, but you say it emerged from the data. Isn't that back to front?
viva_questions.model_answer: It is set out in Chapter 2 because the methodology literature allows a framework drawn from the fieldwork to be presented before the findings, and Chapter 3 says how it came about: the first coding broke the four pillars, the second tested the working claim, and the third coded every transcript against the five concepts. A framework that emerged in that order can be shown to have emerged (2.7; 1.6; 3.4).

viva_questions.q: Which link did not emerge in the same way?
viva_questions.model_answer: The holder. The first four came out of the data before any theory named them; the fifth was drawn from the interviews read again beside my 2022 and 2023 notes, the locker networks, the rules and Chen's two kinds of overlap. It's a link I propose, not one I found (2.7).

quiz.q: Which framework guided the 2024 fieldwork?
quiz.explanation: The four pillars of the registration (2.7).

quiz.q: What became of trust in the emergent framework?
options: It survived chiefly as something supplied from outside the parties
It became the unit of analysis
It was dropped from the analysis
quiz.explanation: 95 of 117 bound from outside the parties; 6 by their own trust (2.7).

entries.term: Testing a framework: Berger and Patchner's three questions and the critical test
entries.plain: Checks a conceptual framework should pass: is its theory described and tied to the problem, does a theory sit under the question, and do its parts hang together and direct the research.
in_this_thesis: Berger and Patchner (1988, cited in Trafford and Leshem, 2008, p. 85) ask three questions, each answered in 2.7: is the theoretical base clearly described and related to the problem (2.6; 2.4); is there a theory underlying the research question (both halves answered: overlap and binding as conditions; a rule on who holds the shared point beside an access rule by vehicle and hour); is the connection between theory, earlier findings and purpose explicit (Table 2.2; each link serves the objective with its number).

Trafford and Leshem's 'critical' test (2008, p. 87): unity (Table 2.2, 'no theory is asked to do another's job'); direction (Chapter 3: the unit of analysis, the two codebooks, the two units of counting and the two further units follow from the links); meaning (Chapter 6, each finding read back through its link); coherence (Chapter 7's conceptual conclusions) (2.7).
Each concept is a variable with a definition, values and a disconfirming observation: overlap takes yes, no, partly, unclear; binding takes one of ten values; the holder one of six classes (2.7).
entries.why: Offered as the tests a framework should meet in the methodology literature the thesis follows (2.7). No further reason is given.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A bridge load test before opening: anchored at both ends, carries the weight it was built for, and its parts act as one structure.

viva_questions.q: How do you know your framework is a framework and not a list?
viva_questions.model_answer: Trafford and Leshem's critical test. Unity is Table 2.2, each theory with one job; direction is Chapter 3, where the unit of analysis, the codebooks and the units of counting follow from the links; meaning is Chapter 6, where each finding is read back through its link; and coherence is the test Chapter 7 puts to its conceptual conclusions (2.7).

viva_questions.q: What would count against your overlap concept?
viva_questions.model_answer: Either of two things: if firms' willingness could be explained by their size or brand whatever their overlap, or if rivals serving the same customers collaborated with nothing holding them together (2.7; Table 3.5).

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the critical test as 2.7 applies it?
quiz.explanation: The four: unity, direction, meaning, coherence (Trafford and Leshem, 2008, p. 87).

quiz.q: How many values can 'binding' take in 2.7?
quiz.explanation: Neutral third party, grant, regulation/permit/mandate, contract, client's instruction, prior vertical relationship, reciprocal trade, platform's reputation, personal tie, trust alone. Six is the holder classes; four the overlap values.

entries.term: Borrowed concepts: ecology as theory, the red cell as a labelled design guide
entries.plain: Concepts from another field can be used as a source of ideas, provided their fit is argued and no empirical claim rests on the borrowed image itself.
in_this_thesis: Ecology is 'read as a source of concepts rather than of evidence, in the manner Benyus (1997) proposed', with weight carried by Gause (1934), Hardin (1960), Schoener (1974), Carothers and Jaksić (1984) and Kronfeld-Schor and Dayan (2003) (2.6).

'The biology is used as Cornelissen (2005) says a metaphor should be used in organisational theory: as a source of concepts whose fit is argued and tested, with every empirical claim carried by the ecology papers and the interviews, never by the image' (2.6).

The red cell is 'used here as a labelled design guide, not as theory' (2.6); 'The ecology of Chapter 2 is a theoretical perspective, openly declared and held to the same standard as the others. The red cell of 6.3 is an analogy used as a design guide, and the thesis says so' (1.6).

Limits are carried: Gause's tube held creatures that could not choose; Hardin wrote 'we still do not comprehend the exact limits of the principle'; birds' red cells keep their nucleus (Stier et al., 2013), 'so neutrality is a reading of the biology, not its law'; the spleen holds no hearing; inclusions are a poor measure of spleen function (de Porto et al., 2010) (2.6).
entries.why: Cornelissen's account of metaphor (2.6), and 'it uses an image where an image makes an argument better than a definition would' (1.6).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: An architect borrowing the honeycomb: it suggests a strong shape, but the engineer still has to calculate the loads.

viva_questions.q: What is the difference between your ecology and your red cell?
viva_questions.model_answer: They are different kinds of thing. The ecology of Chapter 2 is a theoretical perspective, openly declared and held to the same standard as the others. The red cell is an analogy used as a labelled design guide, and I say so; no empirical claim rests on it (1.6; 2.6).

viva_questions.q: How do you stop a metaphor doing work it shouldn't?
viva_questions.model_answer: I use it as Cornelissen says a metaphor should be used: a source of concepts whose fit is argued and tested, with every empirical claim carried by the ecology papers and the interviews, never by the image. And I carry each source's limits, the red cell's included: birds' red cells keep their nucleus, so neutrality is a reading of the biology, not its law (2.6).

quiz.explanation: Benyus supplies the design vocabulary; Colinvaux the big fierce animal; Zahavi the handicap (2.6).

A labelled design guide, not theory

entries.term: Trafford and Leshem's frame (Stepping Stones)
entries.plain: A guide to doing a doctorate with the viva in mind. It fixes the order in which a design is explained (paradigm, approach, methodology, methods) and supplies checklists for the design, the framework and the claim.
in_this_thesis: Chapter 3 sets its choices out 'in the order Trafford and Leshem (2008, ch. 6) recommend': the paradigm (critical realist), then the approach (retroductive), then the methodology (a design in four stages, qualitative at its core), then the methods (3.1).
Table 3.1 answers the six questions they put to a research design (2008, p. 91): what the research wants to discover, why, when and over what period, how, where and who (3.1).
The conceptual framework is tested with Berger and Patchner's three questions as they cite them (p. 85) and with the test they call critical (p. 87): unity, direction, meaning and coherence (2.7).
Figure 3.3 audits the whole design in the form Rose (1982) proposed, as they carry it (pp. 103-104) (3.7).
Every change of plan is explained, because they hold that a change of plan must be explained in the thesis (pp. 99, 104) (3.8).
The contribution is claimed as 'modest in the way Trafford and Leshem (2008, p. 141) ask': each form traceable to a chapter, a count and an appendix row (7.2).
entries.why: The thesis does not say why it adopts Trafford and Leshem as its frame. It uses their order and their tests at each point listed; the reference list gives the book's full title, 'Stepping stones to achieving your doctorate: by focusing on your viva from the start'.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative frame.
entries.analogy: A building inspector's checklist: it does not design the house, but it fixes the order in which the plans are shown and the questions each must answer.

viva_questions.q: Why is your methodology chapter ordered paradigm, approach, methodology, methods?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because that's the order Trafford and Leshem recommend, and it makes each choice follow from the one before: a critical realist paradigm, so a retroductive approach, so a staged design qualitative at its core, then the methods. Table 3.1 answers their six questions of a design, and the rest of Chapter 3 is the long form of each answer (3.1).

viva_questions.q: You call your contribution modest. What do you mean?
viva_questions.model_answer: Trafford and Leshem ask that a claim be modest in the sense of traceable. Each of my four forms of contribution is traceable to a chapter, a count and an appendix row, and each count to the files it was made from (7.2).

quiz.q: In what order does Chapter 3 set out its choices?
quiz.explanation: The order Trafford and Leshem (2008, ch. 6) recommend: critical realist paradigm, retroductive approach, a four-stage design, then the methods (3.1).

quiz.q: What does Table 3.1 answer?
options: The four questions Lincoln and Guba put to qualitative work
The six questions Trafford and Leshem put to a research design
The eight questions put to the Ghent documents
The three questions Berger and Patchner put to a framework
quiz.explanation: Six questions (2008, p. 91): what, why, when, how, where, who. Lincoln and Guba's four are answered in 3.7, Berger and Patchner's three in 2.7, and the eight questions to the documents in 3.5.

entries.gap: Why this frame and not another is not stated.

entries.term: Research paradigm (ontology, epistemology, mode of inference)
entries.plain: A paradigm is a set of starting assumptions: what exists (ontology), how it can be known (epistemology), and so how to reason from evidence (mode of inference). It decides what will count as a finding.
in_this_thesis: Table 3.2 compares three paradigms 'in the terms Guba and Lincoln (1994) use to compare paradigms, adapted' (3.1).

Guba and Lincoln's four positions are reduced to two, positivism and constructivism, 'the latter labelled interpretivist here as it commonly is'; the third column is drawn from the critical realist literature (Fleetwood, 2005; Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992; Easton, 2010) (3.1).
The rows compared are ontology, epistemology, mode of inference, what counts as a finding, how findings generalise, the researcher's position, and where this thesis sits (Table 3.2).
Adopted: critical realist. Rejected: positivist and interpretivist, each with its reason in the last row (Table 3.2).
The seven rows are taught one by one: each lesson reads its row across the three columns, in the table's own words (Table 3.2).

Sources: the positivist and interpretivist columns follow Guba and Lincoln (1994, pp. 105–117), whose constructivism is labelled interpretivist here; the third column follows the sources named in each cell. (Table 3.2)
entries.why: 'Critical realism was chosen for three reasons, and each rival position fails one of them' (3.1); the three reasons are set out under critical realism. The thesis says that Guba and Lincoln's four positions 'are reduced to two, positivism and constructivism' (3.1), but not why.
entries.not_this: Positivism and interpretivism, both rejected in Table 3.2. Guba and Lincoln's other two positions are not discussed.
entries.analogy: Choosing which instrument you will trust before you go out to measure: a tape measure, a conversation and an accident investigator's reconstruction each make different things count as evidence.

viva_questions.q: State your ontology and your epistemology, one sentence each.
viva_questions.model_answer: Ontologically, there is one reality, stratified, in which mechanisms exist whether or not they fire, so the markets, the customers and the binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them. Epistemologically, that reality is independent of us, but our knowledge of it is fallible and theory-laden, so accounts, documents and numbers have to be read for what they can and cannot show (Table 3.2; 3.1).

viva_questions.q: Guba and Lincoln compare four paradigms. Why do you compare only three?
viva_questions.model_answer: I adapted their table to the choice I actually made. I kept the two positions my choice was made against, positivism and constructivism, which I label interpretivist as it commonly is, and drew the third column from the critical realist literature. My reasons are stated against those two; I don't argue the other positions out one by one (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: In Table 3.2, which paradigm's mode of inference is 'induction: accounts built up from what participants say'?
quiz.explanation: Positivist is deduction, interpretivist is induction, critical realist is retroduction (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: How does Table 3.2 adapt Guba and Lincoln (1994)?
options: It replaces constructivism with critical theory
It adds pragmatism as a fourth column
It reduces their four positions to two and adds a critical realist column
It keeps all four positions and ranks them
quiz.explanation: Positivism and constructivism (labelled interpretivist) are kept; the third column comes from the critical realist literature (3.1).

entries.gap: Why Guba and Lincoln's four positions are reduced to two is not stated.

entries.term: Positivism and interpretivism, in plain words
entries.plain: Positivism holds that there is one reality, which a researcher standing outside can measure: you turn an idea into a hypothesis, test it on numbers and generalise from a sample to a population. Interpretivism holds that realities are made in people's meanings: the researcher builds an account up from what participants say, together with them, and leaves the reader to judge where it applies.
in_this_thesis: Positivism in Table 3.2's words: 'One reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement'; 'The observer stands outside the observed; knowledge is objective'; 'Deduction: hypotheses tested against measurement'; findings generalise 'Statistically, from sample to population' (Table 3.2).

Interpretivism in Table 3.2's words: 'Multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings'; 'Knowledge is made between researcher and participant; findings are created'; 'Induction: accounts built up from what participants say'; and on generalising, 'They do not; transferability is the reader's judgement on the description' (Table 3.2).
Interpretivist is Guba and Lincoln's constructivism under its common name: 'the latter labelled interpretivist here as it commonly is' (3.1).
What a positivist design would have needed here, and lacked: 'a full list of operators to draw a sample from and a tested way to measure willingness to collaborate, and the field has neither' (3.1).
What an interpretivist design would not do: claim that 'the markets, the customers and the binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them' (3.1).

With hindsight, a positivist design 'would have measured what this thesis counted, the overlap of two operators' markets against their willingness across a sample, and it would have said less about why'; an interpretivist one 'would have read the twenty-six for the meaning of collaboration to each and said nothing about the mechanism' (7.4).
entries.why: Because the thesis is defined against them: Table 3.2 'sets the position beside the two it was chosen against' (3.1). In the viva: say what each one is in a sentence before you say why you chose neither.
entries.not_this: Critical realism, the third column of Table 3.2, which the thesis adopted.
entries.analogy: Finding out why a town's buses run late. The positivist counts: timetables against arrival times over hundreds of journeys, then a statistic. The interpretivist listens: drivers' and passengers' own stories of what lateness means to them. Each tells you something; neither, on its own, names the cause.

viva_questions.q: In one sentence each, what are positivism and interpretivism?
viva_questions.model_answer: Positivism holds there is one reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement, studied by testing hypotheses against measurement and generalising statistically from sample to population. Interpretivism holds there are multiple realities, held in people's meanings, studied by building accounts up from what participants say, with transferability left to the reader's judgement (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: Which paradigm tests hypotheses against measurement and generalises from a sample to a population?
quiz.explanation: Positivist: 'Deduction: hypotheses tested against measurement'; findings generalise 'Statistically, from sample to population' (Table 3.2). Constructivism is the interpretivist column under Guba and Lincoln's name (3.1).

quiz.q: Which paradigm builds accounts up from what participants say and leaves transferability to the reader?
quiz.explanation: Interpretivist: 'Induction: accounts built up from what participants say'; 'They do not; transferability is the reader's judgement on the description' (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: In Table 3.2, where does the interpretivist researcher stand?
options: Part of the research tool, examining their own influence openly
Outside the field, reading only documents and numbers
With a point of view, but not creating what is real
Outside the research, letting the design remove bias
quiz.explanation: Interpretivist: 'Part of the research tool; the researcher's own influence is examined openly (reflexivity)'. Positivist: 'Stands outside the research; the design removes bias' (Table 3.2).

entries.term: Table 3.2, row by row: the whole table in one walk
entries.plain: Table 3.2 sets three ways of doing research side by side, one per column: positivist, interpretivist and critical realist, the last being this thesis's. Each of its seven rows asks one question, and you read a row from left to right to see how each way answers it.
in_this_thesis: The table is 'Table 3.2 Three paradigms compared, and where this thesis sits'; its columns are 'Positivist', 'Interpretivist' and 'Critical realist (this thesis)' (Table 3.2).

Row 1, ontology: what exists? Positivist: 'One reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement'. Interpretivist: 'Multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings'. Critical realist: 'One reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real; mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Fleetwood, 2005)' (Table 3.2).

Row 2, epistemology: how can we know it? Positivist: 'The observer stands outside the observed; knowledge is objective'. Interpretivist: 'Knowledge is made between researcher and participant; findings are created'. Critical realist: 'Reality is independent of us; our knowledge of it is fallible and theory-laden (Fleetwood, 2005; Sayer, 2000)' (Table 3.2).

Row 3, mode of inference: how do we reason? Positivist: 'Deduction: hypotheses tested against measurement'. Interpretivist: 'Induction: accounts built up from what participants say'. Critical realist: 'Retroduction: what must be so for the observed regularity to be possible (Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992)' (Table 3.2).

Row 4, what counts as a finding. Positivist: 'A relationship between variables, stated so it could be falsified'. Interpretivist: 'A credible interpretation, thick enough for a reader to recognise the setting'. Critical realist: 'A mechanism, named and shown to have operated in the case (Easton, 2010; Wynn and Williams, 2012)' (Table 3.2).

Row 5, how findings generalise. Positivist: 'Statistically, from sample to population'. Interpretivist: 'They do not; transferability is the reader's judgement on the description'. Critical realist: 'To the mechanism, not the population; it may fire elsewhere under other conditions (Easton, 2010)' (Table 3.2).

Row 6, the researcher's position. Positivist: 'Stands outside the research; the design removes bias'. Interpretivist: 'Part of the research tool; the researcher's own influence is examined openly (reflexivity)'. Critical realist: 'Has a point of view but does not create what is real; examines their own influence while still holding that mechanisms exist (Fleetwood, 2005; Finlay, 2002)' (Table 3.2).

Row 7, where this thesis sits. Positivist: 'rejected: no register to draw a sample from and no established measure of willingness to test'. Interpretivist: 'rejected: overlap and binding are held to be real, not only reported'. Critical realist: 'adopted: a regularity in 26 accounts read back to the mechanism, and tested against the cases that should break it' (Table 3.2).

Under the table: 'Sources: the positivist and interpretivist columns follow Guba and Lincoln (1994, pp. 105–117), whose constructivism is labelled interpretivist here; the third column follows the sources named in each cell.' (Table 3.2)
entries.why: Because the table shows the choice beside the two it was made against: it 'sets the position beside the two it was chosen against, in the terms Guba and Lincoln (1994) use to compare paradigms, adapted' (3.1). In the viva: if you can read any row across, you can answer a paradigm question by pointing to its cell.
entries.not_this: Guba and Lincoln's own comparison of four positions: the thesis keeps two of them and adds a critical realist column (3.1).
entries.analogy: A comparison chart in a phone shop: three phones side by side, with rows for battery, camera and price. You read across a row to compare one feature, and the last row is the verdict: the one you bought.

viva_questions.q: Walk me through Table 3.2, one row at a time.
viva_questions.model_answer: Ontology: one reality for the positivist, multiple realities for the interpretivist, and for me one reality, stratified, in which mechanisms exist whether or not they fire. Epistemology: objective knowledge, knowledge made with the participant, and for me fallible, theory-laden knowledge of a reality independent of us. Inference: deduction, induction and, for me, retroduction. A finding: a relationship between variables, a credible interpretation, or for me a mechanism shown to have operated. Generalising: to a population, to the reader's judgement, or for me to the mechanism. Position: outside the research, part of the research tool, or for me a point of view that does not create what is real. And the verdict: positivism and interpretivism rejected, critical realism adopted (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: How many rows does Table 3.2 have, counting 'Where this thesis sits'?
quiz.explanation: Ontology, epistemology, mode of inference, what counts as a finding, how findings generalise, the researcher's position, and where this thesis sits (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: Reading Table 3.2 across a row, in which order do the columns come?
quiz.explanation: The third column is 'Critical realist (this thesis)' (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: In which row of Table 3.2 is the positivist cell 'Statistically, from sample to population'?
quiz.explanation: Positivist: 'Statistically, from sample to population'. Interpretivist: 'They do not; transferability is the reader's judgement on the description'. Critical realist: 'To the mechanism, not the population; it may fire elsewhere under other conditions (Easton, 2010)' (Table 3.2).

entries.term: Table 3.2, row 1: ontology (what exists)
entries.plain: Ontology is the question of what exists before anyone studies it. Read the row across: the positivist says there is one reality you can measure; the interpretivist says there are many, made in people's heads; the critical realist says there is one, in layers, with causes that exist even when nothing happens.
in_this_thesis: Positivist: 'One reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement' (Table 3.2).
Interpretivist: 'Multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings' (Table 3.2).
Critical realist, this thesis: 'One reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real; mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Fleetwood, 2005)' (Table 3.2).

Sources: the positivist and interpretivist columns follow Guba and Lincoln (1994, pp. 105–117), whose constructivism is labelled interpretivist here; the third column follows the sources named in each cell. (Table 3.2)

The same claim in the thesis's own setting: 'There is a real world of last-mile markets whose structures (who competes with whom for which customers, who can bind whom) exist whether or not any participant describes them accurately' (3.1).
entries.why: 'Second, the pattern is taken to be real, not just something participants said: the markets, the customers and the binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them, and an interpretivist design would not make that claim' (3.1). In the viva: this row is why interpretivism is rejected, so be ready to say what you hold to be real.
entries.not_this: The positivist and interpretivist answers in the same row of Table 3.2, both rejected.
entries.analogy: Before a football match: is there one true score you can count (positivist), a different match for every fan (interpretivist), or one match whose result comes from things the scoreboard never shows, such as fitness and tactics (critical realist)?

viva_questions.q: Read me the ontology row of Table 3.2.
viva_questions.model_answer: Positivist: one reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement. Interpretivist: multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings. Mine, critical realist: one reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real, in which mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Table 3.2; Fleetwood, 2005).

viva_questions.q: Your participants each describe the market differently. Doesn't that mean there are many realities?
viva_questions.model_answer: No. Their descriptions differ, but I hold that there is one reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real. The markets, the customers and the binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them. The accounts are fallible evidence of that reality, read for what they can and cannot show (Table 3.2; 3.1).

quiz.q: In the 'Ontology' row of Table 3.2, which column reads: 'Multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings'?
quiz.explanation: Positivist: 'One reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement'. Interpretivist: 'Multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings'. Critical realist: 'One reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real; mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Fleetwood, 2005)' (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: In the 'Ontology' row of Table 3.2, what does the critical realist cell say about mechanisms?
options: They are made between researcher and participant
They exist only when someone reports them
They exist whether or not they fire
They can be measured directly by surveys
quiz.explanation: 'One reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real; mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Fleetwood, 2005)' (Table 3.2). To fire is to work: 3.1 says the mechanism 'may work elsewhere'.

quiz.q: How many realities does the critical realist cell of the 'Ontology' row say there are?
options: Two: the observer's and the observed's
quiz.explanation: Critical realist: 'One reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real'. 'Multiple realities' is the interpretivist cell (Table 3.2).

entries.term: Table 3.2, row 2: epistemology (how it can be known)
entries.plain: Epistemology is the question of how we can know what exists. Read the row across: the positivist stands outside and measures; the interpretivist makes knowledge together with the participant; the critical realist says the world is there whatever we think, but what we know of it can be wrong and is shaped by the ideas we bring.
in_this_thesis: Positivist: 'The observer stands outside the observed; knowledge is objective' (Table 3.2).
Interpretivist: 'Knowledge is made between researcher and participant; findings are created' (Table 3.2).
Critical realist, this thesis: 'Reality is independent of us; our knowledge of it is fallible and theory-laden (Fleetwood, 2005; Sayer, 2000)' (Table 3.2).

'Theory-laden' means shaped by the ideas the researcher brings. The thesis gives its own case: the framework of 2024 was built on the field's four pillars, and 'the guide asked about trust because the field did' (3.7).
entries.why: 'Knowledge of that world is fallible and comes through accounts, documents and numbers that must be read for what they can and cannot show' (3.1). In the viva: if asked how interviews can show something real, this row is the answer, because accounts are fallible evidence of a real world.
entries.not_this: The positivist and interpretivist answers in the same row of Table 3.2, both rejected.
entries.analogy: A match on television: one viewer trusts the camera completely (positivist), one says the match is what the players and fans make of it (interpretivist), one says the match really happened but every camera angle can miss something (critical realist).

viva_questions.q: And your epistemology, row two of the table?
viva_questions.model_answer: Positivist: the observer stands outside the observed and knowledge is objective. Interpretivist: knowledge is made between researcher and participant, so findings are created. Mine: reality is independent of us, but our knowledge of it is fallible and theory-laden, so accounts, documents and numbers have to be read for what they can and cannot show (Table 3.2; 3.1).

viva_questions.q: If your knowledge is theory-laden, how do you stop your own theory deciding the answer?
viva_questions.model_answer: By asking for evidence against as well as for. The interviews were searched as carefully for evidence against the mechanism as for evidence for it. And the four pillars I started with did not survive the data: they became findings. Knowledge is fallible and theory-laden, so the design lets the evidence correct the theory (3.1; 3.7).

quiz.q: In the 'Epistemology' row of Table 3.2, which column reads: 'The observer stands outside the observed; knowledge is objective'?
quiz.explanation: Positivist: 'The observer stands outside the observed; knowledge is objective'. Interpretivist: 'Knowledge is made between researcher and participant; findings are created'. Critical realist: 'Reality is independent of us; our knowledge of it is fallible and theory-laden (Fleetwood, 2005; Sayer, 2000)' (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: What does the critical realist cell of the 'Epistemology' row mean by calling our knowledge 'fallible and theory-laden'?
options: It can be wrong, and is shaped by the ideas we bring
It is certain once enough people agree on it
It is created by the researcher and participant
It is objective because the observer stands outside
quiz.explanation: 'Reality is independent of us; our knowledge of it is fallible and theory-laden (Fleetwood, 2005; Sayer, 2000)' (Table 3.2). 'Findings are created' is the interpretivist cell; 'knowledge is objective' the positivist.

quiz.q: According to 3.1, through what does knowledge of the world of last-mile markets come?
quiz.explanation: 'Knowledge of that world is fallible and comes through accounts, documents and numbers that must be read for what they can and cannot show' (3.1).

entries.term: Table 3.2, row 3: mode of inference (how to reason)
entries.plain: The mode of inference is how you reason from evidence to a claim. Read the row across: deduction tests a guess against numbers; induction builds a picture up from what people say; retroduction asks what must be true underneath for the pattern you keep seeing to be possible.
in_this_thesis: Positivist: 'Deduction: hypotheses tested against measurement' (Table 3.2).
Interpretivist: 'Induction: accounts built up from what participants say' (Table 3.2).
Critical realist, this thesis: 'Retroduction: what must be so for the observed regularity to be possible (Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992)' (Table 3.2).
3.1 explains induction in brackets: 'retroduction, not induction (building a general rule from repeated observations)' (3.1).

And says what retroduction asks: 'Faced with a pattern that keeps recurring, it does not ask what caused it in one case but what must be true for it to keep happening; the answer is a mechanism, which is then checked against the cases where it should have worked and did not' (3.1).
entries.why: 'Third, the explanation sought is a mechanism that can be tested against the cases that should break it, which is retroduction, not induction (building a general rule from repeated observations)' (3.1). In the viva: name all three, deduction, induction and retroduction, and say which column each belongs to.
entries.not_this: The positivist and interpretivist answers in the same row of Table 3.2, both rejected.
entries.analogy: Cooking: deduction is checking a recipe by baking it; induction is collecting what every cook says about the dish; retroduction is tasting the same flavour in many dishes and working out which ingredient must be there for it.

viva_questions.q: Which mode of inference do you use, and what are the other two?
viva_questions.model_answer: Retroduction: what must be so for the observed regularity to be possible. The positivist column is deduction, hypotheses tested against measurement; the interpretivist is induction, accounts built up from what participants say. I reason from a pattern that recurs across cases to the mechanism that would produce it, and test it against the cases that should break it (Table 3.2; 3.1).

viva_questions.q: Isn't retroduction just a guess?
viva_questions.model_answer: It is an inference from the pattern to the mechanism that would produce it, and it does not stop there. The mechanism is then checked against the cases where it should have worked and did not, and the interviews were searched as carefully for evidence against it as for it. Because it is retroduced and not observed, I offer it as a proposition (3.1; 3.7).

quiz.q: In the 'Mode of inference' row of Table 3.2, which column reads: 'Retroduction: what must be so for the observed regularity to be possible (Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992)'?
quiz.explanation: Positivist: 'Deduction: hypotheses tested against measurement'. Interpretivist: 'Induction: accounts built up from what participants say'. Critical realist: 'Retroduction: what must be so for the observed regularity to be possible (Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992)' (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: Which mode of inference does Table 3.2 give the positivist column?
quiz.explanation: Positivist: 'Deduction: hypotheses tested against measurement'. Interpretivist: induction. Critical realist: retroduction (Table 3.2). Triangulation is reading sources against one another, not a mode of inference (3.1).

quiz.q: In 3.1, what question does retroduction put to a pattern that keeps recurring?
options: What it means to each of the participants
What caused it in this one case
What must be true for it to keep happening
quiz.explanation: 'Faced with a pattern that keeps recurring, it does not ask what caused it in one case but what must be true for it to keep happening' (3.1).

entries.term: Table 3.2, row 4: what counts as a finding
entries.plain: This row says what a result has to look like to count. Read it across: for the positivist, a link between two measured things that could be proved wrong; for the interpretivist, a believable, detailed account; for the critical realist, a named cause shown to have worked in the case.
in_this_thesis: Positivist: 'A relationship between variables, stated so it could be falsified' (Table 3.2).
Interpretivist: 'A credible interpretation, thick enough for a reader to recognise the setting' (Table 3.2).
Critical realist, this thesis: 'A mechanism, named and shown to have operated in the case (Easton, 2010; Wynn and Williams, 2012)' (Table 3.2).
The thesis names its mechanism: what was observed is treated 'as the visible result of deeper causes, overlap and binding, which play out differently in different settings' (3.1).
And shows it operated, in Wynn and Williams's terms: 'the mechanism is overlap and binding; the corroboration is the second reading of every transcript and the counts of 4.2 to 4.5' (3.1).
entries.why: 'the answer is a mechanism, which is then checked against the cases where it should have worked and did not' (3.1). In the viva: when asked what you found, name the mechanism, overlap and binding, and show where it operated in the cases.

entries.term: Table 3.2, row 5: how findings generalise
entries.plain: This row says how far a result reaches beyond the cases studied. Interpretivist: 'They do not; transferability is the reader's judgement on the description' (Table 3.2).

The phrase in plain words, from 3.1 itself: 'what it generalises to is the mechanism, which may work elsewhere, not a population' (3.1). So 'fire' means 'work': the mechanism actually producing its effect.

'Under other conditions' sits with two other lines: in the ontology row, 'mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Fleetwood, 2005)' (Table 3.2), and in 3.1, overlap and binding 'play out differently in different settings' (3.1).

entries.plain: This row says where the researcher stands. Interpretivist: 'Part of the research tool; the researcher's own influence is examined openly (reflexivity)' (Table 3.2).

'Has a point of view': the author brought his own picture to the interviews, 'the image of the big fierce animal (1.6)', and 'The twenty-six did not sustain it' (4.2).
