entries.term: Why critical realism: three reasons, and a rival failing each
entries.plain: 3.1 gives three reasons for choosing critical realism, and each rival position fails one of them. Positivism fails the first (the field has no list of operators to sample from and no tested measure of willingness), interpretivism fails the second (it would not claim the pattern is real), and the third asks for retroduction, reasoning back from the pattern to its cause, not induction.
in_this_thesis: 'Critical realism was chosen for three reasons, and each rival position fails one of them' (3.1).

Reason 1, which positivism fails: 'First, what needs explaining is a pattern across twenty-six accounts, a refusal to collaborate that comes back wherever the parties' customers overlap. A positivist design would have needed a full list of operators to draw a sample from and a tested way to measure willingness to collaborate, and the field has neither' (3.1).

Reason 2, which interpretivism fails: 'Second, the pattern is taken to be real, not just something participants said: the markets, the customers and the binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them, and an interpretivist design would not make that claim' (3.1).

Reason 3, the reasoning needed: 'Third, the explanation sought is a mechanism that can be tested against the cases that should break it, which is retroduction, not induction (building a general rule from repeated observations)' (3.1). In Table 3.2, induction is the interpretivist column's mode of inference and deduction the positivist's.

The same verdicts in the last row of Table 3.2: positivist 'rejected: no register to draw a sample from and no established measure of willingness to test'; interpretivist 'rejected: overlap and binding are held to be real, not only reported'; critical realist 'adopted: a regularity in 26 accounts read back to the mechanism, and tested against the cases that should break it' (Table 3.2).

The cost, stated straight after: 'The cost of this choice is set out in 3.7: a mechanism named from twenty-six accounts is a proposition, and what it generalises to is the mechanism, which may work elsewhere, not a population' (3.1).
With hindsight, in 7.4: 'the critical realist choice was made because the question was about mechanisms and the evidence was accounts' (7.4).
entries.why: Because the thesis argues its paradigm against the two alternatives instead of assuming it: 'each rival position fails one of them' (3.1). In the viva: give the three reasons in order, name the rival that fails each of the first two, and state the cost before you are asked.

entries.term: Critical realism
entries.plain: The view that there is a real world of structures and causal mechanisms that exist whether or not we see them, and that our knowledge of it is fallible. Research tries to explain what produces the patterns we observe.
in_this_thesis: Named as the paradigm in the abstract ('A critical realist, theory-building design') and first in Chapter 3 (3.1).

Its assumptions are stated (Bhaskar, 2008; Sayer, 2000): a real world of last-mile markets whose structures (who competes with whom for which customers, who can bind whom) exist whether or not any participant describes them accurately; knowledge of it is fallible and comes through accounts, documents and numbers; explanation is retroductive (3.1).
The refusals and the few collaborations that did work are treated 'as the visible result of deeper causes, overlap and binding, which play out differently in different settings' (3.1).

Consequences for the design: 'the interviews were searched as carefully for evidence against the mechanism as for evidence for it'; the mechanism was tested against 'the one city that already shares out delivery hours by law', and the holder against the 117 arrangements, forty-three locker networks and the rules; and 'Chapter 2 presents the framework as coming out of the evidence rather than being laid over it' (3.1).

'The closest example of this approach is Easton (2010), who made the case for critical realism in research on industrial networks, the ties between firms that trade with one another, and this thesis follows him' (3.1).

Each rival fails one of the three reasons; the last row of Table 3.2 says how: positivist 'rejected: no register to draw a sample from and no established measure of willingness to test'; interpretivist 'rejected: overlap and binding are held to be real, not only reported'; critical realist 'adopted: a regularity in 26 accounts read back to the mechanism, and tested against the cases that should break it' (Table 3.2).
entries.why: Three reasons, and 'each rival position fails one of them' (3.1). First, 'what needs explaining is a pattern across twenty-six accounts, a refusal to collaborate that comes back wherever the parties' customers overlap', and 'a positivist design would have needed a full list of operators to draw a sample from and a tested way to measure willingness to collaborate, and the field has neither'. Second, 'the markets, the customers and the binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them, and an interpretivist design would not make that claim'. Third, 'the explanation sought is a mechanism that can be tested against the cases that should break it, which is retroduction, not induction'. In 7.4: chosen 'because the question was about mechanisms and the evidence was accounts'. The stated cost: 'a mechanism named from twenty-six accounts is a proposition, and what it generalises to is the mechanism, which may work elsewhere, not a population' (3.1).
entries.not_this: Positivism ('no register to draw a sample from and no established measure of willingness to test') and interpretivism ('overlap and binding are held to be real, not only reported') (Table 3.2).
entries.analogy: An accident investigator treats witness statements as fallible, but assumes the brakes, the road and the weather were real, and works back to the mechanism that explains why crashes keep happening at the same bend.

viva_questions.q: What does critical realism let you claim that interpretivism would not?
viva_questions.model_answer: That overlap and binding are real: the markets, the customers and the binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them. An interpretivist reading would give me credible interpretations of what collaboration means to each participant, but it would say nothing about the mechanism (3.1; Table 3.2; 7.4).

viva_questions.q: What does the choice cost you?
viva_questions.model_answer: A mechanism named from twenty-six accounts is retroduced, not observed, so it is a proposition, and what it generalises to is the mechanism, which may work elsewhere, not a population. That is why Chapter 7 offers propositions with falsifiers for others to test (3.1, 3.7, 7.2).

viva_questions.q: Who is your methodological precedent?
viva_questions.model_answer: The closest example of this approach is Easton (2010), who made the case for critical realism in research on industrial networks, and I follow him. Wynn and Williams (2012) turn the position into principles for case research, and Chapter 3 is arranged so that each principle can be pointed to (3.1).

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the three reasons 3.1 gives for choosing critical realism?
options: It removes the need for coding
The field has no full list of operators to sample from and no tested measure of willingness
It lets findings generalise to every European city
quiz.explanation: The other two reasons: the pattern is taken to be real, not just something participants said; and the explanation sought is a mechanism tested against the cases that should break it (3.1).

quiz.q: Which work does 3.1 call the closest example of this approach?
quiz.explanation: Easton made the case for critical realism in research on industrial networks; Guba and Lincoln supply the comparison table (3.1).

quiz.q: In the thesis's critical realist reading, what are overlap and binding?
quiz.explanation: What was observed is treated 'as the visible result of deeper causes, overlap and binding, which play out differently in different settings' (3.1).

entries.term: Stratified reality: the empirical, the actual and the real
entries.plain: Critical realists split reality into three layers: the real (structures and mechanisms, whether or not they are active), the actual (events that happen, seen or unseen) and the empirical (what is observed or experienced). A mechanism can exist without firing.
in_this_thesis: Table 3.2, ontology row, critical realist column: 'One reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real; mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Fleetwood, 2005)'.

The thesis does not map the three layers onto its own data in one place. The pieces are in 3.1: the mechanism is overlap and binding; the events are the arrangements of Appendix H and the refusals of Chapter 4; and knowledge 'comes through accounts, documents and numbers that must be read for what they can and cannot show'.
entries.why: It is given as part of the critical realist position (Fleetwood, 2005) and is not otherwise discussed. The thesis does not say how each layer bears on its design.
entries.not_this: Positivist ontology: 'One reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement'. Interpretivist ontology: 'Multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings' (Table 3.2).
entries.analogy: A magnet's pull is real even with no metal nearby (the real); a paperclip jumping to it is an event (the actual); your seeing the paperclip move is the empirical.

viva_questions.q: You say reality is stratified. Where are the real, the actual and the empirical in your thesis?
viva_questions.model_answer: The real is the mechanisms, overlap and binding. The actual is the events: the arrangements of Appendix H and the refusals of Chapter 4. The empirical is what I could get at: accounts, documents and numbers, which is why each is read for what it can and cannot show (3.1; Table 3.2).

viva_questions.q: Why does it matter that a mechanism can exist without firing?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because I set the mechanism against the cases in which it should have fired and did not. Overlap can be present and still not produce a refusal, where a wall, a penalty or an owner with no stake outweighs the exposure. The mechanism is still operating; it is outweighed (3.1; 1.5).

quiz.q: Which source does Table 3.2 cite for reality 'stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real'?
quiz.explanation: Fleetwood (2005), in the critical realist column (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: In a stratified ontology, which layer holds mechanisms that may not be firing?
quiz.explanation: Mechanisms belong to the real; events to the actual; observations to the empirical (Table 3.2).

beats.narration: Critical realism sees one reality in three layers, like the floors of one building.

beats.narration: Top floor, the empirical: what we can observe. Interviews, documents, numbers.
beats.on_screen: A notebook, a folded city plan and a small bar shape on the top floor.

beats.narration: Middle floor, the actual: events that happen, whether or not anyone sees them.
beats.on_screen: Stylised vans meeting at a hub; one meeting hidden behind a wall.

beats.narration: Ground floor, the real: mechanisms that produce events, even when they are not firing.

beats.narration: The thesis reads down from what was said, through events, to mechanisms.

entries.gap: The thesis states the stratified ontology but never maps the three layers onto its own evidence. Have the mapping ready.

entries.term: Mechanism and regularity
entries.plain: A regularity is a pattern that recurs across cases. A mechanism is what produces it. Critical realist research names the mechanism and checks it against cases where it should have produced the pattern.
in_this_thesis: The regularity: 'a refusal to collaborate that comes back wherever the parties' customers overlap', across twenty-six accounts (3.1).
The mechanisms named: overlap and binding (3.1).
What counts as a finding under critical realism: 'A mechanism, named and shown to have operated in the case (Easton, 2010; Wynn and Williams, 2012)' (Table 3.2).

The mechanism was tested against the cases that should break it: 'the one city that already shares out delivery hours by law', and the holder against 'the 117 arrangements, forty-three locker networks and the rules that say when a point is neutral' (3.1).
How it generalises: 'To the mechanism, not the population; it may fire elsewhere under other conditions (Easton, 2010)' (Table 3.2).
entries.why: 'Faced with a pattern that keeps recurring, it does not ask what caused it in one case but what must be true for it to keep happening; the answer is a mechanism, which is then checked against the cases where it should have worked and did not' (3.1; Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992).
entries.not_this: Positivist finding: 'A relationship between variables, stated so it could be falsified'. Interpretivist finding: 'A credible interpretation, thick enough for a reader to recognise the setting' (Table 3.2).
entries.analogy: A rash that keeps appearing on the same patients is the regularity; the allergy is the mechanism; the doctor then checks patients who ate the food and had no rash.

viva_questions.q: What is the regularity, and what is the mechanism?
viva_questions.model_answer: The regularity is a refusal that recurs wherever the parties' customers overlap, across twenty-six accounts. The mechanisms are overlap and binding: rivals refuse to pool what could expose their customers unless a wall, a penalty or an owner with no stake in those customers outweighs that exposure (3.1; 1.5).

viva_questions.q: Your propositions each relate two variables. Isn't that positivist?
viva_questions.model_answer: A positivist finding is a relationship between variables stated so it could be falsified and tested against measurement. Mine are propositions about mechanisms, drawn from the cases, each with its falsifier in Table 7.1, offered for others to test. Testing them as hypotheses in a deductive design is the seventh further study, not something this thesis claims to have done (Table 3.2; 7.2; 7.5).

quiz.q: Under critical realism, what counts as a finding (Table 3.2)?
options: A theme present in most transcripts
A statistically significant relationship between variables
A mechanism, named and shown to have operated in the case
A credible interpretation thick enough to recognise the setting
quiz.explanation: The second option is the positivist finding, the third the interpretivist one (Table 3.2).

quiz.q: Which two mechanisms does 3.1 name?
quiz.explanation: Trust, efficiency, innovation and sustainability are the four pillars the data replaced; size and brand are the clauses of the working claim that fell (3.1, 3.4).

entries.term: Positivism and interpretivism (the two paradigms rejected)
entries.plain: Positivism treats reality as measurable and tests hypotheses against measurement, generalising from a sample to a population. Interpretivism treats reality as constructed in people's meanings and builds understanding from what participants say.
in_this_thesis: Table 3.2 gives each position's ontology, epistemology, mode of inference (deduction; induction), what counts as a finding, how findings generalise (statistically; they do not, transferability is the reader's judgement) and the researcher's position (stands outside the research; part of the research tool).
The interpretivist column follows Guba and Lincoln's constructivism, 'labelled interpretivist here as it commonly is' (3.1).

Where this thesis sits: positivist 'rejected: no register to draw a sample from and no established measure of willingness to test'; interpretivist 'rejected: overlap and binding are held to be real, not only reported' (Table 3.2).

Critique with hindsight (7.4): a positivist design 'would have measured what this thesis counted, the overlap of two operators' markets against their willingness across a sample, and it would have said less about why'; an interpretivist one 'would have read the twenty-six for the meaning of collaboration to each and said nothing about the mechanism'.
entries.why: Each fails one of the three reasons for critical realism (3.1): positivism needs a full list of operators to draw a sample from and a tested way to measure willingness to collaborate, and the field has neither; interpretivism would not claim that the markets, customers and binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them.
entries.not_this: These are the alternatives; critical realism was adopted.
entries.analogy: Positivism is a census with a tape measure; interpretivism is a collection of life stories; the question needed an investigator who uses the stories to reconstruct what actually happened.

viva_questions.q: Could a positivist design have done better?
viva_questions.model_answer: It would have measured what I counted, the overlap of two operators' markets against their willingness across a sample, and said less about why. And it could not have started: there is no register of operators to sample from and no established measure of willingness (Table 3.2; 7.4).

viva_questions.q: Your evidence is participants' accounts. Aren't you really an interpretivist?
viva_questions.model_answer: I treat the accounts as fallible evidence about something real, not as the reality. An interpretivist design would read the twenty-six for the meaning of collaboration to each and say nothing about the mechanism; I hold that overlap and binding exist however well or badly a participant describes them (3.1; 7.4).

quiz.q: Why does Table 3.2 reject positivism?
options: No register to draw a sample from and no established measure of willingness
quiz.explanation: Table 3.2, last row (3.1).

quiz.q: According to 7.4, what would an interpretivist design have said about the mechanism?
options: It would have tested it statistically
It would have generalised it to a population
It would have measured it across a sample
quiz.explanation: It 'would have read the twenty-six for the meaning of collaboration to each and said nothing about the mechanism' (7.4).

entries.term: Retroduction
entries.plain: Reasoning backwards from a recurring pattern to what must be true for that pattern to occur, then checking that explanation against the cases that should break it.
in_this_thesis: 'Explanation is retroductive: from a pattern that recurs across cases to the mechanism that would produce it' (3.1).
Start: the regularity in twenty-six accounts and one city's record (3.1).
Ask: not 'what caused it in one case' but 'what must be true for it to keep happening' (3.1; Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992).
Answer: a mechanism, overlap and binding (3.1).

Test: check the mechanism 'against the cases where it should have worked and did not'; 'the interviews were searched as carefully for evidence against the mechanism as for evidence for it'; the mechanism tested against Ghent, and the holder against the 117 arrangements, forty-three locker networks and the rules (3.1).
Output: a proposition, because 'a mechanism inferred from accounts is retroduced and not observed' (7.4).
entries.why: 'Critical realism reasons by retroduction' (3.1), and 'the explanation sought is a mechanism that can be tested against the cases that should break it, which is retroduction, not induction' (3.1).
entries.not_this: Deduction (positivist: hypotheses tested against measurement) and induction (interpretivist: accounts built up from what participants say) (Table 3.2). The thesis does not mention abduction.
entries.analogy: A mechanic hears the same knock in many cars, works back to what must be loose for that knock to occur, then checks cars where that part is tight to confirm the knock is absent.

viva_questions.q: Explain retroduction to someone outside research.
viva_questions.model_answer: It's reasoning back from a pattern to what must be so for the pattern to recur. I saw refusals recur wherever rivals' customers overlapped, asked what must be true for that, and answered with overlap and binding. Then I set that answer against the cases that should break it, which is why the evidence against was coded as deliberately as the evidence for (3.1).

viva_questions.q: How is retroduction different from induction?
viva_questions.model_answer: Induction builds an account up from what participants say. Retroduction asks what must be so for an observed regularity to be possible, names a mechanism and tests it against the cases where it should have fired and did not: here Ghent, the 117 arrangements, forty-three locker networks and the rules (Table 3.2; 3.1).

viva_questions.q: Isn't what you describe really abduction?
viva_questions.model_answer: I name my mode of inference as retroduction, the mode critical realism gives this kind of work, following Danermark and colleagues and Sayer, and the thesis does not discuss abduction. What I can state exactly is what I did: from the regularity to the mechanism that would produce it, then tested against the cases that should break it (3.1).

quiz.q: What question does retroduction put to a regularity, as 3.1 states it?
options: How often it appears in a random sample
What it means to each participant
What must be true for it to recur
What caused it in one case
quiz.explanation: It does not ask 'what caused it in one case' but 'what must be true for it to keep happening' (3.1).

quiz.q: What does 7.4 say is the cost of a mechanism inferred from accounts?
options: It is retroduced and not observed
It must be tested by regression
It cannot be written as a proposition
quiz.explanation: Hence the propositions of 7.2, offered for others to test (7.4).

beats.narration: Across twenty-six interviews, one pattern keeps returning: rivals who share customers refuse to pool.
beats.on_screen: A stylised city map; pairs of vans with overlapping customer areas turn away from each other.

beats.narration: Retroduction runs backwards: what must be true for this pattern to keep happening?
beats.on_screen: The scene rewinds like a film reel to a single question-mark shape.

beats.narration: The answer is a mechanism: overlap, with nothing outside to outweigh the exposure.
beats.on_screen: Two overlapping circles; an empty slot where a clasp could sit.

beats.narration: Then the test: look for the cases that should break it.
beats.on_screen: A magnifying glass sweeps across rows of arrangements, a city gate and a locker bank.

beats.narration: Where something binds rivals from outside, they collaborate. The mechanism survives.

entries.gap: Abduction is not discussed. If an examiner raises it, say what you did rather than debate labels.

entries.term: Deduction and induction
entries.plain: Deduction starts from a theory and tests its predictions against data. Induction starts from the data and builds general statements up from it.
in_this_thesis: Table 3.2 assigns deduction to positivism ('hypotheses tested against measurement') and induction to interpretivism ('accounts built up from what participants say').
Stage one, the 2022-23 systematic review, was 'deductive under the four pillars of the registration: trust, efficiency, innovation, sustainability' (3.1).
Stage two, the interviews, were 'read inductively and coded three times' (3.1).
The survey's open answers were 'coded inductively, in the manner Braun and Clarke (2006) describe' (3.6).
The overall mode is retroduction, 'not induction' (3.1).
The seventh further study would 'test the propositions of 7.2 as hypotheses in a deductive design in a market this thesis did not sample' (7.5).
entries.why: For the overall mode, see retroduction (3.1). The thesis does not say why the 2023 review was run deductively under the four pillars, beyond their being the pillars of the registration.
entries.not_this: Neither is the overall mode; the thesis adopts retroduction.
entries.analogy: Deduction is checking yesterday's forecast against today's sky; induction is keeping a diary of skies until a pattern shows.

viva_questions.q: Where in the research is there deduction, and where induction?
viva_questions.model_answer: The 2023 review was deductive under the four pillars of the registration. The interviews were read inductively, and the survey's open answers coded inductively. The overall mode is retroduction. Deduction returns at the end, as the further study that would test my propositions as hypotheses (3.1, 3.6, 7.5).

viva_questions.q: If the interviews were read inductively, why is your framework not simply inductive?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because the reading did not stop at themes. The first coding broke the pillars, the second tested the working claim and recorded the evidence against as well as for, the third coded every transcript against the five concepts, and the mechanism was then set against Ghent, the 117 arrangements, the locker networks and the rules (3.1, 3.4).

quiz.q: Under which framework was the 2023 systematic review deductive?
options: The four pillars: trust, efficiency, innovation, sustainability
The holder classes of codebook version 3
quiz.explanation: The pillars of the registration; the review found what its string could see (3.1).

quiz.q: What does 7.5 propose as the seventh further study?
options: Testing the propositions as hypotheses in a deductive design
A larger survey on the four pillars
quiz.explanation: In a market the thesis did not sample, with the operator pair as the unit (7.5).

entries.gap: Why the 2023 review was deductive under the pillars is not argued.

entries.term: Theory-building (not hypothesis-testing)
entries.plain: Research that develops explanations and propositions from cases rather than testing ready-made hypotheses. Testing the propositions is left for later work.
in_this_thesis: The abstract calls the design 'critical realist, theory-building'.
'Because it takes a critical realist view, this research builds theory rather than testing it' (3.1).

'Theory is developed here, not tested as hypotheses against measurement: the framework of 2.7 was drawn from the interviews, its fifth link from the interviews read again beside the locker networks and the rules, and it is offered in Chapter 7 as propositions, each of two variables, for others to test' (3.1).
Statistical tests appear in the later stages, but the locker difference 'fits the link but does not test it' (1.5).

'Because the design was theory-building, the contribution is offered as propositions rather than as tested hypotheses, each a single statement relating two variables, under the conditions it names, that others may test in their own context' (7.2).
entries.why: It follows from the paradigm: 'Because it takes a critical realist view, this research builds theory rather than testing it' (3.1).
entries.not_this: Testing hypotheses against measurement (3.1).
entries.analogy: Drawing the first reliable chart of a coastline from sailors' logs; sounding every bay is the next voyage.

viva_questions.q: You ran Fisher's exact test and a permutation test. How is this theory-building?
viva_questions.model_answer: The tests sit in the later stages, for the fifth link, and they show a difference by owner class that is consistent with the proposition, not a test of it. The design is qualitative at its core, with descriptive counts and statistical tests in its later stages, and the contribution is offered as propositions for others to test (Table 3.1; 5.2; 7.2).

viva_questions.q: What theory did you build?
viva_questions.model_answer: A five-link chain: overlap, the boundary of sharing, the binder, power and the holder; the first four found in the evidence, the fifth proposed. It is offered as five propositions, P1 to P5, each relating two variables, each with its falsifier in Table 7.1 (2.7; 7.2).

quiz.q: Because the design was theory-building, how is the contribution offered?
options: As a single theory with no conditions
As tested hypotheses with effect sizes
As propositions, each relating two variables
quiz.explanation: Each is a single statement relating two variables, under the conditions it names (7.2).

quiz.q: From what was the fifth link drawn?
options: The interviews read again beside the locker networks and the rules
quiz.explanation: 3.1; the permit register was not read (3.5).

entries.term: Wynn and Williams's principles for critical realist case research
entries.plain: Five principles for doing case research the critical realist way: describe the events, describe the structure and context, infer the mechanism, check it against evidence, and compare across sources.
in_this_thesis: Wynn and Williams (2012) 'turn the position into principles for case research': explicate the events, explicate the structure and context, retroduce the mechanism, corroborate it empirically, triangulate across sources (3.1).
Chapter 3 'is arranged so that each can be pointed to' (3.1):
Events: the arrangements of Appendix H and the refusals of Chapter 4.
Structure and context: the markets the parties compete in and the cities they deliver into.
Mechanism: overlap and binding.
Corroboration: the second reading of every transcript and the counts of 4.2 to 4.5.
Triangulation: the review, the interviews, the documents and the survey read against one another.
entries.why: The thesis presents them as the operational form of its paradigm; it gives no further reason.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative set of principles.
entries.analogy: A five-part accident report: what happened, the road conditions, the cause, the evidence that confirms it, and whether skid marks, witnesses and camera footage agree.

viva_questions.q: How does your design meet Wynn and Williams's principles?
viva_questions.model_answer: Each can be pointed to. The events are the arrangements of Appendix H and the refusals of Chapter 4; the structure and context are the markets the parties compete in and the cities they deliver into; the mechanism is overlap and binding; the corroboration is the second reading of every transcript and the counts of 4.2 to 4.5; and the triangulation is the review, interviews, documents and survey read against one another (3.1).

viva_questions.q: What exactly is your corroboration?
viva_questions.model_answer: The second reading of each half, made without sight of the first, which agreed on 112 of 130 stances, and the counts of 4.2 to 4.5, which show how widely each pattern holds and where it does not (3.1; 3.4).

quiz.q: In 3.1's mapping, what are the 'events'?
options: The arrangements of Appendix H and the refusals of Chapter 4
quiz.explanation: Structure and context are the markets and cities; the mechanism is overlap and binding (3.1).

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the principles as 3.1 lists them?
options: Estimate the effect size in a population
quiz.explanation: The five: explicate the events, explicate the structure and context, retroduce the mechanism, corroborate it empirically, triangulate (3.1).

entries.term: Triangulation
entries.plain: Checking a claim against different kinds of evidence. If separate sources point the same way, the claim is stronger; if one disagrees, that is reported.
in_this_thesis: 'The triangulation is the review, the interviews, the documents and the survey read against one another' (3.1).

On what binds: 95 of the 117 arrangements are bound from outside the parties, while survey respondents rate trust highly (89 of 119 at 4 or 5) and, among the 45 who said how they keep it, name formal contracts, third-party coordination and public authority support beside joint planning (4.4; 5.3).
On the holder: three kinds of evidence, the 117 arrangements recoded, the locker networks and the rules (1.5).
On power: the update's count rests partly on a decision rule that assumes the claim, so it is tested instead on the interviews and on who began the 117 arrangements (2.2; 4.5).
The survey 'is set beside them, not in their place' (3.6).
entries.why: It is one of Wynn and Williams's principles (3.1). The thesis gives no further reason.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Fixing a position from three landmarks rather than one: any single bearing can be off, but where three lines cross the fix can be trusted.

viva_questions.q: Your survey tests no link. How can it triangulate?
viva_questions.model_answer: It sits beside the links rather than testing them. It shows what organisations say about trust next to what they report using to keep it: 89 of 119 rate trust at 4 or 5, and among the 45 who said how they keep it, formal contracts, third-party coordination and public authority support are named beside joint planning. What binds is shown by the 117 arrangements, 95 of them bound from outside (3.6; 5.3; 4.4).

viva_questions.q: Give an example where your sources pull in different directions.
viva_questions.model_answer: Trust. Survey respondents rate it highly; the arrangements show 95 of 117 bound from outside the parties and six by their own trust. I report both, and read the survey as what people say matters and what they say they use, not as what binds (5.3; 4.4).

quiz.q: Which four sources does 3.1 name as triangulated?
options: The review, the interviews, the documents and the survey
ScienceDirect, Scopus, Web of Science and TRID
Three codings and a second reading
quiz.explanation: Read against one another (3.1).

quiz.q: How does 3.6 position the survey against the 117 arrangements?
options: As a replacement where the interviews were thin
As a population estimate of the arrangements
Beside them, not in their place
As the main test of link 3
quiz.explanation: What holds an arrangement together is shown by the 117 arrangements; the survey records report, not conduct (3.6).

entries.term: Staged design in four stages (multiphase)
entries.plain: Running research in steps, so that what each step finds shapes the next one.
in_this_thesis: Stage 1, 2022 and 2023: the systematic review, deductive under the four pillars; what its string could not see became the gap of 1.1 (3.1).

Stage 2, 2024 into 2025: twenty-six interviews in eleven countries, held July to September 2024, built on the four pillars, read inductively and coded three times between 2024 and 2026, with the survey running beside them from 22 February 2024 to 30 April 2025; the pillars became findings and the five links emerged across the three codings (3.1).

Figure 3.1, Stage 2: 'Each collaboration described became a row: 117 arrangements (Appendix H)'. So the 117 arrangements come from the interviews: 'each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration that a participant described is one row of Appendix H' (3.1).

Stage 3, 2025 and 2026: 'the documents of one city that gives out delivery hours by permit, read for the fifth link as it was first framed (a city giving set hours to named companies)', and the review re-run with corrected strings (3.1).

Stage 4, October 2026: the fifth link in its final form, the holder: the 117 arrangements recoded, the rules and forty-three locker networks in sixteen countries reviewed, the networks compared, and a scenario built (3.1).
Figure 3.1 draws the stages 'in the multiphase form the design literature uses for sequential fieldwork (Creswell and Plano Clark, 2018)' (3.1).
Overall: 'qualitative at its core, with descriptive counts and statistical tests in its later stages' (Table 3.1).
entries.why: 'Each stage's evidence feeding the next' (3.1). Maxwell's (2013) point, 'that the parts of a design act on one another rather than in sequence, is met in 3.8, where what changed between the stages is set out with its reason' (3.1). The thesis does not say why it describes the design as staged rather than as mixed methods.
entries.not_this: The thesis does not call itself mixed methods; the phrase appears only in the title of Creswell and Plano Clark's book in the reference list.
entries.analogy: A relay where each runner's split sets the next runner's route: the review handed a gap to the interviews, the interviews handed a candidate rule to the documents, and so on.

viva_questions.q: Is this a mixed-methods study?
viva_questions.model_answer: I describe it as a staged design under a critical realist paradigm, qualitative at its core, with descriptive counts and statistical tests in its later stages, drawn in the multiphase form Creswell and Plano Clark use for sequential fieldwork. The survey is descriptive and gives scale; no link of the chain rests on it (Table 3.1; 3.1; 3.8).

viva_questions.q: What did each stage hand to the next?
viva_questions.model_answer: The review's blind spot became the gap the interviews went after. The interviews broke the four pillars and produced the links. The third stage tested what the interviews had raised: the first form of the fifth link in Ghent's documents, and the field's newest work with corrected strings. The fourth tested the fifth link in its final form, the holder (3.1).

viva_questions.q: The survey ran alongside the interviews. Doesn't that break 'each stage feeds the next'?
viva_questions.model_answer: It does, and I record it as change 2 in Table 3.8. The ethics application planned the survey to follow the qualitative phase; it opened on the day of approval and ran beside the interviews on the four pillars, so it asks what the guide asked and not what the interviews found. That is why it is read for scale only (3.6; 3.8).

quiz.q: When was the fourth stage, testing the holder, carried out?
quiz.explanation: September 2022 is the first review's search; July to September 2024 the interviews; April 2017 Ghent's plan taking effect (3.1).

quiz.q: How does Table 3.1 describe the design?
options: An experiment with a control group
Qualitative at its core, with descriptive counts and statistical tests in its later stages
Quantitative at its core, with qualitative illustration
quiz.explanation: Table 3.1, 'How?'.

quiz.q: What did stage 3 read Ghent's documents for?
options: The holder of the shared point
The fifth link as first framed: a city giving set hours to named companies

entries.term: Figure 3.1, and where the 117 arrangements come from
entries.plain: Figure 3.1 is the map of the research: four stages from top to bottom, with what was done in each on the left and what it handed to the next on the right. Its Stage 2 box shows that the 117 arrangements come from the interviews: every collaboration a participant described became one row of Appendix H.
in_this_thesis: The figure is 'Figure 3.1 The four stages of the research and the evidence each fed to the next'; its two columns are headed 'What was done' and 'Evidence fed to the next' (Figure 3.1).

Stage 2, 2024 to 2025, 'Interviews, read inductively': '26 interviews, 30 people, 11 countries'; 'Each collaboration described became a row: 117 arrangements (Appendix H)'; 'Coded three times, the last against five concepts (3.4)' (Figure 3.1).

3.1 says the same in words: 'each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration that a participant described is one row of Appendix H, described by whether the parties' markets overlapped, what was pooled and what withheld, what bound it, who began it, its status at interview and whether it used time' (3.1).

The row rule: 'a scheme described by two participants becomes two rows, each pointing to the other, because what is counted is the description, not the scheme. A count of rows is therefore a count of accounts of arrangements, not of separate arrangements' (3.1).
Stage 4, October 2026, came back to the same rows: 'The 117 arrangements coded again for who holds the shared point (4.4)' (Figure 3.1).

Figure 3.1 is drawn 'in the multiphase form the design literature uses for sequential fieldwork (Creswell and Plano Clark, 2018), with the evidence of each stage feeding the questions of the next' (3.1).
entries.why: Because the counts of 4.4 and 4.5 rest on the rows of Appendix H (3.7), and Stage 4 coded the same 117 again for the holder. In the viva: say they come from the interviews, then give the row rule, so that 117 is never taken for 117 separate schemes.
entries.not_this: A count of separate schemes: 'a count of rows is therefore a count of accounts of arrangements, not of separate arrangements' (3.1).
entries.analogy: A school trip diary: each pupil writes up every outing they went on, and each write-up becomes one page. Two pupils describing the same museum visit make two pages, so a count of pages counts write-ups, not visits.

viva_questions.q: Where do your 117 arrangements come from?
viva_questions.model_answer: From the interviews. Each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration that a participant described became one row of Appendix H, and Figure 3.1 shows it in Stage 2. A scheme described by two participants is two rows, each pointing to the other, so 117 is a count of accounts of arrangements, not of separate arrangements (Figure 3.1; 3.1).

viva_questions.q: Why not count each scheme once?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because what is counted is the description, not the scheme: a row is one participant's account of one arrangement. Limiting each case to what the participant described, and no further, is the discipline Miles, Huberman and Saldaña ask for. And wherever the text needs the number of separate arrangements, it says so (3.1).

quiz.q: In which stage of Figure 3.1 did each collaboration described become a row?
quiz.explanation: Stage 2, the interviews; Stage 4 coded the same 117 again for who holds the shared point (Figure 3.1).

quiz.q: What does a count of the 117 rows count?
options: Separate arrangements, not accounts of them

Interview transcripts, not the arrangements in them
quiz.explanation: 'A count of rows is therefore a count of accounts of arrangements, not of separate arrangements, and wherever the text needs the number of separate arrangements, it says so' (3.1).

entries.term: Two units of counting: the transcript and the row (and the row rule)
entries.plain: When a study counts, it must say what one unit is. Here one transcript (one participant's testimony) and one row (one account of one arrangement) are counted separately and never mixed.
in_this_thesis: Transcript: each of the twenty-six read as a whole and given a stance on each of the five concepts (supports, contradicts, mixed, silent), so 'a count of transcripts is a count of accounts' (3.1).
Every count of stances is 'a count of transcripts, not of mentions' (4.1).

Row: one row of Appendix H per description of an arrangement. The row rule: 'a scheme described by two participants becomes two rows, each pointing to the other', so 'a count of rows is therefore a count of accounts of arrangements, not of separate arrangements' (3.1).

A half: a first listing of 39 items (accounts of 37 arrangements); the appendix gives those 39 rows and adds 17 the listing left out, 56 rows, holding between 51 and 52 unique schemes once two repeated descriptions are merged. B half: 61 items, 61 rows. Total: 117 (3.4).
Two further units for the fifth link: the locker network counted by ownership period (47 periods of 43 networks) and the rule, read for how it defines a neutral point (3.1).
entries.why: Transcripts: 'because a transcript is one participant's testimony and a participant who said a thing three times said it once' (3.4). Rows: 'because what is counted is the description, not the scheme' (3.1).
entries.not_this: Counting mentions (4.1).
entries.analogy: Counting witnesses versus counting statements about each incident: two witnesses describing the same crash give two statements, and the report says so.

viva_questions.q: Why is 117 not the number of arrangements?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because a row is one participant's account of one arrangement. A scheme described by two participants is two rows, cross-referenced, since the unit is the description. In the A half, the 56 rows hold between 51 and 52 unique schemes; where the text needs the number of arrangements, it says so (3.1; 3.4).

viva_questions.q: Why count by transcript rather than by mention?
viva_questions.model_answer: A transcript is one participant's testimony, and a participant who said a thing three times said it once. So every count of stances in Chapters 4 and 5 is a count of transcripts (3.4; 4.1).

quiz.q: A scheme described by two participants becomes how many rows of Appendix H?
quiz.explanation: The unit is the description, not the scheme (3.1).

quiz.q: How many rows does the A half contribute to Appendix H?
quiz.explanation: 39 items in the first listing (accounts of 37 arrangements) plus 17 added; the B half contributes 61 (3.4).

entries.term: Recording what changed: Table 3.8, Maxwell's interactive model and the Rose audit
entries.plain: Writing down every change to a design, with its reason, so a reader can see the design adjusted to evidence rather than being bent to a conclusion.
in_this_thesis: Table 3.8 lists five changes: 1, the four-pillar interview guide became five-link coding (2024 to 2026); 2, the survey ran alongside the interviews, not after them (2024 to 2025); 3, the review was re-run with corrected strings (2026); 4, the 2023 full-text stage was re-run (2026); 5, the fifth link was re-specified from hours allocated between operators to the holder of the shared point beside an access rule by vehicle and hour (October 2026).

'None of the five was a change of question. The first four were changes of instrument, made because the instrument had shown its limit; the fifth was a change of the proposed answer, made because the first answer did not survive the tests put to it' (3.8).

Change 5's reasons: Ghent expected no fall in suppliers' traffic in the hours its windows leave open (Stad Gent, 2016, p. 112), and 'a rule that must know who is acting costs more to watch than one that bars an act whoever does it' (Ostrom, 1990, p. 204) (Table 3.8).

Figure 3.3 audits the design after Rose (1982), as Trafford and Leshem carry it (2008, p. 103): theory, propositions, design, fieldwork, results, with feedback from results back to propositions (3.7).
Internal consistency (fieldwork against design) is checked before external consistency (conclusions against theory) (p. 104): the first is the work of Chapters 3 to 5, the second of Chapter 6 (3.7).
'The feedback arrows of Figure 3.3 are these five changes' (3.8).
In 3.1: 'Maxwell's (2013) point, that the parts of a design act on one another rather than in sequence, is met in 3.8, where what changed between the stages is set out with its reason' (3.1).
entries.why: Trafford and Leshem 'hold that a change of plan must be explained in the thesis, and that accounting for it shows a reader how the research audited itself as it went (2008, pp. 99, 104)'; Maxwell's interactive model (2013), 'in which goals, framework, questions, methods and validity act on one another rather than following in sequence, is the form the five changes took' (3.8).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A ship's log that records each change of course and the reason, so nobody can later say the ship simply drifted to where it landed.

viva_questions.q: What is the difference between a change of instrument and a change of answer?
viva_questions.model_answer: A change of instrument changes how I asked or looked, made because the instrument had shown its limit: the pillars becoming five-link coding, the survey running alongside, the strings corrected, the 2023 full-text stage re-run. A change of answer changes what I proposed: the fifth link moving from hours allocated between operators to the holder, because the first answer did not survive the tests put to it (3.8).

viva_questions.q: What is Figure 3.3 for?
viva_questions.model_answer: It audits the whole design in the form Rose proposed, as Trafford and Leshem carry it: theory, propositions, design, fieldwork, results, with feedback arrows back to the propositions. Internal consistency is checked in Chapters 3 to 5 before external consistency in Chapter 6, and the feedback arrows are the five changes of Table 3.8 (3.7; 3.8).

quiz.q: In the Rose audit as the thesis applies it, which is checked first?
options: The translation of the Ghent extracts
External consistency of the conclusions against theory
Internal consistency of the fieldwork against the design
quiz.explanation: Trafford and Leshem's order (2008, p. 104): internal in Chapters 3 to 5, external in Chapter 6 (3.7).

quiz.q: What are the feedback arrows of Figure 3.3?

entries.term: Maxwell's interactive model: the parts of a design act on one another
entries.plain: Maxwell (2013) sees a research design not as a straight line from question to method to answer but as parts that push and pull on one another, so that a change in one can change the others. The thesis draws its stages in sequence in Figure 3.1 and shows the push and pull in 3.8, where each change between the stages is set out with its reason.
in_this_thesis: 'Maxwell's (2013) point, that the parts of a design act on one another rather than in sequence, is met in 3.8, where what changed between the stages is set out with its reason' (3.1).

The parts, as 3.8 names them: 'Maxwell's interactive model (2013), in which goals, framework, questions, methods and validity act on one another rather than following in sequence, is the form the five changes took, each a method or an answer revised when a question outgrew it' (3.8).

The five changes of Table 3.8: the four-pillar interview guide became five-link coding; the survey ran alongside the interviews, not after them; the review was re-run with corrected strings; the 2023 full-text stage was re-run; and the fifth link was re-specified, from hours allocated between operators to the holder of the shared point beside an access rule by vehicle and hour (Table 3.8).

One part acting on another, change 1: why, 'the data broke the pillars; the links recurred across transcripts'; effect on the design, 'the codebook of Table 3.5; the framework of 2.7 presented as emergent' (Table 3.8).
What did not move: 'None of the five was a change of question' (3.8).

Why Figure 3.1 still reads as a line: it 'draws the four stages in the multiphase form the design literature uses for sequential fieldwork (Creswell and Plano Clark, 2018), with the evidence of each stage feeding the questions of the next' (3.1).
entries.why: Trafford and Leshem 'hold that a change of plan must be explained in the thesis, and that accounting for it shows a reader how the research audited itself as it went (2008, pp. 99, 104)' (3.8), and Maxwell's model is the form those changes took. In the viva: if asked whether the design was planned or made up as you went, say it was staged, and that every change is recorded with its reason, none of them a change of question.
entries.not_this: A design whose parts simply follow one another, which is what Maxwell's point is set against: parts that 'act on one another rather than following in sequence' (3.8).
entries.analogy: Planning a family holiday: the budget, the dates, the destination and the travel all affect one another. If the flights cost more than you thought, the dates or the destination change; you do not fix each in turn and never look back.

viva_questions.q: Figure 3.1 is a straight line of four stages. Isn't that the opposite of Maxwell?
viva_questions.model_answer: Figure 3.1 draws the stages in the multiphase form used for sequential fieldwork, with the evidence of each stage feeding the questions of the next. Maxwell's point, that the parts of a design act on one another rather than in sequence, is met in 3.8. Table 3.8 sets out the five changes between the stages, each with its reason, and the feedback arrows of Figure 3.3 are those five changes (3.1; 3.8).

viva_questions.q: Did your question change as the design changed?
viva_questions.model_answer: No. None of the five was a change of question. The first four were changes of instrument, made because the instrument had shown its limit; the fifth was a change of the proposed answer, made because the first answer did not survive the tests put to it (3.8).

quiz.q: What is Maxwell's (2013) point, as 3.1 states it?
options: A design is judged only by the validity of its final results
The parts of a design act on one another rather than in sequence
Each stage of a design should be finished before the next
A design should be fixed in full before any fieldwork begins
quiz.explanation: 'Maxwell's (2013) point, that the parts of a design act on one another rather than in sequence, is met in 3.8' (3.1).

quiz.q: Where does 3.1 say Maxwell's point is met?
options: In 3.8, where what changed between the stages is set out

In 3.6, where the survey's questions are set out
In 3.2, where the review's strings are set out
quiz.explanation: 'is met in 3.8, where what changed between the stages is set out with its reason' (3.1).

quiz.q: In 3.8, which parts does Maxwell's interactive model say act on one another?
options: Goals, framework, questions, methods and validity

entries.term: Semi-structured interview (the guide and the working script)
entries.plain: An interview with a fixed set of themes but a free order and free follow-up questions, so the conversation can follow what the participant knows.
in_this_thesis: The instrument approved by the School's ethics committee on 22 February 2024 asked fourteen questions under seven headings, two to a heading (3.3; Appendix A).

Three headings framed the conversation ('Background and Experience with HC', 'Challenges and Solutions', 'Future Perspectives'); the four between them were the pillars of the registration: 'Trust and Partnership', 'Operational Efficiency', 'Innovation in Collaboration', 'Sustainability Outcomes' (3.3).

A working script of twenty-three prompts in ten stages, from introduction and consent through role, collaborations known, drivers, blocks, outcomes and whom else to ask, sat beside the guide in every interview (3.3).

The guide was built in the sequence Kallio and colleagues (2016) describe, from prerequisites and prior knowledge to a preliminary guide and its complete form (the fourteen-question guide and the twenty-three-prompt script) (3.3).
The interviews were conducted as Brinkmann and Kvale (2015) describe the form: 'a guide that fixes the themes and leaves the order and the follow-up to the conversation' (3.3).

The guide had allowed forty-five to sixty minutes; the median was forty-three, and fourteen closed sooner, 'most because the participant had said what they had come to say, though a call is easier to end than a visit' (3.3).
entries.why: The script 'let the conversation follow the participant rather than the headings' (3.3). 'The guide asked about trust because the field did; what the participants answered is in Chapter 4, and it is why the pillars are findings in this thesis rather than its frame' (3.3). The thesis does not set the semi-structured form against structured or unstructured interviews.
entries.not_this: No alternative interview form is named. In hindsight (7.4): 'a guide written after the fact would have asked about overlap and time directly and found less than it was told, because the participants brought both unprompted'.
entries.analogy: A walking tour with a list of landmarks but no fixed route: every landmark gets visited, in whatever order the guide's companion leads.

viva_questions.q: Your guide was built on four pillars you later abandoned. Doesn't that taint the data?
viva_questions.model_answer: The guide asked about trust because the field did, and that is the evidence of where the research began; I quote its headings as they stood. The working script let the conversation follow the participant, and what came back broke the pillars: they became findings, not the frame. And a guide written after the fact would have found less than I was told, because participants brought overlap and time unprompted (3.3; 7.4).

viva_questions.q: Fourteen interviews ended before the forty-five minutes you planned. Is that a problem?
viva_questions.model_answer: Most ended because the participant had said what they had come to say, though a call is easier to end than a visit, and I say so. Sixteen of the twenty-six ran forty minutes or more, and each transcript's length and quality flags are given in Table 4.1 (3.3; 4.1).

quiz.q: How many questions, under how many headings, did the approved guide ask?
quiz.explanation: Twenty-three prompts in ten stages is the working script; thirteen in five sections is the draft survey (3.3; 3.6).

quiz.q: Whose description of the semi-structured form does 3.3 follow?
quiz.explanation: Kallio and colleagues (2016) supply the sequence for building the guide (3.3).

entries.gap: Why semi-structured rather than structured or unstructured is not argued.

entries.term: Purposive (purposeful) sampling
entries.plain: Choosing participants deliberately because they know about the question, rather than at random. The aim is information-rich cases, not a statistically representative sample.
in_this_thesis: Participants 'were chosen purposively for the kinds of party the question needed (those who run collaborations, those who convene, fund or regulate them, and those who study or broker them), and were found through the projects and publications in which they had done so' (3.3).
'The sampling was purposeful in Patton's sense (2015), for information-rich cases of each kind of party' (3.3).

The mix: eight public bodies, four consultancies (one a neutral trustee, heard through two staff), six academics (three had worked in industry), four carriers (three from inside one, one the retiring adviser to a small cargo-bike operator; two of the four in one country), and one each for a manufacturing site host, a shipper-side pooling platform, an environmental coalition and a European association of cities (3.3; Table 3.1).
Thirty people in twenty-six interviews: twenty-three with one person, two with a pair, one with three (3.3).
'Twenty-six is a purposive set, not a sample of a population' (3.3).
entries.why: 'The mix was chosen for the question rather than for the industry. If the thing to be explained is who begins a collaboration and what binds it, then the people who convene, fund, regulate, study and broker collaborations had to be in the room, not carriers alone' (3.3).
entries.not_this: A sample of a population (3.3); Table 3.2 notes there is 'no register to draw a sample from'.
entries.analogy: To learn why a bridge failed you ask the engineers, inspectors and builders who worked on it, not a random sample of drivers who crossed it.

viva_questions.q: Why not interview mostly carriers, since the thesis is about them?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because the question is who begins a collaboration and what binds it, so the people who convene, fund, regulate, study and broker collaborations had to be in the room, not carriers alone. Carriers, at four voices, are the one kind I call thin, and the others describe carrier behaviour they have watched for years (3.3; 3.7).

viva_questions.q: Is twenty-six representative?
viva_questions.model_answer: It isn't meant to be. It's a purposive set chosen for information-rich cases of each kind of party, not a sample of a population, and the findings generalise to the mechanism, not to a population (3.3; 3.1).

quiz.q: Whose sense of purposeful sampling does 3.3 follow?
quiz.explanation: Biernacki and Waldorf describe the chain referral of the second stage (3.3).

quiz.q: How many of the twenty-six interviews speak for a public body?
quiz.explanation: Four carriers, four consultancies, six academics (3.3; Table 3.1).

entries.term: Snowball (chain-referral) sampling
entries.plain: Asking each participant to name others who should be heard, and following those names. It reaches people you could not find alone, but the chain runs along each referrer's own network.
in_this_thesis: 'Each was asked at the close whom else the research should hear, and the referrals were followed until the kinds of party were covered and the accounts had begun to repeat' (3.3). The working script's last stages include whom else to ask (3.3; Appendix A).
The second stage of sampling 'was chain referral of the kind Biernacki and Waldorf (1981) describe' (3.3).
Their named bias, 'that referrals run along the referrer's own network', was 'met here by starting the chains from each of the three kinds of party, in eleven countries, rather than from one' (3.3).
The same bias is named for the survey, whose link was passed along the author's networks and those of the people it was passed to (3.6).
entries.why: The thesis gives the bias and the counter-measure; it does not say why chain referral was used beyond following the referrals 'until the kinds of party were covered and the accounts had begun to repeat' (3.3).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative. Its own term is 'chain referral'; 'snowball' appears only in the title of Biernacki and Waldorf's paper.
entries.analogy: Finding good tradespeople by asking each one you hire who else they'd trust: you reach people no directory lists, but you stay inside their circle unless you start from several circles.

viva_questions.q: Snowball samples stay inside one network. How did you deal with that?
viva_questions.model_answer: That is the bias Biernacki and Waldorf name, that referrals run along the referrer's own network. I met it by starting the chains from each of the three kinds of party, in eleven countries, rather than from one (3.3).

viva_questions.q: When did you stop following referrals?
viva_questions.model_answer: When the kinds of party were covered and the accounts had begun to repeat; that is the data saturation of 3.3, reached by kind of party and not by count (3.3).

quiz.q: How did the thesis counter the bias of chain referral?
options: By interviewing only people with no referrer
By stopping at a fixed number of twelve
By starting chains from each of the three kinds of party, in eleven countries

quiz.q: Which other part of the research carries the same referral-chain bias?
quiz.explanation: Its link was shared along the author's networks and passed on (3.6).
