entries.term: Information power (how many interviews are enough)
entries.plain: The idea that a study needs fewer interviews the more information each one holds for its aim: a narrow aim, well-chosen participants, guiding theory and strong conversations all reduce the number needed.
in_this_thesis: Malterud, Siersma and Guassora (2016) 'hold that the number of interviews a study needs falls as its aim narrows, as the sample's specificity to that aim rises, as the study is guided by theory, as the dialogue is strong and as the analysis is of cases rather than across them' (3.3).

On the first four, this study's need was low: its aim was narrow; its participants were chosen for having convened, funded, regulated, brokered or refused the very thing at issue; its coding was against a stated framework; and sixteen of the twenty-six interviews ran forty minutes or more (3.3).
On the fifth it was higher, 'since the analysis runs across cases' (3.3).
entries.why: Given as the argument for why twenty-six was enough, beside saturation (3.3).
entries.not_this: Guest, Bunce and Johnson's (2006) dozen-interview finding, not relied on (see saturation). The phrase 'information power' appears only in the title of Malterud and colleagues' paper; the body of 3.3 uses their five dimensions without naming the concept.
entries.analogy: How many witnesses you need depends on who they are: five people who stood at the junction tell you more than fifty who heard about it later.

viva_questions.q: How did you decide twenty-six interviews was enough?
viva_questions.model_answer: On Malterud and colleagues' five dimensions. The aim was narrow; the participants were chosen for having convened, funded, regulated, brokered or refused the very thing at issue; the coding was against a stated framework; and sixteen of the twenty-six ran forty minutes or more. Only the last dimension raised the need, because my analysis runs across cases. Beside that, data saturation was reached by kind of party (3.3).

viva_questions.q: Which dimension worked against you?
viva_questions.model_answer: The analysis strategy. Malterud and colleagues say fewer interviews are needed where analysis is of cases rather than across them, and mine runs across cases, so on that dimension the need was higher (3.3).

quiz.q: On which of Malterud and colleagues' dimensions was this study's need higher?
options: The coding was against a stated framework
Participants were specific to the aim
quiz.explanation: The other three, and strong dialogue, lowered the need (3.3).

quiz.q: How many of the twenty-six interviews ran forty minutes or more?
quiz.explanation: Fourteen closed sooner than the forty-five the guide allowed (3.3).

entries.gap: The thesis argues Malterud's dimensions but never uses the term 'information power' in its text. Use the term if asked, then give the five dimensions.

entries.term: Saturation (data saturation, reached by kind of party)
entries.plain: The point at which new interviews stop adding anything new. Different authors mean different things by it, so a study should say which kind it reached.
in_this_thesis: Saunders and colleagues (2018) 'distinguish four things saturation can mean, theoretical, inductive thematic, a priori thematic and data saturation' (3.3).

'What was reached here is the fourth in their terms, ‘identifying redundancy in the data’, the point at which a new participant of a kind described arrangements and refusals the set already held' (3.3).
'It was reached by kind of party and not by count, which is why the carriers, at four voices, are the one kind 3.7 calls thin' (3.3).

Guest, Bunce and Johnson's (2006) finding that most themes appear within the first dozen interviews 'is not relied on, because it was reached on a homogeneous sample, and this one was chosen to be the opposite' (3.3).
entries.why: As above: saturation is defined so the claim can be checked, and judged by kind of party because the sample was deliberately varied (3.3).
entries.not_this: Guest, Bunce and Johnson's dozen-interview rule (3.3).
entries.analogy: Tasting a soup from every pot in a kitchen: you stop when each pot's next spoonful tastes like the last, not after a fixed number of spoonfuls overall.

viva_questions.q: Did you reach saturation?
viva_questions.model_answer: Data saturation in Saunders and colleagues' sense, identifying redundancy in the data: the point at which a new participant of a kind described arrangements and refusals the set already held. It was reached by kind of party, not by count, which is why the carriers, at four voices, are the one kind I call thin (3.3; 3.7).

viva_questions.q: Most themes appear within twelve interviews, according to Guest and colleagues. Why not cite that?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because their finding was reached on a homogeneous sample, and mine was chosen to be the opposite, so I don't rely on it (3.3).

quiz.q: Which of Saunders and colleagues' four kinds of saturation does the thesis claim?
quiz.explanation: 'Identifying redundancy in the data' (3.3).

quiz.q: Why is Guest, Bunce and Johnson's dozen-interview finding not relied on?
options: It was reached on a homogeneous sample
quiz.explanation: This sample was chosen to be the opposite (3.3).

entries.term: Online interviews, automatic transcripts and quotation conventions
entries.plain: How the conversations were held, recorded and turned into text, and the rules for quoting from that text.
in_this_thesis: Held online between July and September 2024, all twenty-six conducted by the author in English; recorded on the call, twenty-four with video and two as audio (3.3).
Eight to seventy-four minutes; twenty hours and five minutes in all; median forty-three; 146,778 words of speech, appended summaries excluded (3.3).

Transcripts were made automatically from the recordings and prepared as McLellan, MacQueen and Neidig (2003) advise: kept as made, appended summaries removed, timestamps retained, so the minute and second of every quotation in Chapters 4 and 5 can be found in Appendix H or I (3.3).

Quotation rules: British spelling; a repeated word and a filler such as 'yeah' removed without marking; every other omission marked with an ellipsis; square brackets either replace an identifying name, place, employer or time of day, or restore a garbled word where its sense was plain, the passage being left unquoted where it was not (3.3).
In one interview, A9, answers were typed in afterwards rather than transcribed, and it is read as low confidence throughout (3.3; Table 4.1).
Every quotation was checked by the author against its transcript before it was used (3.3). 'One flag runs through all twenty-six: the transcripts are automatic' (4.1).
entries.why: Online 'because the participants sat in eleven countries, and the video call has been found to serve qualitative interviewing well where distance would otherwise exclude the people the question needs (Archibald et al., 2019; Lobe, Morgan and Hoffman, 2020)' (3.3).
entries.not_this: Face-to-face interviews are implied but not named; 3.3 notes 'a call is easier to end than a visit'.
entries.analogy: A court stenographer's record with timestamps: anyone can go to the exact minute a quoted line was spoken.

viva_questions.q: Your transcripts are automatic. How do you know the quotations are right?
viva_questions.model_answer: Every quotation was checked against its transcript before use, timestamps were kept so each can be found to the minute and second, a garbled word is restored in square brackets only where its sense is plain, and the passage is left unquoted where it isn't. Quality flags for each transcript are in Table 4.1 (3.3; 4.1).

viva_questions.q: Did interviewing online cost you anything?
viva_questions.model_answer: Some interviews were shorter: fourteen closed before the forty-five minutes the guide allowed, most because the participant had said what they came to say, though a call is easier to end than a visit. Against that, the video call let me reach people in eleven countries whom distance would otherwise have excluded (3.3).

quiz.q: What was the total speech in the twenty-six transcripts?
quiz.explanation: Appended summaries excluded (3.3).

quiz.q: Which transcript is read as low confidence throughout because answers were typed in afterwards?
quiz.explanation: B8 is the poorest recording; A5 eight minutes of prepared answers; B10 outside the domain (Table 4.1).

entries.term: Pseudonymisation and anonymisation
entries.plain: Removing or disguising details that would identify participants, and replacing names with codes.
in_this_thesis: Participants are identified by codes A1 to A13 and B1 to B13, in the order the transcripts were filed and divided into the two halves read separately in the second and third codings (3.3).
No participant and no employer is named in any chapter; organisations are described by type; where a participant's own description would identify them, it was made generic in Table 3.4 (3.3).
Table 3.4 gives the eleven countries as a set, not against each code (3.3).
A city or public scheme is named only where it is a matter of public record and more than one person could have described it; a role that would narrow to one person was widened (3.3).
The transcripts were pseudonymised, with names, employers and places replaced by the codes, before the second coding began (3.4).
entries.why: 'These choices follow Saunders, Kitzinger and Kitzinger (2015), who show that anonymising interview data is a set of judgements rather than a procedure, and the judgements made here are stated so that a reader can see what was traded for what' (3.3).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Blurring faces and number plates in a street photograph while keeping the street recognisable enough to tell the story.

viva_questions.q: How did you protect participants when the sector is small?
viva_questions.model_answer: Codes instead of names; no employer named; organisations by type; descriptions made generic where they would identify; the countries given as a set, not against codes; public schemes named only where on public record and describable by more than one person; and narrow roles widened. Following Saunders, Kitzinger and Kitzinger, I treat anonymising as judgements and state them (3.3).

viva_questions.q: When were the transcripts pseudonymised?
viva_questions.model_answer: Before the second coding began, with names, employers and places replaced by the codes of Table 3.4 (3.4).

quiz.q: Whose work does 3.3 cite for treating anonymisation as a set of judgements?
quiz.explanation: Saunders and colleagues (2018) is the saturation paper (3.3).

quiz.q: How does Table 3.4 give the eleven countries?
options: As a set, not against each code

entries.term: Ethics approval and consent (including verbal consent)
entries.plain: Formal permission from a university ethics committee before research with people, and each participant's informed agreement to take part and be recorded.
in_this_thesis: The School of Architecture and the Built Environment's ethics committee, Faculty of Science and Engineering, approved the study as Category A on 22 February 2024, with the guide, the participant information sheet and the consent form, on condition that the final questions be approved by the supervisory team before data collection began, 'which was done' (3.3; Appendices B, C).

Every participant received the information sheet and consent form; twenty-seven of the thirty returned the form signed; three (A5, the second participant in A9, and B8) consented verbally, on the recording, B8 at the close of the call; B8 had been sent the sheet, which said the interview would be recorded and that recording could be declined (3.3).

The survey ran under the same approval; its first item asked respondents to confirm they had read the information sheet, and the six who answered No are excluded; it asked for no name and no organisation; the optional email answers were not read (3.6).
entries.why: 'Ethics was part of the design and not a clearance obtained for it' (3.3). Verbal consent follows the ESRC, which holds that 'in some contexts verbal consent may be ethically preferable to written consent' and that 'Where possible this should include audio-recorded consent' (Economic and Social Research Council, 2026) (3.3).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A building permit and the householder's signed agreement: the first says the work may be done at all, the second that this person agreed to it.

viva_questions.q: Three participants didn't sign a consent form. Is that a problem?
viva_questions.model_answer: They consented verbally, on the recording, as Appendix B records. That follows the ESRC guidance that verbal consent may be ethically preferable in some contexts and should, where possible, be audio-recorded. B8 consented at the close of the call, having been sent the information sheet, which said the interview would be recorded and that recording could be declined (3.3).

viva_questions.q: What condition did the ethics approval carry?
viva_questions.model_answer: That the final questions be approved by the supervisory team before data collection began, which was done (3.3).

quiz.q: When was the study approved, and in which category?
quiz.explanation: 19 February 2024 is the draft survey's date (3.3; 3.6).

quiz.q: How many of the thirty participants returned the consent form signed?
quiz.explanation: Three consented verbally on the recording; twenty-four is the number recorded with video (3.3).

entries.term: The comparator interview and out-of-domain transcripts kept in the denominator
entries.plain: A comparator is a case from outside the main boundary, kept to contrast with the rest. Out-of-domain transcripts are interviews that turned out to be about something else; keeping them in the count avoids quietly improving the numbers.
in_this_thesis: India's one interview (A1) 'was held as a comparator from outside Europe; it stands, like every transcript, in each count of twenty-six, contributes three rows to Appendix H, read as comparators, and is drawn on only where the text says so' (3.3; 1.4).
Two transcripts, B10 (an engineer on interurban weight enforcement) and B11 (a site host who had 'not really' looked at logistics), 'proved on reading to lie outside the domain' (3.7; 4.1).

They are kept in the set and in Table 3.4; both codings record them as silent on most concepts; they stand in every denominator of twenty-six; their eight rows stand in the 117; 'no finding in Chapters 4 and 5 rests on them alone' (3.7).
Table 4.1 flags every transcript's quality: for example A2 'not specifically urban', A5 eight minutes of prepared answers, A9 typed answers, B8 the poorest recording (4.1).
entries.why: The thesis states the treatment but not an explicit reason for keeping out-of-domain transcripts in the denominator. Its stated rule is that no finding rests on them alone (3.7).
entries.not_this: Dropping them from the count is not done, and the thesis does not discuss it.
entries.analogy: Keeping the two jurors who slept through a trial in the headcount, and saying so, rather than reporting a unanimous verdict from ten.

viva_questions.q: Why keep two out-of-domain interviews in your denominator of twenty-six?
viva_questions.model_answer: They stand in every count, both codings record them as silent on most concepts, and no finding rests on them alone. Keeping them in means a count of twenty-six is every interview I held, not a set chosen after reading (3.7; 4.1).

viva_questions.q: Why is there an Indian interview in a European thesis?
viva_questions.model_answer: As a comparator from outside Europe. It stands in every count of twenty-six, contributes three rows to Appendix H read as comparators, and is drawn on only where the text says so (3.3; 1.4).

quiz.q: Which two transcripts lie outside the domain?
quiz.explanation: A1 is the comparator; A9 low confidence; B8 the poorest recording; A5 prepared answers (4.1).

quiz.q: How many rows of Appendix H do the two out-of-domain transcripts contribute?
quiz.explanation: They stand in the 117 (3.7).

entries.gap: The reason for keeping out-of-domain transcripts in the denominator is implied, not stated. Say it plainly if asked.
story_refs: EQ ch1: Why Europe, when one of your interviews is in India?

entries.term: Interviewer effects: seeded themes, relayed positions and the five cautions
entries.plain: An interviewer can shape answers by suggesting ideas or repeating what others said. Good practice records where that happened and does not count it as the participant's own view.
in_this_thesis: Each coding recorded, transcript by transcript, the themes the interviewer introduced and the positions he relayed between interviews, 'and neither is counted as a participant's view' (4.1).
Brand, raised by the interviewer in five interviews, was declined in all five, and is counted as declined, not as absent; it was raised unprompted in eight, three of them first-hand (3.4; 4.6).

Relayed positions: the shipper-responsibility thesis relayed to two as something others had said; one participant's case narrated to another; the claim that small operators collaborate hard put to two, who did not take it up (4.1).
Where a participant took up a seeded theme, as B5 took up the trustee, it is counted with the seeding noted (4.1).

Five cautions of the second coding are carried into the thesis as written: brand declined in five of five; relayed positions mean agreement across transcripts partly reflects the interviewer; one recording substantially incomplete; one participant's successes were proposals; one case not yet running at interview (3.4).
entries.why: The interviewer 'is the reader most exposed to his own expectation, which Miles, Huberman and Saldaña name among the first threats to a qualitative analysis' (3.4). Recording seeded and relayed themes is part of reflexivity (3.7).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A detective noting which details he mentioned to a witness first, so a later 'match' with his own theory isn't mistaken for corroboration.

viva_questions.q: You raised brand yourself. How did you stop that colouring the result?
viva_questions.model_answer: Brand was put by me in five interviews and declined in all five, and it is counted as declined, not as absent. It was raised unprompted in eight, three first-hand, and it is reported as the minority finding it is (3.4; 4.6).

viva_questions.q: You relayed one participant's views to another. Doesn't that make agreement across transcripts partly your doing?
viva_questions.model_answer: Partly, yes, and that is one of the five cautions carried into the thesis as written. Each coding recorded where I relayed a position or seeded a theme, neither is counted as a participant's view, and where a participant took a seeded theme up, it is counted with the seeding noted (3.4; 4.1).

quiz.q: How is brand counted, given the interviewer raised it?
options: It was removed from the analysis
As supported, since it was discussed
quiz.explanation: Raised by the interviewer in five interviews, declined in all five (3.4; 3.7).

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the five cautions of the second coding?
options: The binder carries no agreement figure
No Dutch speaker checked the translations
quiz.explanation: The other options are real limits, but stated elsewhere (3.6, 3.5, 3.4).

story_refs: EQ ch4: You raised brand yourself. Why does the visibility finding survive at all?

entries.term: Thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke) and the first coding
entries.plain: Reading qualitative data closely, labelling passages with codes, and grouping the codes into themes that describe patterns across the data.
in_this_thesis: 'The twenty-six transcripts were coded three times, in the thematic manner Braun and Clarke (2006) describe, and the order matters, because each coding was made to test the one before it' (3.4).
The first coding was made by the author in 2024 and 2025, after the interviews, under the guide's four pillar headings (3.4).

It is 'where the pillars broke': trust appeared only as something borrowed from outside the parties; efficiency as the driver participants named and compulsion as the one that moved them; innovation as a facilitator; sustainability as a by-product (3.4).

From it the author wrote the working claim of 2026: the last mile is a brand asset; size sorts willingness; working arrangements run on substitutes for trust; power sits with shippers and cities; time can do what pooling was asked to (3.4).
The survey's open answers were also coded inductively in Braun and Clarke's manner, into six themes and a code for answers with nothing of substance (3.6).
entries.why: The thesis does not say why it chose thematic analysis over other qualitative approaches; it says each coding was made to test the one before (3.4).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative qualitative method.
entries.analogy: Sorting a heap of letters into piles by what they are about, then noticing the piles you expected don't fit and new piles forming.

viva_questions.q: What did the first coding produce?
viva_questions.model_answer: Two things. It broke the four pillars: trust appeared only as something borrowed from outside the parties, efficiency as the named driver with compulsion as what actually moved firms, innovation as a facilitator and sustainability as a by-product. And it produced the working claim of 2026, which the second coding was built to test (3.4).

viva_questions.q: Why thematic analysis?
viva_questions.model_answer: I coded the transcripts in the thematic manner Braun and Clarke describe, in a sequence where each coding tested the one before: thematic under the pillars first, then codebook codings against the claim and then the five concepts. The thesis doesn't argue thematic analysis against other approaches; what it shows is that sequence (3.4).

quiz.q: Under which headings was the first coding made?
Which of these was a clause of the working claim of 2026?
quiz.explanation: Size and brand were the clauses the second coding did not sustain (3.4).

entries.gap: Why thematic analysis rather than another approach is not argued.

entries.term: The three codings of the transcripts
entries.plain: The transcripts were coded three times, each coding built to test the one before it, so the framework can be shown to have come from the data.
in_this_thesis: First coding (2024 and 2025, by the author): under the four pillar headings; the pillars broke; the working claim of 2026 was written from it (3.4).

Second coding (September 2026): a codebook coding (Miles, Huberman and Saldaña, 2014) built to test the working claim, not Table 3.5; transcripts pseudonymised first; coded in two halves, A1 to A13 and B1 to B13, each read in full without the notes of the first coding; for every clause and transcript it recorded a stance, the exact words, their place and the evidence against as well as for (3.4).

Result: two clauses, brand and size, were not sustained; two regularities the claim had not named, overlap and the boundary of sharing, appeared; the codebook of Table 3.5 was rewritten from these results (3.4).

Third coding: against Table 3.5, again in two halves of thirteen, so that 'every count in Chapters 4 and 5 is a count against the concepts the thesis actually claims and not against the claim it abandoned'; each half coded a second time without sight of its first codes (3.4).
Figure 3.2 draws the sequence (3.4).
entries.why: 'Each coding was made to test the one before it' (3.4). The second was made 'to test what the first had produced before anything was built on it'; the third so that counts are against the concepts actually claimed (3.4). 'A framework that emerged in that order can be shown to have emerged, and one that had been imposed could not' (1.6). The guide's headings were not used for the second coding 'because the guide's four headings were the hypothesis the data had already overturned, and coding the transcripts under them would have measured the hypothesis rather than the data' (3.4).
entries.not_this: Coding once, or coding under the guide's headings throughout (rejected, 3.4).
entries.analogy: Drafting a map, sending a second surveyor out with the draft to find where it is wrong, then sending a third with the corrected map to count what lies where.

viva_questions.q: Why three codings rather than one?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because each tested the one before. The first, under the pillars, broke them and produced a working claim. The second tested that claim, and two clauses, brand and size, fell while overlap and the boundary of sharing appeared. The third coded every transcript against the rewritten codebook, so every count is against what I actually claim, not the claim I abandoned (3.4).

viva_questions.q: Isn't rewriting the codebook from the second coding's results circular?
viva_questions.model_answer: The third coding counts against concepts the second coding found, yes; that is the point, so that the counts are against what the thesis claims. The check against the coding itself is the second, blind reading of each half, which agreed on 112 of 130 stances, and every difference is listed (3.4; Table 3.6).

viva_questions.q: When was the second coding done, and against what?
viva_questions.model_answer: In September 2026, against the working claim of 2026, not against Table 3.5, on pseudonymised transcripts, in two halves, each read in full without the first coding's notes (3.4).

quiz.q: What was the second coding built to test?
options: The working claim written from the first coding
quiz.explanation: 'It was that claim, not Table 3.5, which the second coding was built to test' (3.4).

quiz.q: Which two regularities did the second coding produce that the claim had not named?
options: Overlap and the boundary of sharing
quiz.explanation: Brand and size were the clauses it did not sustain (3.4).

beats.narration: The same twenty-six transcripts were coded three times. Each coding tested the one before.
beats.on_screen: Twenty-six stylised pages in a fan; three coloured highlighters waiting.

beats.narration: First, under the four pillars the interviews were designed around. The pillars broke.
beats.on_screen: Four columns labelled by icons (handshake, gauge, bulb, leaf) crack and tilt.

beats.narration: From that reading came a working claim: brand, size, substitutes for trust, power, time.
beats.on_screen: Five small cards drop onto the table.

beats.narration: Second, the claim was tested without the first coding's notes. Brand and size fell.
beats.on_screen: Two cards flip face down; two new cards rise: overlapping circles and a dividing line.

beats.narration: Third, every transcript was coded against the rewritten codebook, and each half read twice.
beats.on_screen: Pages pass under a lamp twice; ticks appear in a grid.

beats.narration: So every count is against what the thesis claims, not what it abandoned.
beats.on_screen: The grid settles into five tidy columns.

entries.term: Codebook coding and the codebook of Table 3.5
entries.plain: Coding text against a written codebook that defines each code and says exactly when a passage counts for or against it, so a second reader can apply the same rules.
in_this_thesis: The second coding was 'a codebook coding of the kind Miles, Huberman and Saldaña (2014) describe' (3.4).

Table 3.5, the transcript codebook, gives five concepts, each with a definition, a SUPPORTS-when rule, a CONTRADICTS-when rule and an example: overlap; the boundary of sharing; what binds; where the power sits; time (3.4).

Example rules: overlap SUPPORTS when 'willingness is explained by the presence or absence of overlap' and CONTRADICTS when 'size or brand explains willingness regardless of overlap, or rivals for the same customers collaborate without a binder'; what binds CONTRADICTS when 'peer trust alone' sustains a working arrangement (Table 3.5).

Terms fixed alongside it: a binder is 'whatever holds an arrangement together once it is formed and does not depend on the goodwill of the parties'; a reciprocal hostage (Williamson, 1983); a gain-share (3.4).
The transcripts stay coded for time as Table 3.5 defines it, though the fifth link now rests on the holder (3.4).
The 117 arrangements were coded against a second codebook, in versions 2 and 3 (Appendix L) (3.4).
entries.why: Codebook work allows the agreement check O'Connor and Joffe (2020) recommend (3.4). The second coding was a codebook coding 'made to test what the first had produced before anything was built on it' (3.4).
entries.not_this: Open, uncodified coding, which is what the first coding under the pillars was (3.4).
entries.analogy: A marking scheme for an exam: it says what earns the mark and what loses it, so two examiners can mark the same script independently.

viva_questions.q: Why are the transcripts still coded for time when the fifth link is now the holder?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because the counts of Chapters 4 and 5 were made against that definition. The holder was coded afterwards, in the 117 arrangements, against a separate codebook (3.4; 2.7).

viva_questions.q: What would make a transcript contradict the overlap concept?
viva_questions.model_answer: If size or brand explained willingness regardless of overlap, or if rivals for the same customers collaborated without a binder; Table 3.5 states both (Table 3.5).

quiz.q: How many concepts does the transcript codebook of Table 3.5 hold?
quiz.explanation: Overlap, the boundary of sharing, what binds, where the power sits, time (Table 3.5).

quiz.q: In 3.4, what is a binder?
options: The party that holds the shared point
The party that began the arrangement
Whatever holds an arrangement together once formed and does not depend on the parties' goodwill
quiz.explanation: The holder is a separate role (4.4).

entries.term: Negative case analysis (evidence against, required)
entries.plain: Deliberately looking for, and recording, the cases that go against your emerging explanation, rather than only the ones that fit.
in_this_thesis: The second coding 'was required to record, for every clause of it and every transcript, a stance, the exact words and their place in the transcript, and the evidence against as well as for, which is the negative case analysis Lincoln and Guba (1985) ask of a qualitative reading, built into the coding protocol rather than left to the reader's conscience' (3.4).
'Disconfirming evidence was required of both codings, so that the counts in Chapter 4 report what cut against the chain ... as well as what supported it' (3.7).
Under critical realism 'the interviews were searched as carefully for evidence against the mechanism as for evidence for it' (3.1).

Examples reported: three accounts that cut against the substitution (B11, A2, B9) set out in 4.4; one transcript contradicting overlap, from outside the last mile (7.1); brand counted as declined (3.4).
entries.why: It is what Lincoln and Guba ask of a qualitative reading (3.4) and what retroduction needs: a mechanism 'tested against the cases that should break it' (3.1).
entries.not_this: Leaving disconfirmation 'to the reader's conscience' (3.4).
entries.analogy: A building inspector who must sign off a list of every crack found, not just a certificate that the walls look fine.

viva_questions.q: How did you make sure you looked for evidence against yourself?
viva_questions.model_answer: It was built into the protocol: for every clause and every transcript the coding had to record the evidence against as well as for, the negative case analysis Lincoln and Guba ask for. So the counts report what cut against the chain, and 4.4 sets out the three accounts that cut against the substitution (3.4; 3.7; 4.4).

viva_questions.q: Name one case that cut against you.
viva_questions.model_answer: The founding co-operative is peer trust pure, and it is the case that dissolved (B9); two distribution directors who played golf together sustained a back-haul between rivals (A2), which is personal trust, though it also sat inside a trade body. None of the three was coded as contradicting; in each, the same account also names a binder from outside, and 4.4 sets that out (4.4).

quiz.q: Whose call for negative case analysis does 3.4 cite?
Where was negative case analysis built in?
options: Into the coding protocol of the second coding
quiz.explanation: 'Rather than left to the reader's conscience' (3.4).

story_refs: EQ ch4: Tell me about the one transcript that contradicts overlap.

entries.term: Coding in two halves (A1 to A13 and B1 to B13)
entries.plain: Splitting the transcripts into two sets and coding each separately, so a misreading in one set is less likely to spread to the whole.
in_this_thesis: The codes A1 to A13 and B1 to B13 follow the order the transcripts were filed and divided into two halves (3.3).
The second coding read each half in full against the working claim, separately (3.4).
The third coding was 'again made in two halves of thirteen transcripts each'; 'because the two halves are different transcripts, their counts are summed, not compared' (3.4).
Each half was then coded a second time for the agreement check: A half 53 of 65, B half 59 of 65 (3.4; Table 3.6).
entries.why: In the second coding, 'the halves were coded separately so that a systematic misreading in either would show as a difference between the halves' (3.4).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Two bakers each making half the batch from the same recipe: if one loaf tastes off, you know which half to check.

viva_questions.q: Why split the transcripts into halves?
viva_questions.model_answer: So that a systematic misreading in either would show as a difference between the halves. In the third coding the halves' counts are summed, not compared, because they are different transcripts; the check on the coding itself is the second, blind reading of each half (3.4).

viva_questions.q: If the halves are different transcripts, how would a difference between them reveal a misreading?
viva_questions.model_answer: The thesis gives that reason for the second coding and, for the third, sums the halves rather than comparing them. The check I rest on is within each half: each was coded twice, blind, and agreed on 53 of 65 and 59 of 65 stances, with every difference listed (3.4; Table 3.6).

quiz.q: In the third coding, how are the two halves' counts combined?
options: Only the B half is used
quiz.explanation: Because the two halves are different transcripts (3.4).

quiz.q: What did the A half's two readings agree on?
quiz.explanation: 59 of 65 is the B half; 112 of 130 the total (Table 3.6).

entries.gap: The thesis says the halves were split so a misreading would show as a difference between them, but in the third coding the halves are summed, not compared, and it does not say how a real difference between two sets of transcripts would be told apart from a misreading.

entries.term: The second reading, blind to the first
entries.plain: Coding the same material a second time without seeing the first set of codes, then comparing the two, to check that the codebook can be applied consistently.
in_this_thesis: The third coding's check was 'the agreement that O'Connor and Joffe (2020) recommend for codebook work, obtained by coding each half a second time against the same codebook without sight of its first codes' (3.4).
'Each coding of a half was made from the transcripts and Table 3.5 alone, to the author's written criteria of 3.2' (3.4).
Result: 112 of 130 stances read the same way twice, 86 per cent; A half 53 of 65, B half 59 of 65 (3.4; Table 3.6).
The eighteen differences fall on twelve transcripts; five of the eighteen on two transcripts, B8 and B10 (Table 3.6 note).
'Where the readings differed Chapter 4 gives both': Table 4.9 for the first four concepts, Chapter 5 for time (3.4; 4.1).

The second reading moved numbers at the margins, not their direction: overlap 15 to 12 supporting (mixed 5 to 7); boundary 16 to 21 (mixed 6 to 2); binds 24 to 25; power 18 to 16 (mixed 5 to 8); time 5 to 6 (4.1).
entries.why: It is the agreement O'Connor and Joffe recommend for codebook work (3.4); it is also part of the answer to the exposure 'that the author interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim the later codings tested' (3.7).
entries.not_this: A chance-corrected coefficient for this check (see raw agreement).
entries.analogy: Re-marking a pile of essays a month later with the first marks hidden, then laying both sets of marks side by side.

viva_questions.q: What changed when each half was read a second time?
viva_questions.model_answer: The numbers moved at the margins but not their direction. Overlap went from fifteen supporting to twelve, with mixed rising from five to seven; the boundary from sixteen to twenty-one; what binds from twenty-four to twenty-five; power from eighteen to sixteen; time from five to six. Wherever the readings differ, Chapter 4 gives both (4.1; Table 4.9).

viva_questions.q: Who made the second reading?
viva_questions.model_answer: Each reading of a half was made from the transcripts and Table 3.5 alone, without sight of the other reading's codes, to my written criteria, and every decision was logged and checked by me (3.4; 3.2).

quiz.q: After the second reading, how many transcripts supported overlap?
quiz.explanation: Fifteen in the first reading; twenty-one and sixteen are the boundary's (4.1).

quiz.q: On which two transcripts do five of the eighteen differences fall?
quiz.explanation: B8 fits neither pole cleanly; both readings placed B10 outside the domain (Table 3.6 note).

beats.narration: A codebook is only useful if it gives the same answer twice.
beats.on_screen: One transcript page and a closed codebook on a desk.

beats.narration: Each half was coded, then coded again with the first codes hidden.
beats.on_screen: A sheet of ticks slides under a cover; a fresh sheet is filled beside it.

beats.narration: Then the two readings were laid side by side.
beats.on_screen: The cover lifts; two grids of ticks align.

beats.narration: They matched on 112 of 130 stances.
beats.on_screen: Most cells glow; eighteen cells blink.

beats.narration: Every one of the eighteen differences is listed, and both readings reported.
beats.on_screen: Each blinking cell drops into a short list, both marks shown.

entries.gap: The thesis does not name who made each reading; it says each was made from the transcripts and the codebook alone, to the author's written criteria, and checked by the author. Answer in those words.

entries.term: Intercoder agreement as raw agreement (112 of 130)
entries.plain: Raw agreement is the simple share of decisions on which two codings match. Unlike some measures, it does not adjust for matches that would happen by chance.
in_this_thesis: 'Over the twenty-six, 112 of 130 stances were read the same way twice, an agreement of eighty-six per cent' (3.4). 130 = 26 transcripts x 5 concepts.
By concept (Table 3.6): overlap 20 of 26; boundary 20; what binds 25; power 22; time 25.
By half: A1 to A13, 53 of 65; B1 to B13, 59 of 65 (Table 3.6).

The largest share of the A half's differences, five of twelve, falls on the boundary concept, 'where freight or operating data pooled under a binder can be read as crossing the line or as held at it'; every such difference runs the same way, so 'the two readings agree on the facts and differ on one rule' (3.4; Table 3.6 note).
A transcript counts as agreement when both readings give the same stance; qualifiers such as 'weak' or 'qualified' do not count as disagreement (Table 3.6).
entries.why: 'The figure is reported as raw agreement and not as a chance-corrected coefficient, because with four possible stances, thirteen transcripts to a half and a fifth concept, time, on which most transcripts are silent, a coefficient would say less than the list of the eighteen differences themselves, which Table 3.6 gives by concept and by half and the paragraph beneath it by transcript' (3.4).
entries.not_this: A chance-corrected coefficient such as Krippendorff's alpha, used instead for the 117 arrangements (3.4).
entries.analogy: Two referees reviewing the same match footage: you could compute a statistic, but with few calls it is clearer to list the eighteen they disagreed on.

viva_questions.q: Eighty-six per cent raw agreement doesn't correct for chance. Why should I trust it?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because with four possible stances, thirteen transcripts to a half and a fifth concept on which most transcripts are silent, a coefficient would say less than the list of the eighteen differences, which I give by concept, by half and by transcript. And on the boundary, where most differences fall, the two readings agree on the facts and differ on one rule, which Chapter 4 reports both ways (3.4; Table 3.6).

viva_questions.q: Where do the readings disagree most?
viva_questions.model_answer: On overlap and the boundary, twenty of twenty-six each. In the A half, five of twelve differences fall on the boundary, all the same way: the first reading counted freight or data pooled under a binder as mixed, the second as satisfying the concept (Table 3.6; 3.4).

quiz.q: Why is the transcript agreement reported as raw agreement?
options: With four stances, thirteen transcripts a half and a mostly silent fifth concept, a coefficient would say less than listing the differences
Krippendorff's alpha cannot be computed for text

quiz.q: On which concepts did the two readings agree on 25 of 26 transcripts?
quiz.explanation: Overlap 20, boundary 20, binds 25, power 22, time 25 (Table 3.6).

entries.term: Krippendorff's alpha
entries.plain: A measure of how far two codings agree beyond what chance alone would produce. 1 means perfect agreement; 0 means no better than chance.
in_this_thesis: Used for the 117 arrangements 'because there the unit is the arrangement, the cases number 117 and the codes are nominal', against Krippendorff's bar of '.800 for firm conclusions and .667 for tentative ones (2004, p. 241)' (3.4).

Codebook version 2: market commonality .84, footprint .84, outcome .87 (firm); the wall .76 (tentative); the penalty .54 over all 117, though the passes never disagree on it among rivals not far from the customer; stage of the chain .59, volume of flows .55, what crosses .65 (below the tentative bar) (3.4).

Version 3: holder's class .88; rivalry among co-users .85; whether the holder sells delivery .87 over all 117, 'partly built in because rival and joint holders sell by definition', and .72 (tentative) on the helper rows; the derived neutral holder .84 (3.4).
The initiator, re-checked in both passes of October 2026: 98 of 117 rows, alpha .80 (3.4).

Elsewhere: the re-run of the 2023 full-text stage, thirty of thirty-one on subject, alpha .91 (3.2); the locker owners, .87 on class and .81 on neutral against rival-held, over forty-seven ownership periods (3.5).
entries.why: Unit is the arrangement, 117 cases, nominal codes (3.4).
entries.not_this: Raw agreement, used for the transcripts (3.4); Cohen's kappa, used for the survey's open answers (3.6).
entries.analogy: Two people guessing coin tosses will agree half the time by luck; alpha only gives credit for agreement beyond that luck.

viva_questions.q: Several of your version 2 variables fall below .667. What follows?
viva_questions.model_answer: I report them as they fell. The penalty is .54 over all 117, though the passes never disagree on it among rivals not far from the customer, the rows that matter; stage of the chain, volume and what crosses fall below too. Every disagreement was listed, the rows where a difference changes a result isolated, and each settled against the codebook with its reason recorded (3.4).

viva_questions.q: Your 'holder sells delivery' alpha is .87. Isn't that flattered?
viva_questions.model_answer: Partly, and I say so: it is partly built in because rival and joint holders sell by definition. On the helper rows, where the code carries information, it is .72, tentative (3.4).

quiz.q: What alpha does Krippendorff set for firm conclusions?
quiz.explanation: .667 is the bar for tentative conclusions (Krippendorff, 2004, p. 241).

quiz.q: What was the alpha for the holder's class in codebook version 3?
quiz.explanation: .76 is the wall (v2), .54 the penalty (v2), .72 'sells delivery' on helper rows (3.4).

quiz.q: Why is alpha used for the arrangements but not the transcripts?
options: Alpha only works on survey data
The unit is the arrangement, the cases number 117 and the codes are nominal

entries.term: Directed content analysis (the 117 arrangements)
entries.plain: Coding text against categories fixed in advance from a theory, with a written rule for each value, rather than letting categories emerge from the reading.
in_this_thesis: 'The 117 arrangements were coded again in October 2026, for the fifth link, by directed content analysis (Hsieh and Shannon, 2005)' (3.4).
'A written codebook fixed the values and the decision rule for each variable, and each code was taken from the row of Appendix H and its passage in the transcript, with the quotation recorded' (3.4).
The codebook ran in versions 1 to 3, piloted and coded twice (see codebook versions) (3.4; Appendix L).
The aim in 4.4: 'so that what binds an arrangement could be set against the refusal of 4.2 on the same rows' (4.4).
entries.why: The thesis says what the coding was for (the fifth link, and setting what binds against the refusal on the same rows, 4.4) but does not say why the directed form was chosen over other forms of content analysis.
entries.not_this: The thematic and codebook codings of the transcripts, which are a different exercise on a different unit (3.4).
entries.analogy: Filling in a standard inspection form for every building on a street: the boxes are fixed in advance, and each tick must point to what the inspector saw.

viva_questions.q: Why directed content analysis for the arrangements?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because by October 2026 the variables were set by the fifth link: who holds the shared point, whether it sells delivery, whether co-users are rivals, beside the wall, the penalty and the flows. A written codebook fixed the values and the decision rule for each, and every code was taken from the row and its transcript passage with the quotation recorded. The thesis doesn't argue the directed form against other forms of content analysis (3.4).

viva_questions.q: What did each code rest on?
viva_questions.model_answer: On the row of Appendix H and its passage in the transcript, with the quotation recorded, so each code can be traced to the words it came from (3.4).

quiz.q: Whose account of directed content analysis does 3.4 cite?
quiz.explanation: Braun and Clarke is thematic analysis; Miles and colleagues the codebook coding; Bowen document analysis.

quiz.q: When were the 117 arrangements coded by directed content analysis?

entries.gap: Why directed content analysis rather than another form is not stated.

entries.term: Codebook versions 1 to 3, the pilot, and settling disagreements
entries.plain: Writing the coding rules, trying them on a few cases, revising them, then coding everything twice and resolving every disagreement against the written rules.
in_this_thesis: Version 1 was piloted on ten rows coded independently twice; 'the two codings raised the same problems and seven changes followed', giving version 2 (3.4).

Version 2 records for each arrangement the parties' market commonality and footprint, the stage of the chain they share, where the saving comes from, the volume of the flows, what crosses between them, the wall that keeps them apart, any penalty for staying out, and the outcome; all 117 rows coded twice, in two passes (3.4).
In version 2 the wall counted a trustee and a helper's position among its values; version 3 'moved both to the holder of the shared point' (3.4).

Version 3 records the class of whoever controls the point where the parties' parcels, data or customer contact meet (receiver, no-stake third party, helper, public body, rival party or joint holder), whether that holder sells delivery to the parties' customers, and whether its co-users are rivals; piloted on the same ten rows, extended by eleven rules, and coded twice over all 117, 'each pass made from Appendix H and the transcripts without sight of the earlier codes or of the other pass' (3.4).
Settlement: 'Every disagreement was listed, the rows on which a difference changes a result were isolated, and each was settled against the codebook with its reason recorded' (3.4).
'Each change to the codebook is dated in Appendix L, and where a change alters a result both results are reported'; Chapter 4 reports the two versions side by side (3.4).
entries.why: Version 3 separates the holder from the wall 'so that a neutral third party is a binder in Table 3.5 and, where it controls the point at which the parties meet, a holder in version 3' (3.4). The pilot exists to find problems before the full coding (3.4).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Testing a new form on ten customers, fixing the confusing questions, then giving it to everyone, with two clerks entering each form separately and a supervisor resolving every mismatch against the instructions.

viva_questions.q: Why did you need a third version of the codebook?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because in version 2 the wall counted a trustee and a helper's position among its values, which mixed two roles. Version 3 moved both to the holder of the shared point, so a neutral third party is a binder in Table 3.5 and, where it controls the point the parties meet at, a holder. Chapter 4 reports both versions side by side (3.4).

viva_questions.q: How were disagreements between passes resolved?
viva_questions.model_answer: Every disagreement was listed, the rows where a difference changes a result were isolated, and each was settled against the codebook with its reason recorded. Every change to the codebook is dated in Appendix L, and where a change alters a result, both results are reported (3.4).

quiz.q: How many rows were used to pilot the arrangement codebook?
quiz.explanation: Version 1 was piloted on ten rows coded independently twice; seven changes followed (3.4).

quiz.q: What did version 3 separate from the wall?
options: The holder of the shared point

quiz.q: How many rules was version 3 extended by after its pilot?
quiz.explanation: Seven is the number of changes after version 1's pilot (3.4).

entries.term: Scott's four tests for documents: authenticity, credibility, representativeness, meaning
entries.plain: Four questions to ask of any document used as evidence: is it genuine, is it believable for the use made of it, is it typical of what it stands for, and is its meaning understood correctly.
in_this_thesis: 'Read as documents, they pass the four tests Scott (1990) sets, and the passing is stated because it bounds the use made of them' (3.5).
Authentic: 'the city's own plans, published under its name, held as the PDFs from which Appendix J reproduces the extracts used'.
Credible 'for the use made of them, which is as the regime's statement of what it allocates and what it expected, not as evidence of what happened on the street'.
Representative 'of the regime's written record and not of the regime, since the permit register and the enforcement records were not read, which 3.7 carries as a limit'.
Meaning: held to the Dutch by translating only the extracts used and setting the Dutch beside the English in Appendix J (Temple and Young, 2004).
The rules read for the holder 'pass Scott's tests as the Ghent plans do, as the issuing bodies' own texts and as statements of the rule rather than of its working' (3.5).
entries.why: 'The passing is stated because it bounds the use made of them' (3.5).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Checking a will: is it genuine, is it the testator's considered wish, is it the latest version, and do we read its old-fashioned wording correctly.

viva_questions.q: How did you judge the Ghent documents as evidence?
viva_questions.model_answer: Against Scott's four tests. They are authentic, the city's own plans under its name; credible for the use I make of them, as the regime's statement of what it allocates and expected, not of what happened on the street; representative of the written record, not the regime, because I didn't read the permit register; and their meaning is held to the Dutch, with the Dutch beside every English rendering in Appendix J (3.5).

viva_questions.q: The plans represent the city's written record, not the regime itself. What does that cost you?
viva_questions.model_answer: It means I know the regime as the city states it, not as the street lives it. The permit register and enforcement records weren't read, and 3.7 and 7.4 carry that as a limit (3.5; 7.4).

quiz.q: For what use are the Ghent plans called credible?
options: As evidence of what happened on the street
As a count of deliveries by window
As the regime's statement of what it allocates and what it expected

quiz.q: Why are the plans representative of the record but not of the regime?
options: The permit register and enforcement records were not read

entries.term: Translation and checking the Dutch extracts
entries.plain: When evidence is in another language, making each translation checkable: translating only what is used, checking it several ways, and printing the original beside it.
in_this_thesis: Both Ghent documents are in Dutch; only the extracts used were translated (3.5).

'Each rendering was made for this thesis and checked by the author against the Dutch original, against a second translation made independently of the first, and against a dictionary; no Dutch speaker checked them, which 7.4 carries as a limit' (3.5).
Appendix J sets the Dutch beside the English, 'so that the reader, not the author, has the last word on each' (7.4).
The survey's four open answers in Spanish, French, German and Italian were rendered into English, and Appendix K sets each original beside its rendering (3.6).
entries.why: Meaning 'was held to the Dutch by translating only the extracts used and setting the Dutch beside the English in Appendix J so that a reader can check each rendering, which is the practice Temple and Young (2004) ask of research that crosses a language' (3.5).
entries.not_this: Checking by a Dutch-speaking reader, not done and stated as a limit (7.4).
entries.analogy: A bilingual menu: the original dish name sits beside the translation, so anyone who reads both can catch a mistake.

viva_questions.q: You don't speak Dutch. How can I trust your renderings?
viva_questions.model_answer: Each was checked against the Dutch original, against a second translation made independently of the first, and against a dictionary. No Dutch speaker checked them, and I carry that as a limit. That's why Appendix J sets the Dutch beside every rendering, so the reader, not me, has the last word (3.5; 7.4).

viva_questions.q: Did you translate the whole of both plans?
viva_questions.model_answer: No, only the extracts used, which keeps every rendering checkable against its original in Appendix J; that is Temple and Young's practice for research that crosses a language (3.5).

quiz.q: Which check was NOT applied to the Dutch renderings?
quiz.explanation: Stated as a limit in 7.4.

quiz.q: Where can the Dutch and English be read side by side?
quiz.explanation: Appendix K does the same for the survey's open answers (3.5; 3.6).

entries.term: The survey: a self-administered web questionnaire, read for scale
entries.plain: A questionnaire people fill in themselves online. Here it describes how common certain views and practices are among respondents; it does not test the thesis's links.
in_this_thesis: 'A self-administered web questionnaire of the kind Dillman, Smyth and Christian (2014) describe, a Google Form titled ‘Horizontal Collaboration in Urban Logistics’' (3.6).

Created 22 February 2024, the day the study was approved; first response that day, last on 30 April 2025; of 132 responses, 36 arrived before July 2024, 37 during the interviews (July to September 2024) and 59 from October 2024 to April 2025 (3.6).

The questions are the author's own, built on the four pillars; they 'ask what the interview guide asked, not what the interviews went on to find': nothing on market overlap, on what is pooled and withheld, on who can change how deliveries run, or on hours set by a city (3.6).

The draft of 19 February 2024 went to the ethics committee (Appendix C.4); the supervisors approved the final questions; the final form keeps the draft's thirteen questions in order and largely in its words, adds a consent item, and revises some answer lists (3.6).
Table 3.7 gives every item in the words respondents saw, its answer form and the number answering (3.6).
It records 'what organisations say matters and what they say they use, which is report and not observed conduct' (3.6).
entries.why: 'This thesis uses it for scale' (3.6); it is 'used here to give scale to what the interviews heard of trust, not to measure the industry' (3.6). It asks about the pillars because it opened on the day of approval on the draft's questions, before the interviews produced the links (3.8, change 2).
entries.not_this: The survey the ethics application planned: built on the qualitative phase's findings and analysed by correlation and regression (3.8; Appendix C.1).
entries.analogy: A show of hands at a trade conference: it tells you what the room says, not what each firm actually does back at the depot.

viva_questions.q: What does the survey add?
viva_questions.model_answer: Scale and a contrast. It asked through the four pillars, so it tests no link. It shows what organisations say about trust beside what they report using to keep it: 89 of 119 rate trust at 4 or 5, and among the 45 who named their means, formal contracts, third-party coordination and public authority support stand beside joint planning. And 36 of 109 collaborate now (5.3; 3.6).

viva_questions.q: Why wasn't the survey built on your five links?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because it opened on the day of approval, 22 February 2024, on the draft's questions as the supervisors approved them, before the interviews produced the links. I record that as change 2 in Table 3.8 and read the survey for scale only (3.6; 3.8).

quiz.q: Over what period did the survey run?
quiz.explanation: It opened before the interviews, ran through them and went on after (3.6).

quiz.q: Which of these did the survey NOT ask?
options: Whether a company's partners serve the same customers in the same place
quiz.explanation: It put no question on overlap (3.6).

story_refs: EQ ch3: Your survey asks about the four pillars, not your links. Why include it?

entries.term: Self-selected, non-probability sample (no response rate)
entries.plain: A sample in which people chose to respond after seeing a link, rather than being drawn at random from a known list. It cannot represent a wider population, and no response rate can be calculated.
in_this_thesis: Population: organisations in urban logistics of the kinds 1.1 admits; 'No register of them exists and none was drawn on' (3.6).

The link was shared on LinkedIn; by email to industry contacts; with the interview participants and through them their networks; through GREEN-LOG and other project networks; on the Universities' Transport Study Group email list; at events; and with research contacts (3.6).
'The respondents are therefore a non-probability sample that selected itself', with the referral-chain bias Biernacki and Waldorf (1981) name (3.6).
Some respondents may be among the thirty interviewed; the form asked for no name, so the overlap cannot be counted, and 'the survey is not a sample independent of the interviews' (3.6).
'No response rate can be computed, since no one knows how many saw the link, and none is claimed' (3.6).
The questionnaire did not ask for a country; four open answers were in Spanish, French, German and Italian; the eleven countries are not claimed for the respondents (3.6).
entries.why: The thesis does not give a reason for distributing this way; it states the consequences (3.6).
entries.not_this: A probability sample from a register, impossible because no register exists (3.6).
entries.analogy: A suggestion box at a conference: useful to hear what people say, but you can't tell how many walked past without writing anything.

viva_questions.q: What's your survey's response rate?
viva_questions.model_answer: None can be computed and none is claimed, because nobody knows how many saw the link. The sample selected itself through LinkedIn, email, the interview participants and their networks, project networks including GREEN-LOG, the UTSG list and events, so it's a non-probability sample with the referral-chain bias Biernacki and Waldorf name (3.6).

viva_questions.q: Could your survey respondents include your interviewees?
viva_questions.model_answer: Possibly. The link went to interview participants while they were being interviewed, and the form asked for no name, so the overlap can't be counted. The survey is not a sample independent of the interviews, and I say so (3.6).

quiz.q: Why can no response rate be computed?
options: No one knows how many saw the link

quiz.q: Which of these did the questionnaire NOT ask for?
quiz.explanation: So the respondents cannot be placed by country (3.6).

entries.term: Piloting (what was piloted and what was not)
entries.plain: Trying an instrument on a small number of cases first, to find problems before using it in full.
in_this_thesis: Arrangement codebook version 1: 'a pilot on ten rows coded independently twice, in which the two codings raised the same problems and seven changes followed' (3.4).
Version 3: 'piloted on the same ten rows, extended by eleven rules' (3.4).

The survey: 'It was not piloted' (3.6); 'two irregularities a pilot might have caught are in the record: the skip after the question on present collaboration was not applied, and the durations recorded run from ‘1-3 years’ to ‘More than 5 years’ with nothing between' (3.6).

The interview guide: built in the sequence Kallio and colleagues (2016) describe, from prerequisites to a preliminary guide and its complete form, and its final questions approved by the supervisory team (3.3); the thesis does not describe a pilot interview.
entries.why: The pilots of the codebook found problems that led to changes (3.4). The thesis does not say why the survey was not piloted.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A dress rehearsal: the codebook had two, the survey went on stage without one, and the programme notes say what went wrong.

viva_questions.q: Was the survey piloted?
viva_questions.model_answer: No. I name the two irregularities a pilot might have caught: the skip after the question on present collaboration wasn't applied, and the durations jump from '1-3 years' to 'More than 5 years'. Both are reported as they stand (3.6).

viva_questions.q: Was your interview guide piloted?
viva_questions.model_answer: The guide was built in the sequence Kallio and colleagues describe, from prerequisites and prior knowledge to a preliminary guide and its complete form, and the supervisory team approved the final questions before data collection. The thesis doesn't describe a pilot interview (3.3).

quiz.q: Which instrument was piloted on ten rows?
What followed the first pilot of the arrangement codebook?
quiz.explanation: Eleven rules extended version 3 after its pilot (3.4).

entries.gap: Whether the interview guide was piloted is not stated; why the survey was not piloted is not stated.

entries.term: Quality in qualitative research: credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability
entries.plain: The qualitative counterparts of validity and reliability: is the account believable (credibility), can a reader judge where it applies (transferability), could the trail be followed (dependability), and does it rest on the data rather than the researcher (confirmability).
in_this_thesis: 'Four questions are commonly put to qualitative work of this kind, credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability (Lincoln and Guba, 1985), and each is answered here with what was done' (3.7).

Credibility: three codings, the last two from the transcripts alone without the first coding's notes; each half read twice in the third coding, the second blind, agreeing on 112 of 130; every quotation verified against its transcript; disconfirming evidence required of both codings (3.7).

Transferability: eleven countries and the kinds of party the question needed, each described 'thickly enough, in Geertz's sense (1973), by code and by type, for a reader to judge where the findings travel' (3.7).

Dependability: every screening decision and card logged in Appendices E and H; every coded stance in Appendix I; the codes of the 117 and their settlements in Appendix L; the locker networks and test runs in Appendix M; every claim of the fifth link traced in a register Appendix O describes (3.7).
The register: 'Every claim the fifth link makes was entered in a register with its evidence, the source and page or the data file and row, and the step of the argument it supports' (3.5).
Confirmability: 'the coding's cautions (3.4) are carried into the text as written' (3.7).
The word 'validity' appears once, in Maxwell's interactive model (3.8); the thesis frames quality in Lincoln and Guba's terms.
entries.why: They are the questions 'commonly put to qualitative work of this kind' (3.7).
entries.not_this: Positivist validity and reliability are not used as the frame (3.7). Member checking (returning findings to participants) is not mentioned.
entries.analogy: A food hygiene inspection with four headings: is it safe, could it be served elsewhere, are the records kept, and is the kitchen judged on its own state rather than the chef's word.

viva_questions.q: How do you establish validity?
viva_questions.model_answer: I answer Lincoln and Guba's four questions. Credibility: three codings, the last two from the transcripts alone, each half read twice blind, 112 of 130, every quotation verified, evidence against required. Transferability: eleven countries and the kinds of party described thickly enough for a reader to judge where findings travel. Dependability: every decision logged in Appendices E, H, I, L and M, and the register of Appendix O. Confirmability: the coding's cautions carried into the text as written (3.7).

viva_questions.q: What is the register?
viva_questions.model_answer: Every claim the fifth link makes was entered with its evidence, the source and page or the data file and row, and the step of the argument it supports, so each claim can be traced. I hold it, and Appendix O describes it (3.5; 3.7).

viva_questions.q: Did you take your findings back to participants?
viva_questions.model_answer: The thesis doesn't describe member checking. Its credibility rests on the three codings, the blind second reading, verifying every quotation against its transcript and requiring the evidence against (3.7).

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Lincoln and Guba's four criteria as 3.7 applies them?
quiz.explanation: The fourth is transferability (3.7).

quiz.q: How does 3.7 answer confirmability?
options: The coding's cautions are carried into the text as written
A Dutch speaker checked the translations

entries.gap: Member checking is not mentioned, and the full register and systematised-review log are held by the author rather than appended.

entries.term: Reflexivity (six objects)
entries.plain: The researcher's continual examination of how they themselves shaped what they found, and what they did about it.
in_this_thesis: Reflexivity 'in Finlay's sense (2002) of the researcher's continual examination of how they shaped what they found, has six objects here' (3.7).
1: the 2023 review, whose string reproduced the field's blind spot until the corrected strings exposed it.
2: the framework of 2024, built on the four pillars, which the data overturned; 'the guide asked about trust because the field did'.
3: the theme the interviewer seeded: brand, raised in five interviews, declined in all five, counted as declined.
4: the positions relayed between interviews, so agreement across transcripts is partly the interviewer's doing; the second coding marked where it happened.
5: the author's first picture of the fifth link, hours allocated by a city to named companies, taken apart by his own questioning (Ostrom, 1990, p. 204; Stad Gent, 2016, p. 112).

6: GREEN-LOG: in 2023 the author spent six months on spatio-temporal demand prediction for another of its living labs (work package 2, task 2.2); the thesis draws on none of that work and cites the Athens living lab from its published evaluation (3.7; 1.6).

What was done about each 'is the method itself': string corrected and both trails kept; pillars made findings; seeded theme counted against; relayed positions marked; first picture tested and replaced (3.7).
'The exposure no procedure removes is that the author interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim the later codings tested' (3.7).
entries.why: Finlay (2002), as above; and in 1.6, the order of emergence is set out 'because a framework that came out of the data is a stronger claim to conceptualisation than one fixed before the data arrived, as long as the thesis shows how it came about'.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A referee reviewing footage of his own decisions, noting where his position on the pitch may have hidden a foul.

viva_questions.q: What are the objects of your reflexivity?
viva_questions.model_answer: Six: the 2023 review's string, which reproduced the field's blind spot; the four-pillar framework the data overturned; brand, which I seeded and which was declined in all five interviews; the positions I relayed between interviews; my own first picture of the fifth link, hours for named companies, which my questioning took apart; and my six months on GREEN-LOG, which the thesis draws on nowhere (3.7).

viva_questions.q: What exposure can't your procedures remove?
viva_questions.model_answer: That I interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim the later codings tested. My answer is the two later codings made without the first coding's notes, the blind second reading of every transcript, and the requirement of evidence against; 3.4 says how far that reaches (3.7).

quiz.q: In whose sense does 3.7 use reflexivity?
quiz.explanation: Geertz supplies thick description; Rose the design audit (3.7).

entries.term: Counting in a qualitative study
entries.plain: Qualitative studies can report counts to show how widely a pattern holds and where it does not, without treating the count as a statistical test.
in_this_thesis: 'The counts are used in the way Hannah and Lautsch (2011) allow a qualitative study to count, to show how widely a pattern holds across the set and where it does not, never as a test of it, and each is tied to the file and the row it came from' (3.4).
'Every count in Chapters 4 and 5 comes from those files and not from memory of them' (3.4).
Stances are counted by transcript, arrangements by row (3.4; 4.1).
'These are counts of rows of Appendix H, made from participants' accounts, not of measured deliveries' (4.4).
entries.why: Hannah and Lautsch (2011), as quoted (3.4).
entries.not_this: Counts as tests (3.4).
entries.analogy: A head gardener noting that blight appeared on eleven of twelve rows: a tally that shows how far the problem spread, not a laboratory trial.

viva_questions.q: You report counts and percentages. Isn't that quantitative?
viva_questions.model_answer: The counts show how widely a pattern holds across the set and where it doesn't, as Hannah and Lautsch allow a qualitative study to count, never as a test of it. Each is tied to the file and row it came from, and they are counts of participants' accounts, not of measured deliveries (3.4; 4.4).

viva_questions.q: How do I know a count wasn't made from memory?
viva_questions.model_answer: Every count in Chapters 4 and 5 comes from the coding files and Appendix H, not from memory of them, and every figure of the fifth link from the coding files, analysis outputs and locker tables of October 2026 (3.4).

quiz.q: Whose account of counting in qualitative research does 3.4 follow?
What are the counts of Appendix H rows counts of?

entries.term: Coding the binder and the initiator of each arrangement
entries.plain: For each arrangement, recording what held it together (the binder) and who started it (the initiator), as two separate codes.
in_this_thesis: Appendix H was built after the second coding by listing every collaboration a participant described, one row per description (3.4).

'Each row carries one binder and one initiator.' The binder is what, on the participant's account, held the arrangement once formed; a second binder is given in brackets and not counted; 'a party that only made the introduction or a rule that only supplied the occasion is not counted as a binder' (3.4).
The initiator is the party the participant said began the arrangement, coded apart from whoever holds it (3.4).
The ninety-five rows bound from outside (4.4) rest on the binder; the forty-two rows begun by a city or public body and the nineteen by a carrier (4.5) rest on the initiator (3.4).

Both were assigned once, by hand, in building the appendix. 'The binder was not coded a second time, so unlike the codes of October 2026 it carries no agreement figure'; the initiator was re-checked in both passes of October 2026, read the same way in 98 of 117 rows (alpha .80) (3.4; 3.7).
The A half's first listing recorded every mechanism a participant named, while the appendix gives one binder per row, so the two tallies differ and 4.4 gives both (3.4).
entries.why: The thesis says what was done and states the gap as a limit (3.7); it does not say why the binder was not coded a second time.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: For each marriage on a register, noting who proposed and what keeps it going, and keeping the two columns separate.

viva_questions.q: Your 95 of 117 rests on a code assigned once. How reliable is it?
viva_questions.model_answer: It carries no agreement figure, and I state that as a limit in 3.7. The binder was assigned once, by hand, from the participant's account, with clear rules: one binder per row, a second in brackets and not counted, and an introducer or a rule that only supplied the occasion not counted. The initiator, re-checked in both passes of October 2026, agreed in 98 of 117 rows, alpha .80 (3.4; 3.7).

viva_questions.q: Why keep the initiator separate from the holder?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because who began an arrangement and who controls the point where the parties meet are different roles. The initiator is coded apart from whoever holds it, and 4.4 shows the binder is not the holder either (3.4; 4.4).

quiz.q: Which of these carries no agreement figure?
quiz.explanation: The binder was assigned once; the initiator was re-checked, 98 of 117, alpha .80 (3.4).

quiz.q: How many of the 117 rows were begun by a city or public body?
quiz.explanation: Nineteen by a carrier; 95 is rows bound from outside; 35 the neutral-third-party binders in Table H.3 (3.4; 4.5).

entries.gap: Why the binder was not coded a second time is not stated; the limit is.

entries.term: Separating size from overlap: mirror pairs and the count by size
entries.plain: To show that overlap, not size, sorts willingness, you need cases where size is held steady and overlap changes, and a count showing willing and unwilling firms at every size.
in_this_thesis: Sub-objectives 1A and 1B ask how willingness varies with operator size and with market overlap; 'the fieldwork was built to separate' them (4.2; 1.3).
Mirror pairs: 'the cases in which the same firm, or the same kind of firm, said yes and no in the same breath, one answer for each side of the line'; ten are set out in Table 4.2 (4.2).
Example: the same small cargo-bike firm refused a rival in its own city and was piloting with one in another town: 'It's not their city. There's no market competition' (B9) (4.2).

The count by size across both halves (Table 4.3): 'Read down either half, willing and unwilling firms appear at every size; read beside the overlap column of Appendix H, the willing cases are those in which the parties do not compete for the same customers or, where they do, something outside them stands between them' (4.2).
Overlap as the condition of refusal: 15 for, 1 against, 5 mixed, 5 silent (third coding); 12/0/7/7 (second reading) (Table 4.9).
The survey cannot separate size from overlap, because it asked nothing about overlap (5.3; 3.6).
entries.why: The hypothesis carried into 2024 was size (the big fierce animal), and the twenty-six 'did not sustain it' (4.2). The codebook's falsifier for overlap is that 'size or brand explains willingness regardless of overlap' (Table 3.5).
entries.not_this: Size as the variable that sorts willingness (the author's 2022 idea, corrected) (1.6; 4.2).
entries.analogy: To show it is the weather, not the driver, that causes skids, find the same driver skidding on ice and not on a dry road.

viva_questions.q: How did you separate size from overlap with only twenty-six interviews?
viva_questions.model_answer: Two ways. Mirror pairs, ten of them, where the same firm or the same kind of firm says yes and no, and what differs is whether the parties want the same customers in the same place. And the count by size across both halves, where willing and unwilling firms appear at every size, the willing ones being those without overlap or with something outside binding them (4.2; Tables 4.2 and 4.3).

viva_questions.q: Your survey shows larger firms collaborate more. Doesn't that favour size?
viva_questions.model_answer: The survey asked nothing about overlap, so it cannot tell size from overlap, and it measures whether a firm collaborates at all, with anyone, anywhere. Link 1 concerns with whom and where, which the interviews answered. One reading consistent with them is that a large firm has more places where its partners are not its rivals, but the survey can't test it (5.3).
