entries.term: Crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (csQCA)
entries.plain: A method for comparing a modest number of cases as combinations of conditions. In the crisp-set form each condition is simply present or absent, and the analysis asks which conditions, or combinations, go with an outcome.
in_this_thesis: 'The settled codes were compared by crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (Ragin, 1987, 2008), which asks which conditions are present wherever an outcome is, and which combinations of them are followed by it wherever they occur' (3.4).
Thresholds 'at the conventional thresholds (Schneider and Wagemann, 2012)': a combination sufficient at a consistency of 0.8, the run repeated at 0.75 and 0.9; a condition necessary at 0.9 (3.4).
Rows tested: rivals not far from the customer (at the last leg, at the door or at no stage named): 22 in one replication and 21 in the other; outcome: running at interview (4.4).
With a wall or a penalty, running in 11 of 13 and 11 of 12; with neither, 3 of 8 and 2 of 8 (4.4).
Kept to rows where something that could expose customers, brand, data or freight crossed: 7 of 8 running with a wall or penalty against 1 of 6 with neither; 8 of 9 against 1 of 7 (4.4).
The one exception that runs: two bike couriers' joint bid (H.2 56), with no wall and no penalty (4.4).
Appendix L lists the minimised combinations found sufficient; the main text reports the running counts and the necessity result, not those combinations.
entries.why: The thesis does not say why it chose QCA, or the crisp-set form, for the 117; it says what the method asks (3.4).
entries.not_this: Regression is ruled out only for the locker test ('with so few periods no regression was run', 3.5); no alternative is named for the 117.
entries.analogy: A doctor reviewing a ward's charts as yes/no ticks (smoker, diabetic, over sixty) to see which ticks appear in every patient who recovered.

viva_questions.q: Why QCA?
viva_questions.model_answer: QCA asks which conditions are present wherever an outcome is, and which combinations are followed by it wherever they occur, which is the shape of my question about the arrangements: what is there whenever rivals near the customer keep running. The thesis states what the method asks and its conventional thresholds; it doesn't argue QCA against other methods (3.4).

viva_questions.q: What were your sufficient combinations?
viva_questions.model_answer: They are listed in Appendix L. In the main text I report the running counts, eleven of thirteen and eleven of twelve with a wall or a penalty against three of eight and two of eight with neither, and the necessity result (4.4; Appendix L).

viva_questions.q: What is the outcome in your QCA?
viva_questions.model_answer: Whether the arrangement was running at interview, among rows between rivals not far from the customer: twenty-two rows in one replication, twenty-one in the other (4.4).

quiz.q: What two questions does crisp-set QCA ask, as 3.4 puts it?

What each participant means by collaboration

quiz.explanation: 11 of 12 in the other; with neither, 3 of 8 and 2 of 8 (4.4).

entries.term: Necessary conditions, consistency and the 0.9 bar
entries.plain: A necessary condition is one that is present whenever the outcome occurs. Consistency is the share of outcome cases that have it; the thesis treats 0.9 (nine in ten) as the bar.
in_this_thesis: A condition is taken as necessary 'at 0.9 (present in at least nine in ten running rows), below which it is reported as present in most running rows' (3.4).
Version 2 (wall includes a trustee or a helper's position): a wall, a penalty or thin flows in 12 of 15 and 12 of 14 running rows, below the bar (4.4).

Version 3 (wall narrowed to data separation, contracts, white labels and physical separation; holder coded on its own): wall, penalty or thin flows in 6 of 10 running rows with a holder code, in both replications (4.4).
Adding a holder with no stake in the parties' customers: 9 of 10, 'which meets the bar' (4.4).
Without rule 1a the three trustee rows drop out and necessity is 6 of 7, with or without the holder, below the bar (4.4; 1.5).
Hence 'the interviews support the holder only under that rule' (4.4; 6.5).
entries.why: 0.9 is given as the conventional threshold (Schneider and Wagemann, 2012) (3.4); no further reason is given.
entries.not_this: Sufficiency, the other QCA relation, taken at 0.8 (3.4).
entries.analogy: If nine of every ten houses that survived a flood had raised floors, raised floors look necessary; if only six of seven did, you can't say that with the same confidence.

viva_questions.q: Nine of ten is exactly on the bar. Isn't that fragile?
viva_questions.model_answer: It meets the bar under rule 1a, and I say plainly that the interviews support the holder only under that rule; without it, it is six of seven, below the bar. That's why the holder is a proposition, not a finding, and why every result is given both ways (4.4; 6.5). Appendix L also shows that dropping each case in turn, the necessity figure ranges from 0.89 to 1.00, lowest without one of the trustee rows.

viva_questions.q: What is the condition whose necessity you test?
viva_questions.model_answer: Among rivals not far from the customer, that a running arrangement has a wall, a penalty, thin flows, or a holder with no stake in their customers. With the holder added, under rule 1a, it is present in nine of ten running rows (4.4; 1.5).

quiz.q: Without rule 1a, what is the necessity count?
quiz.explanation: Below the bar; with rule 1a, 9 of 10 (4.4).

entries.term: Robustness checks and the two replications
entries.plain: Repeating an analysis in ways that should not change the answer if it is sound: running it twice independently, removing one case at a time, recoding doubtful cases the hard way, and re-checking every calculation.
in_this_thesis: Two replications: 'Each pass of version 2 was paired with one of version 3, and the two pairs were run separately, as two replications, and not merged, so that a result must hold in both' (3.4).
Drop-one: 'Each result was checked by dropping each case in turn' (3.4).
Hard recoding: 'and by recoding every helper and every public body as never neutral' (3.4).

Recomputation: 'After the analysis every computation, the agreement figures, the comparison and its checks, was checked again against the settled codes; the faults found, among them a counting error, were corrected, and every figure in this thesis is from the corrected computations, which Appendix L reports' (3.4).
Appendix L reports that, dropping each case in turn, necessity ranges from 0.89 to 1.00 in each replication, lowest without H1-11.
entries.why: Replications are kept apart 'so that a result must hold in both' (3.4). The thesis gives no separate reason for the drop-one and recoding checks.
entries.not_this: Merging the passes into one data set (rejected, 3.4).
entries.analogy: Two engineers each building the bridge model separately, then taking out one strut at a time to see if it still stands.

viva_questions.q: What is a replication in your analysis?
viva_questions.model_answer: One of two separately run pairs of coding passes, a version 2 pass paired with a version 3 pass. They were run separately and not merged, so a result must hold in both, which is why my counts come in pairs, eleven of thirteen and eleven of twelve, for example (3.4; 4.4).

viva_questions.q: You found a counting error. What happened?
viva_questions.model_answer: Every computation was checked again against the settled codes after the analysis; the faults found, among them a counting error, were corrected, and every figure in the thesis is from the corrected computations, which Appendix L reports (3.4).

entries.term: Rule 1a (the trustee rule), and why it is reported both ways
entries.plain: A coding rule added after the results were seen. Because a late rule can bend a result towards what the researcher expects, every result is reported with it and without it.
in_this_thesis: The rule: 'Where a neutral trustee runs a scheme (it selects the members, holds each party's data and hires the operator), the trustee is coded as the holder, and the operator it hires as a helper working for it' (7.4).

Why it arose: once version 3 stopped counting the trustee as a wall, 'the coding rule that gives the holder to whoever holds the goods made the hired operator the holder in the three rows that describe the one trustee-run shipper network (H.1 11, 17 and 37), and the trustee was coded nowhere' (3.7).
'The rule was added after the results were seen' (3.7; 4.4; 7.4). Appendix L dates it to 28 October 2026.
'Rule 1a applies to every row, and every result is reported both with it and without it (4.4, Appendix L)' (3.7).

With it: 9 of 10 running rows meet the necessity bar; neutral holders run in 5 of 6 rows. Without it the three trustee rows drop out, 'because the transcripts do not show whether the operator each trustee hired sells to the parties' customers': 6 of 7, below the bar; neutral holders 2 of 3 (4.4; Table 7.1).
'The interviews support the holder only under that rule' (4.4).

Further research: the rule 'should be applied as it stands to arrangements this thesis did not code, so that the interviews' support for the holder is tested on rows the rule was not written from' (7.5).
entries.why: Both results are given because of the late addition: 'That late addition is why both results are given, here and in Appendix L' (4.4); and the codebook rule that 'where a change alters a result both results are reported' (3.4). The rule itself was needed because, without it, the trustee 'was coded nowhere' (3.7).
entries.not_this: Reporting only the result with the rule (rejected), or dropping the rule (also reported).
entries.analogy: A referee who changes an offside rule at half-time must publish the score under both rules, and the new rule must then be tried in matches it wasn't written for.

viva_questions.q: Your holder result depends on a rule you added after seeing the results. Isn't that circular?
viva_questions.model_answer: It would be if I hid it. The rule was added after the results were seen, I say so in 3.7, 4.4 and 7.4, it applies to every row, and every result is reported with and without it. With it, nine of ten; without it, six of seven, below the bar. So I claim only that the interviews support the holder under that rule, and the next study should apply the rule as it stands to arrangements it wasn't written from (4.4; 7.5).

viva_questions.q: Why was the rule needed at all?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because once version 3 stopped counting the trustee as a wall, the rule that gives the holder to whoever holds the goods sent the holder code to the operator the trustee hired, in the three rows on the one trustee-run shipper network, and the trustee was coded nowhere. Rule 1a codes the trustee as the holder and the operator as its helper (3.7).

viva_questions.q: Why do the three rows drop out entirely without the rule?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because the transcripts don't show whether the operator each trustee hired sells to the parties' customers, so without the rule the holder can't be classed as neutral or not (4.4).

entries.term: Other choices made after the results were seen (thin flows; rows where something crosses)
entries.plain: Any analytic choice made after seeing results is a risk of fitting the analysis to the answer; the safeguard is to say so and show the result both ways.
in_this_thesis: 'Two other choices in the analysis of the 117 were made after the first results were seen: thin flows (a low volume of freight between the parties) as a condition, added for the rural row (H.1 42), and the restriction to rows where something crosses between the parties; both are reported as such (4.4, Appendix L.4)' (3.7).
Thin flows: the rural case, offered as an inference, had neither a wall nor a penalty but thin flows, and is counted as running (4.4).

The restriction: kept to rows where something that would expose customers, brand, data or freight crossed, the contrast is 7 of 8 running with a wall or penalty against 1 of 6 with neither, and 8 of 9 against 1 of 7 (4.4).

The main text does not give the reason for the restriction. Appendix L does: it follows from S + P ≥ L + W, since where nothing crosses, L = 0 and no wall is needed; and it was specified after the counting error was found.
entries.why: Thin flows was added 'for the rural row (H.1 42)' (3.7). For the restriction, see the gap.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A surveyor who moves a boundary marker after the first measurements must mark both lines on the map.

viva_questions.q: Which of your analytic choices came after you saw the results?
viva_questions.model_answer: Three, all reported as such: rule 1a for the trustee schemes; thin flows as a condition, added for the rural row; and the restriction to rows where something crosses between the parties. Each is in 3.7, 4.4 and Appendix L, with results both ways (3.7; 4.4).

viva_questions.q: Why restrict to rows where something crosses?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because where nothing that could expose a party's customers, brand, data or freight crosses between them, there is nothing for a wall to protect: in the condition S + P ≥ L + W, L is zero. The reasoning is set out in Appendix L; the main text reports the restriction as a choice made after the first results (3.7; 4.4).

entries.term: Document analysis (Ghent's plans)
entries.plain: Reading an organisation's own documents systematically, for what they say, what they expected and what they leave out, as evidence in their own right.
in_this_thesis: Ghent was chosen as 'the one European city brought to the author's notice whose access regime writes hours into the permit itself, category by category and in law' (3.5).
'The test was documentary, in the sense Bowen (2009) gives the term: a reading of the city's own record for what it says, what it expected and what it did not count' (3.5).

Two documents, both in Dutch: the draft circulation plan, Ontwerp Circulatieplan Binnenstad Gent, of 24 October 2016, 158 pages (chapter 7: 7.8 time windows, 7.10 permit categories, 7.11 the city's modelled expectation); and the Plan stedelijke logistiek of autumn 2023, 36 pages (3.5).

Eight questions were put to them: what the regime allocates (hours or space); to whom, by category; on what conditions; what 2023 withdrew or added; what the city expected the windows to do to delivery traffic; what frictions it recorded; whether either treats operators as competitors or mentions carriers sharing; and whether 2023 mentions neighbouring cities' windows (3.5). The answers are in 5.2.
'The reading is a document analysis, not a case study in Yin's sense (2018), which would have needed the operators and the register as well as the plans' (3.5).
Belgian participants' accounts of window regimes are used with the other interviews in 5.1, not in the document reading (3.5).

The receiver's opening hours were not observed directly; they are read in participants' accounts and in the city's actor table, whose retailers' row gives 'deliveries within opening hours' as their interest (Stad Gent, 2023, p. 7) (3.5).
entries.why: 'The documents are taken as the regime's own statement of itself, which is exactly what a test of a design proposition needs' (3.5).
entries.not_this: A case study in Yin's sense, which would have needed the operators and the permit register (3.5).
entries.analogy: Judging a company's plan by its own board papers: they tell you what it intended and expected, not what happened on the shop floor.

viva_questions.q: Why Ghent, and why only Ghent?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because it is the one European city brought to my notice whose access regime writes hours into the permit itself, category by category and in law, so it is the operating instance of time-based allocation in the record. It supplies the rule by vehicle and hour's instrument, conditions and costs, not its proof (3.5; 5.2).

viva_questions.q: Why isn't this a case study?
viva_questions.model_answer: A case study in Yin's sense would have needed the operators and the permit register as well as the plans. I read the plans as the regime's own statement of itself, which is what a test of a design proposition needs; what the regime does on the street is the next study's question (3.5; 7.4; 7.5).

viva_questions.q: What did the documents not count?
viva_questions.model_answer: Deliveries by window. The 2016 plan promised evaluations after a year and after nine months to a year; the 2023 plan carries neither, so the expectation that suppliers' traffic would not fall in the open hours is treated as expected, not as found (5.2).

quiz.q: Whose sense of documentary analysis does 3.5 follow?
quiz.explanation: Scott supplies the four tests; Yin the case study it is not; Temple and Young the translation practice (3.5).

quiz.q: How many questions were put to the Ghent documents?
quiz.explanation: Six is Trafford and Leshem's design questions; four Scott's tests; fourteen the interview guide's questions (3.5).

quiz.q: Which date is the draft circulation plan?
quiz.explanation: It took effect on 3 April 2017; the logistics plan is autumn 2023 (3.5; 5.2).

story_refs: EQ ch5: Why Ghent? One city is thin evidence for a rule.

entries.term: Systematised review (the rules and the locker networks)
entries.plain: A review that records its searches, sources, dates and inclusion rules so it can be repeated, without every element of a full systematic review.
in_this_thesis: Both the rules and the locker networks were gathered 'by a systematised review in the sense Grant and Booth give the term (2009, p. 95), a search that records its strings, sources, dates and inclusion rules so that it can be repeated' (3.5).
Every search was run in October 2026; primary legal texts and public bodies' reports first, peer-reviewed studies next, press and industry sources only for dated events (3.5).
Inclusion rules in Appendix M; the full log 'is held by the author and available on request' (3.5; 3.7).

Rules read: the German postal law and its explanatory memorandum, a Swiss city's report, an Austrian ministry's guide, a European programme's framework, the Belgian postal regulator's public inquiry, the European postal regulators' report on access, and, through the press, one German city's funding rule; each read for whether it defines a neutral point by who may use it or by who holds it, and whether it looks again when control changes (3.5).
Finding: 'No rule, statute or study found looks again at a point when control of it changes' (5.2).
entries.why: The thesis defines the form (a search recorded so it can be repeated) but does not say why a systematised rather than a full systematic review was run for this evidence.
entries.not_this: A full systematic review, as used for the literature (3.2), is not used here; the thesis does not compare them.
entries.analogy: A logged survey of every bridge on a river, recording where you looked and what counted, without the full engineering audit of each one.

viva_questions.q: Why a systematised review for the rules and lockers, not a full systematic review?
viva_questions.model_answer: I used Grant and Booth's systematised form: a search that records its strings, sources, dates and inclusion rules so it can be repeated, with a stated order of sources, legal texts and regulators first, peer-reviewed studies next, press only for dated events. The thesis doesn't argue the choice against a full systematic review (3.5).

viva_questions.q: Your search log isn't in the appendices. Why?
viva_questions.model_answer: The inclusion rules, the networks and the test runs are in Appendix M; the full search log is held by me and available on request, as 3.5 and 3.7 say (3.5; 3.7).

quiz.q: Whose definition of a systematised review does 3.5 use?
In the systematised review, which sources were used only for dated events?

entries.gap: Why systematised rather than systematic is not argued, and the full search log is not appended.

entries.term: The locker networks: inclusion rule, ownership periods and the main-carrier denominator
entries.plain: How the set of parcel-locker networks was chosen and what was counted in each, so the comparison by owner can be repeated.
in_this_thesis: Inclusion: 'A network of parcel lockers or staffed pick-up points in Europe or the United Kingdom was included where its owner can be identified and at least one source says which carriers deliver into it, or that it is closed to all but its owner' (3.5).

Result: forty-three networks in sixteen countries; forty-seven ownership periods 'once a network sold during the evidence window is counted once for each owner'; 210 rows of evidence on which carrier delivers where, 'with each country's main carriers as the denominator' (3.5).
Each owner coded twice, independently, as neutral or by the kind of rival holding it: alpha .87 on class, .81 on neutral against rival-held, over forty-seven ownership periods (3.5).
The test uses the twenty-five open networks, 'leaving out each owner's own group': twenty-six ownership periods, twelve neutral-held and fourteen rival-held (3.5; 5.2).
'Its rules were written before the run, and the two added once the networks had been listed are stated in Appendix M' (3.5).
A main carrier for which no source was found is counted as not delivering (5.2).
entries.why: The ownership period is the unit 'so that a network sold during the evidence window counts once for each owner' (3.1). The thesis does not say why each country's main carriers are the denominator.
entries.not_this: Counting by pair of network and carrier, also reported but not relied on (see Fisher's exact test).
entries.analogy: Counting shops by each owner they have had, so a shop sold mid-year appears once under each owner, with each town's main suppliers as the yardstick.

viva_questions.q: Why count ownership periods rather than networks?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because a network sold during the evidence window has two owners, and the test is about who holds it, so it counts once for each owner: forty-seven periods of forty-three networks. Twenty-six periods, from the twenty-five open networks, enter the test (3.1; 3.5; 5.2).

viva_questions.q: A carrier you found no source for is counted as not delivering. Doesn't that bias the result?
viva_questions.model_answer: It could, and I say so. But the count of pairs with evidence, which leaves such carriers out, points the same way: forty-five of forty-eight neutral-held pairs against eighteen of forty-four rival-held (5.2).

quiz.q: How many ownership periods enter the locker test?
quiz.explanation: From the twenty-five open networks; forty-seven periods across all forty-three networks (3.5; 5.2).

quiz.q: What is the denominator for each network's share?

entries.gap: Why main carriers are the denominator is not argued; how the two rules added after listing affected the run is in Appendix M only.

entries.term: Permutation test
entries.plain: A test that asks whether a difference between two groups could be luck, by shuffling the group labels many times and seeing how often a difference as large as the real one turns up.
in_this_thesis: The comparison is 'by a permutation test on the twenty-six ownership periods that enter it, each counted once (Agresti, 2013)' (3.5).
On average 46.0 per cent of a country's main carriers deliver into a network held by a firm that sells no delivery, against 21.3 per cent for rival-held networks; permutation test, p = .008 (5.2).
'The permutation test above, which counts each ownership period once, is the result the thesis rests on (Appendix M.3)' (5.2).
Appendix M gives the detail: a difference of 24.7 points, two-sided, 200,000 relabellings.
'With so few periods no regression was run' (3.5).
The result 'is a difference between types of owner. It fits the link but does not test it' (1.5).
entries.why: It 'counts each ownership period once' (5.2), whereas the pair-level counts are not independent; and with so few periods no regression was run (3.5).
entries.not_this: Fisher's exact test on pairs (reported as indicative) and regression (not run) (3.5; 5.2).
entries.analogy: If twelve red and fourteen blue raffle tickets were drawn, and reds won much more often, you'd reshuffle the colours many times and see how often reds win that much by chance.

viva_questions.q: Why a permutation test, not regression?
viva_questions.model_answer: With twenty-six ownership periods, too few for regression. The permutation test counts each period once, so it doesn't pretend the many pairs of network and carrier are independent; that's why it is the result I rest on: 46.0 against 21.3 per cent, p = .008 (3.5; 5.2).

viva_questions.q: Explain p = .008 here in plain words.
viva_questions.model_answer: If who holds a network made no difference, and I shuffled the neutral and rival labels across the twenty-six periods, a gap as large as the real one, in either direction, would turn up fewer than one time in a hundred (5.2; Appendix M).

viva_questions.q: Does p = .008 show that a neutral holder causes carriers to join?
viva_questions.model_answer: No. It is a difference by owner class at one time, consistent with the proposition and not a test of it; the networks weren't matched on price, size or terms, and cause is left to reading the networks again after each change of holder (5.2; 7.4; 7.5).

quiz.q: What does the permutation test count once?
options: Each pair of network and carrier

quiz.q: What p value does the locker comparison rest on?
quiz.explanation: p < .001 is Fisher's on pairs (indicative); .039 and .18 the sign tests (5.2).

quiz.q: Why was no regression run?
options: Regression is not allowed in theory-building
There were too few ownership periods
quiz.explanation: 'With so few periods no regression was run' (3.5).

entries.term: The p value and statistical significance
entries.plain: A p value is the probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one observed if there were in fact no real difference. A small p means the result would be surprising by chance alone; it does not measure size or cause.
in_this_thesis: Locker test, each ownership period counted once: p = .008 (5.2).
Pairs of network and carrier, Fisher's exact test: p < .001 for both counts, 'indicative' because the pairs are not independent (5.2).
Same carrier, sign test: by carrier group 7 against 2, 10 equal, p = .18; by national name 10 against 2, 9 equal, p = .039 (5.2).
On the group count, 'the difference does not reach significance, so the same-carrier check gives the direction and does not prove it' (5.2).
The survey runs 'no test of significance' (3.6).
entries.why: The thesis reports p values for the locker comparison only, where it has a comparison to test (3.5; 5.2). It does not state the significance level it uses.
entries.not_this: Significance tests on the survey (not run, 3.6).
entries.analogy: A smoke alarm's sensitivity: a reading this high would rarely happen with no fire, but it doesn't tell you how big the fire is or who started it.

viva_questions.q: Your group sign test gives p = .18. Doesn't that undermine the locker result?
viva_questions.model_answer: It gives the direction and doesn't prove it, and I say so. By group, seven carriers lean neutral and two rival, ten equal, which doesn't reach significance; by national name it's ten against two, p = .039, but the arms of one group share an owner, so the group count is the stricter. The result I rest on is the permutation test, p = .008 (5.2).

viva_questions.q: What significance level do you use?
viva_questions.model_answer: The thesis reports the p values and reads them in words, for instance that .18 'does not reach significance'; it doesn't state a level. And each p is read for what it is: a difference by owner class at one time, not a cause (5.2; 7.4).

quiz.q: Which p value comes from the sign test by carrier group?
quiz.explanation: .039 is by national name; .008 the permutation test; < .001 Fisher's on pairs (5.2).

quiz.q: What does the thesis conclude from the same-carrier sign tests?
options: They give the direction and do not prove it
They prove a neutral holder causes carriers to join

entries.gap: No significance level is stated anywhere in the thesis.

entries.term: Fisher's exact test, and why non-independent pairs make it indicative
entries.plain: Fisher's exact test checks whether two yes/no categories are related in a small table of counts. It assumes each counted item is independent; if items are linked, its p value overstates the certainty.
in_this_thesis: The test compares carriers' delivery into neutral-held and rival-held networks 'by Fisher's exact test on the carriers' (3.5).
Pairs with evidence: the carrier delivers in 45 of 48 neutral-held pairs and 18 of 44 rival-held (5.2).
Pairs with each country's main carriers: 41 of 88 and 18 of 86 (5.2).
Fisher's exact test, p < .001 for both (two-sided, Appendix M) (5.2).

'The pairs are not independent, because one network serves several carriers and one carrier faces several networks, so these two p-values are indicative, and the permutation test above, which counts each ownership period once, is the result the thesis rests on' (5.2).
entries.why: The thesis reports both tests and rests on the permutation test because the pairs are not independent (5.2). It does not say why Fisher's exact test in particular was chosen for the pairs.
entries.not_this: Relying on the pair-level p values (rejected as only indicative, 5.2).
entries.analogy: Polling ten members of one family counts as ten votes, but they are not ten independent opinions.

viva_questions.q: Your Fisher's test gives p < .001. Why not lead with it?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because the pairs are not independent: one network serves several carriers and one carrier faces several networks. So those p values are indicative only, and I rest on the permutation test, which counts each ownership period once (5.2).

viva_questions.q: Do the pair counts and the period counts agree?
viva_questions.model_answer: They point the same way: forty-five of forty-eight neutral-held pairs with evidence against eighteen of forty-four rival-held, and forty-one of eighty-eight against eighteen of eighty-six main-carrier pairs, beside 46.0 against 21.3 per cent by period (5.2).

quiz.q: Why are the Fisher p values only indicative?
options: The networks are in sixteen countries
quiz.explanation: One network serves several carriers and one carrier faces several networks (5.2).

quiz.q: In how many of the 48 neutral-held pairs with evidence does the carrier deliver?
quiz.explanation: 18 of 44 rival-held; 41 of 88 is the main-carrier pairs (5.2).

entries.gap: Why Fisher's exact test was chosen for the pairs is not stated.

entries.term: Sign test: holding the carrier fixed
entries.plain: A simple test of direction: for each case, record only whether it leans one way or the other, ignore ties, and ask whether one direction wins more often than a coin toss would give.
in_this_thesis: 'The same carrier, by group and by national name, compared across networks of both kinds by a sign test, which holds the carrier fixed though not a network's price, terms or siting' (3.5).
By carrier group: of the 19 groups facing both kinds, 7 deliver into a larger share of the neutral-held networks, 2 into a larger share of the rival-held, 10 equal; p = .18 (5.2).
By national name: 10 against 2, 9 equal; p = .039 (5.2).

A national name is each name under which a carrier delivers, so the arms of one group, such as DHL's, count apart; 'because those arms share an owner they are not independent of one another, and the count by group is the stricter of the two' (5.2).
'The same-carrier check gives the direction and does not prove it' (5.2).
Holding the network constant as well 'needs locker price, size and service data that the public sources used here do not hold' (7.4).
entries.why: It holds the carrier fixed (3.5), removing differences between carriers from the comparison.
entries.not_this: A quality-matched comparison holding the network fixed too, left to 7.5 (7.4).
entries.analogy: Asking the same shoppers which of two shops they use more, so differences between shoppers drop out.

viva_questions.q: Why test the same carriers separately?
viva_questions.model_answer: To hold the carrier fixed, so the difference isn't just that different carriers face different networks. It doesn't hold a network's price, terms or siting fixed. By group, seven against two with ten equal, p = .18; by national name, ten against two, p = .039. It gives the direction and doesn't prove it (3.5; 5.2).

viva_questions.q: Why is the group count the stricter one?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because a group's national arms share an owner, so they aren't independent of one another; counting by group treats each owner once (5.2).

quiz.q: By carrier group, how did the 19 groups facing both kinds split?
quiz.explanation: 10 against 2 with 9 equal is by national name (5.2).

quiz.q: What does the sign test NOT hold fixed?
options: A network's price, terms or siting

entries.term: 'Consistent with, not a test of': one-time comparison versus cause
entries.plain: A difference found by comparing cases at one moment can fit an explanation without proving it; showing cause needs, for example, watching the same cases before and after a change.
in_this_thesis: The locker result 'is a difference between types of owner. It fits the link but does not test it' (1.5).
'The test compares networks at one time: it shows a difference by owner class, and it neither measures a gradient between pairs of firms nor shows a cause' (5.2).
Holders are coded by class, not by their market commonality with each carrier, so the result is 'consistent with the gradient P5 proposes and not a test of it' (7.4; 3.7).

By owner class the share falls from 46 (neutral) to 42 (retailers with own delivery), 29 (carriers' subsidiaries), 17 (carrier-owned), 15 (postal operators) and none for the one joint network, 'an ordering consistent with a gradient of market commonality ... though the classes are too small to test it' (5.2).

Named threats: published sources may under-record carriers; a neutral network, which lives by selling access, may have more reason to list its carriers; the networks were not matched on price, size or terms, and no public measure of quality was found (5.2; 3.5).

Changes of owner are read both ways: GLS ended its cooperation after Austrian Post took over a telecoms operator's stations (by February 2024), though that may reflect the new owner's terms; De Buren passed to DHL Group in May 2025 with DPD and UPS named on the day of sale and no later statement; myflexbox's sale to Deutsche Post on 1 October 2026 is the baseline (5.2).
'Cause is left to reading the networks again after each change of holder (7.5)' (5.2).
entries.why: As stated in 5.2 and 7.4: a comparison at one time, by class, unmatched on quality, cannot show cause.
entries.not_this: A before-and-after design after each change of holder, and a quality-matched comparison, both left to further research (7.5; 7.4).
entries.analogy: Finding that towns with more fire stations have fewer house fires is consistent with stations preventing fires, but you'd need to watch towns before and after a station opens to know.

viva_questions.q: The locker difference could be price, size or quality. How do you know it's the holder?
viva_questions.model_answer: I don't claim to. The test compares networks at one time, by owner class, unmatched on price, size or terms, because no public measure of quality was found. It shows a difference by owner class consistent with the proposition, and the same-carrier check gives the direction. Cause is left to reading the networks again after each change of holder, with myflexbox's sale as the baseline (5.2; 7.4; 7.5).

viva_questions.q: Your sales evidence cuts both ways. Why include it?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because it is the only evidence of drift by sale, and I read each sale both ways: GLS's exit after Austrian Post's takeover may reflect the new owner's terms; De Buren shows no exit at sale but no later statement either. Two changes of owner are thin, and 3.7 says so (5.2; 3.7).

quiz.q: What does the locker test NOT show, according to 5.2?
options: A direction within the same carriers
A cause, or a gradient between pairs of firms

quiz.q: Which owner class reaches the smallest share of main carriers?
quiz.explanation: 5.2; Figure 5.3.

entries.term: Likert-type items (and their directions)
entries.plain: Questions answered on a numbered scale, here 1 to 5, between two labelled ends, such as 'not important' and 'extremely important'.
in_this_thesis: 'Three items are five-point Likert-type items (Likert, 1932), and they do not run the same way' (3.6).
Success: 1 very successful to 5 very unsuccessful. Importance of trust: 1 not important to 5 extremely important. Likelihood of more collaboration: 1 very likely to 5 very unlikely (3.6).
'Every table that reports them states the direction' (3.6).
The draft's worded scales for success and future engagement became scales of 1 to 5 in the final form (3.6).
Results are reported as counts and percentages, e.g. trust: 68 chose 5 and 21 chose 4, 89 of 119 (75 per cent), none chose 1 or 2 (5.3).
entries.why: The thesis states the items and directions; it does not say why the directions differ.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: Three thermometers, two marked hot at the top and one hot at the bottom: readable, provided every reading says which way up it was.

viva_questions.q: Your three scales run in different directions. Did that cause errors?
viva_questions.model_answer: I state the direction wherever an item is reported: success from 1 very successful to 5 very unsuccessful, trust from 1 not important to 5 extremely important, likelihood from 1 very likely to 5 very unlikely. The thesis doesn't test whether respondents misread the directions; it reports the answers as they stand (3.6; 5.3).

viva_questions.q: How did you summarise the Likert answers?
viva_questions.model_answer: As counts and percentages of those who answered, not as tests: on trust, 68 chose 5 and 21 chose 4, 89 of 119 in all, and no one chose 1 or 2 (5.3; 3.6).

quiz.q: On the trust item, what does 5 mean?
On the likelihood item, what does 1 mean?
quiz.explanation: Success runs 1 very successful to 5 very unsuccessful (3.6).

entries.gap: Why the scales run in different directions, and whether that confused respondents, is not discussed.

entries.term: Descriptive analysis only: counts, percentages and cross-tabulations
entries.plain: Describing what respondents said with counts, percentages and two-way tables, without statistical tests or claims about a wider population.
in_this_thesis: 'The analysis is descriptive: counts, percentages of those who answered each item, and cross-tabulations by company size and by whether the company collaborates now' (3.6).
Percentages are whole numbers in the chapters and to one decimal place in Appendix K (3.6).
'No test of significance is run and nothing is inferred to a population' (3.6).
The 2024 application planned correlation and regression (Appendix C.1); 'neither is run' (3.6).

Example cross-tabulation: collaborating now by size, 14 of 30 large (47 per cent), 13 of 34 medium (38), 9 of 45 small (20); rating trust at 5, 28 of 50 small (56), 19 of 35 medium (54), 21 of 34 large (62) (5.3).
entries.why: Correlation and regression were not run 'because a sample that selected itself supports no estimate beyond itself (Fowler, 2014), and because the survey is used here to give scale to what the interviews heard of trust, not to measure the industry' (3.6).
entries.not_this: Correlation and regression, as planned in 2024 (3.6; 3.8).
entries.analogy: A census of one room: you can say exactly what this room thinks, not what the country thinks.

viva_questions.q: Why no significance tests on the survey?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because a sample that selected itself supports no estimate beyond itself, as Fowler says, and because the survey gives scale to what the interviews heard of trust, not a measure of the industry. The application had planned correlation and regression; neither was run, and Table 3.8 records the change (3.6; 3.8).

viva_questions.q: What is a cross-tabulation, and how did you use it?
viva_questions.model_answer: A table of one answer against another. I cross-tabulated by company size and by whether the company collaborates now: for example, the share collaborating now runs from 9 of 45 small companies to 14 of 30 large, while the share rating trust at 5 is much the same at every size (3.6; 5.3).

quiz.q: Why were correlation and regression not run on the survey?
options: A self-selected sample supports no estimate beyond itself, and the survey is used for scale
The software could not run them

quiz.q: Among large companies, what share collaborate now?
quiz.explanation: Small 9 of 45, medium 13 of 34, overall 36 of 109 (5.3).

entries.term: Item-level denominators and the skip that was not applied
entries.plain: When respondents skip questions, each question is reported out of those who answered it. A 'skip' is a rule that sends some respondents past questions not meant for them; if it fails, unintended people answer.
in_this_thesis: Of 132 responses, six answered No to consent and seven gave consent but nothing more; the other 119 are usable, 'and every one of them is kept, however many items it answered. Each item is reported of those who answered it, with that number beside it' (3.6).
'The form did not apply the draft's skip, and the answers are reported as they stand' (3.6).

36 of the 109 who answered said they collaborate now, but 48 said how long they had been involved (12 of them had answered No) and 48 rated their collaboration's success (36 collaborating now, 12 not); these are 'read as past engagement' (3.6).

Goals were answered by 107, 68 of them not collaborating now, read as goals a company has or would have; mechanisms of trust by 45 (11 not now), benefits by 49 (13), challenges by 93 (53), read as past or expected collaboration (3.6).
'A challenge named by a company that does not collaborate now may be one it met in an earlier attempt or one it expects, and the item cannot tell the two apart' (3.6).
The duration answers run from '1-3 years' to 'More than 5 years', with nothing between; the draft had offered 'More than 3 years' (3.6).
entries.why: The thesis keeps every usable response and reports each item against those who answered (3.6). It does not say why the skip was not applied; it names it among the irregularities a pilot might have caught.
entries.not_this: Dropping partial responses, or forcing the draft's skip after the fact; neither is done.
entries.analogy: A form that says 'married people only, answer section C', but has no gate: you count section C out of whoever filled it in, and say who they were.

viva_questions.q: Twelve companies that don't collaborate rated their collaboration's success. How do you read that?
viva_questions.model_answer: The form didn't apply the draft's skip, so I report the answers as they stand and read them as past engagement. The twelve who chose 4 are the twelve that said they don't collaborate now, all involved for less than a year; the 36 who collaborate now chose 2 or 3 (3.6; 5.3).

viva_questions.q: Why does each survey item have a different denominator?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because I kept every one of the 119 usable responses however many items it answered, so each item is reported of those who answered it, with the number beside it (3.6).

entries.term: Cohen's kappa and the survey's open answers
entries.plain: Cohen's kappa measures agreement between two codings beyond what chance would give, for categorical codes; 1.00 is perfect agreement.
in_this_thesis: The open question, on key factors for success, was answered by 39; answers were coded inductively (Braun and Clarke, 2006) into six themes and a code for answers with nothing of substance; an answer may carry more than one theme; the codebook is in Appendix K (3.6).
Coded twice, independently, against one codebook; the second coding blind, from the codebook and the answers alone (3.6).

'The two codings agreed on all 39 answers (Cohen's kappa 1.00 over 273 coding decisions, seven codes for each answer; Cohen, 1960), reported as O'Connor and Joffe (2020) recommend for codebook work' (3.6).
Limit: 'The codebook was drawn up from these answers in the first coding, which makes agreement easier to reach in so short a set, and the agreement is reported with that limit' (3.6).

Themes (5.3): agreed terms and a party to hold them (10); the means and the money (9); public rules, powers or incentives (7); trust between the partners (6); customers and data stay with their owner (5); the decision placed with another party (3); six said nothing of substance.
The open question came last, after the items on trust, 'so its answers may echo them'; they are read 'as examples of what respondents say and not as a count of the industry's view' (5.3).
entries.why: Reported as O'Connor and Joffe recommend for codebook work (3.6). The thesis does not say why kappa here rather than alpha.
entries.not_this: Krippendorff's alpha, used for the arrangements; raw agreement, used for the transcripts (3.4).
entries.analogy: Two judges scoring the same thirty-nine entries against a rubric one of them helped write: perfect agreement is good, but expected.

viva_questions.q: A kappa of 1.00 looks too perfect.
viva_questions.model_answer: It's reported with its limit: the codebook was drawn up from these same answers in the first coding, which makes agreement easier in so short a set, thirty-nine answers. The second coding was blind, from the codebook and the answers alone, over 273 decisions, seven codes for each answer (3.6).

viva_questions.q: What did the open answers say?
viva_questions.model_answer: The largest theme, in ten answers, was agreed terms and a party to hold them, such as 'a neutral third party running it ... without it falls apart within a year'. Six named trust between the partners. They are thirty-nine voluntary answers, read as examples, not as the industry's view (5.3).

quiz.q: Over how many coding decisions was kappa computed?
quiz.explanation: Seven codes for each of 39 answers (3.6).

options: Agreed terms and a party to hold them
quiz.explanation: 10 answers; means and money 9; public rules 7; trust 6 (5.3).

entries.gap: Why kappa rather than alpha for the open answers is not stated.

entries.term: The scenario model (a scenario, not a forecast)
entries.plain: A worked example that sets out what a policy might cost and save under stated assumptions, with low, central and high values, rather than a prediction of what will happen.
in_this_thesis: For 'one notional council area of 50,000 households, as a scenario and not a forecast' (3.5).

'Each input has a low, a central and a high value, a worst case is added, every input is sourced or marked as an assumption, and only the increment over the redirection to nearby points that already happens is counted' (3.5).
Time valued at the Department for Transport's value for non-work time, £7.08 an hour; car emissions at 0.167 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent a kilometre (3.5).

Central case: about 33,600 depot trips and 28,000 hours of residents' time saved a year (about 9,100 hours by households without a car), worth about £198,000; carriers save about £106,000 on redeliveries; checking 60 points at £700 costs £42,000; net about £262,000 (6.3).
Low case: adds nothing, leaving the cost of checking 30 points at £400, £12,000. Worst case: low benefits with 100 points at £1,500, the council £150,000 a year down (6.3).
'Eight of the thirteen inputs are assumptions, and the result turns on the share of missed parcels redirected and the time each trip saves' (6.3).
A check costs about £400 to £1,500 a point a year (6.3). Inputs, sources and formulas are in Appendix N (3.5).
entries.why: The thesis presents it as setting out 'what the rule proposed in 6.3 ... would cost and save' (3.5). It does not argue for the scenario method against alternatives. 3.7 calls it 'a worked example on an assumed share of what is redirected today'.
entries.not_this: A forecast (3.5; 6.3).
entries.analogy: A household budget drawn up for a lean month, a normal month and a bad month: it shows what depends on what, not what next month will be.

viva_questions.q: Eight of your thirteen inputs are assumptions. What is the scenario worth?
viva_questions.model_answer: It is a worked example, not a forecast, and I say which inputs are assumptions and that the result turns on two of them, the share of missed parcels redirected and the time each trip saves. It shows the range: about £262,000 a year net in the central case, nothing but a £12,000 checking cost in the low case, and £150,000 down in the worst case (6.3; 3.7).

viva_questions.q: Why count only the increment?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because some missed parcels are already redirected to nearby points, so only what the rule adds beyond that redirection is counted (3.5).

quiz.q: In the central case, what is the net value a year?
quiz.explanation: £198,000 of residents' time plus £106,000 carriers' saving minus £42,000 checking; £150,000 down is the worst case (6.3).

quiz.q: What value of time does the scenario use?
quiz.explanation: The Department for Transport's value for non-work time; 0.167 kg is the car emissions factor (3.5).

entries.term: Limitations and the critique with hindsight
entries.plain: An honest list of what the research could not show, with the consequence of each, and what a critic would say with hindsight.
in_this_thesis: The paradigm's cost: 'a mechanism named from twenty-six accounts is retroduced and not observed, so it is a proposition, and it generalises to the mechanism and not to a population' (3.7).

Carriers: four of twenty-six interviews speak for a carrier (three of thirty voices, a fourth an adviser to one); much of what is said of carriers is second-hand, though from people who negotiated with them for years (3.7; 7.4).
Out-of-domain transcripts kept in every denominator; the binder assigned once, with no agreement figure; silence counts may be too high; the survey self-selected, unpiloted and on the pillars (3.7).
Ghent read in documents, not its operators or permit register (3.7; 7.4).

Fifth link: coded by holder class, not pair by pair; 26 ownership periods; much of carriers' use known from regulators and the press; support only under rule 1a; thin flows and the restriction chosen after results; networks not matched on quality; drift by sale rests on two changes of owner, each read both ways; the scenario a worked example; no residents, shopkeepers or employed drivers interviewed; no court has ruled on the rule's proportionality (3.7).
Translations not checked by a Dutch speaker (7.4).

Critique with hindsight: a positivist design would have measured what was counted and said less about why; an interpretivist one would have said nothing about the mechanism; 'a guide written after the fact would have asked about overlap and time directly and found less than it was told, because the participants brought both unprompted' (7.4).
entries.why: The thesis states them with their consequences ('One further limit is stated with its consequence', 7.4); it gives no separate reason for the section.
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A surveyor's report that marks on the map which areas were measured on foot and which were sketched from a distance.

viva_questions.q: What would a critic say with hindsight?
viva_questions.model_answer: That a positivist design would have measured overlap against willingness across a sample and said less about why; that an interpretivist one would have said nothing about the mechanism; and that the fieldwork was designed under a framework the data replaced. Against the last, a guide written after the fact would have found less, because participants brought overlap and time unprompted (7.4).

viva_questions.q: What does your argument need that you did not observe directly?

Both are further studies (3.5; 7.4; 7.5).

entries.term: Generalising to the mechanism, not the population (analytical generalisation)
entries.plain: Instead of claiming a result holds for a whole population, the claim is that a mechanism has been identified that may operate elsewhere, under the right conditions. Methodologists often call this analytical generalisation.
in_this_thesis: Table 3.2, critical realist column: findings generalise 'To the mechanism, not the population; it may fire elsewhere under other conditions (Easton, 2010)'.
'A mechanism named from twenty-six accounts is a proposition, and what it generalises to is the mechanism, which may work elsewhere, not a population' (3.1).
Propositions are 'claimed for the mechanism it names, not for a population (7.4)' (7.2).
7.4: the propositions 'rest on the cases from which they were drawn, are offered as propositions about mechanisms rather than as generalisations about populations, and are open to others to test'.
Transferability is met by thick description, by code and type, for a reader to judge where the findings travel (3.7).
The thesis does not use the phrase 'analytical generalisation'; it says 'generalises to the mechanism'.
entries.why: It is the generalisation critical realism allows (Table 3.2; 7.4): 'The generalisation the paradigm allows is the one the propositions of 7.2 claim' (7.4).
entries.not_this: Statistical generalisation from sample to population (positivist), and no generalisation, transferability left to the reader (interpretivist) (Table 3.2).
entries.analogy: Learning how a lock's mechanism works from a handful of locks: it tells you how any lock of that design can be opened, not how many such locks exist.

viva_questions.q: Is this what's called analytical generalisation?
viva_questions.model_answer: That's the usual label for what I claim, though the thesis puts it in its own words: a mechanism named from twenty-six accounts generalises to the mechanism, not to a population; it may fire elsewhere under other conditions. The propositions rest on the cases they were drawn from and are open to others to test (3.1; Table 3.2; 7.4).

viva_questions.q: How is that different from transferability?
viva_questions.model_answer: Transferability is the reader's judgement on a thick description, and I support it with description by code and type across eleven countries. My claim goes a step further than an interpretivist would, that a mechanism may fire elsewhere under other conditions, and still stops short of a population (3.7; Table 3.2).

entries.term: Propositions and their falsifiers (P1 to P5, Table 7.1)
entries.plain: A proposition is a single testable statement linking two variables. A falsifier is the observation that would show it wrong.
in_this_thesis: Each proposition is 'a single statement relating two variables, under the conditions it names, that others may test in their own context; each is claimed for the mechanism it names, not for a population' (7.2).

P1: unless a wall, a penalty or an owner with no stake outweighs the exposure, willingness falls as the overlap of customer markets rises. Falsifier: a sample with no wall, penalty or neutral holder in which willingness does not fall with overlap at some size band, or in which size sorts willingness where overlap does not (Table 7.1).

P2: the more a shared resource constitutes a party's customer relationship, the less likely it is to be pooled. Falsifier: a working arrangement between rivals in the urban last mile pooling freight, customers or operating data with nothing binding it.

P3: a horizontal collaboration lasts as long as the external arrangement that binds it. Falsifier: an arrangement that outlived its binder on trust alone, or dissolved while its binder stood and its parties still gained.

P4: an instrument aimed at the party that places the order or writes the permit changes flows more than the same instrument aimed at the carrier. Falsifier: an instrument aimed at carriers that moved flows more.

P5: at equal access, a carrier's use of a shared point falls as the holder's market commonality with that carrier rises. Falsifier: no difference in use by holder at equal access, or no change in carriers' partner lists after a sale to a rival.
Each row of Table 7.1 gives what the proposition rests on and its counts, first and second reading (7.2).
entries.why: 'Because the design was theory-building, the contribution is offered as propositions rather than as tested hypotheses' (7.2). A falsifier is 'what a proposition is for' when tested (7.5).
entries.not_this: Tested hypotheses (7.2).
entries.analogy: A recipe card that also says exactly what result would prove the recipe wrong, so the next cook knows what to look for.

viva_questions.q: What would falsify P5?
viva_questions.model_answer: No difference in carriers' use of a point by holder at equal access, or no change in carriers' lists of partners after a point is sold to a rival (Table 7.1; 2.7).

viva_questions.q: Why offer propositions rather than conclusions?
viva_questions.model_answer: Because the design was theory-building. Each proposition is a single statement relating two variables, under the conditions it names, claimed for the mechanism and not for a population, with its falsifier, so others can test it in their own context (7.2).

entries.term: The designs left for further research
entries.plain: The studies that would test what this thesis could only propose, each with its data, its unit and its comparison.
in_this_thesis: 'Seven studies follow from what this thesis could not do, and each is named where the thesis met its limit, with the data it needs, the unit it would count and the comparison it would make' (7.5).
1, measure the physical signal: shippers' carrier choices; unit the award of a contract; branded against unbranded at the same price and time.
2, count the handover: time-stamped delivery records; unit the delivery; a no-stake point against the door or a rival-held point on the same streets.
3, publish the record Ghent's plans do not report: permit and camera counts; unit the cell of a window and a class of operator; before and after a rule by vehicle and hour.
4, the shipper side as a category: the rows of Appendix H and the thirteen papers; unit the arrangement; shipper-begun against carrier-begun.
5, ask the receivers: unit the opening hour; the hour offered against the hour moved.
6, ask whether hours set by a city are acceptable to those they would bind: unit the organisation; a rule by vehicle and hour against hours by class of operator and against no rule.
7, test the propositions as hypotheses 'in a deductive design in a market this thesis did not sample': a survey of operator pairs; unit the pair; each proposition against its falsifier.

For the fifth link: vignettes for planners; use per point against volume; council test parcels for the dot; matched streets before and after (Angrist and Pischke, 2009) from first-attempt records and residents' diaries; re-reading the locker networks after the myflexbox sale with quality, price and terms matched; and applying rule 1a as it stands to arrangements not coded here (7.5).
entries.why: Each is 'named where the thesis met its limit' (7.5).
entries.not_this: The thesis names no alternative.
entries.analogy: A builder's handover note listing which walls were load-tested and how the next team should test the rest.

viva_questions.q: How would you show that a neutral holder causes carriers to join?
viva_questions.model_answer: By a before-and-after design: read the locker networks again after each change of holder, starting from myflexbox's sale on 1 October 2026 as the baseline, with quality, price and terms matched. Holding the network constant needs price, size and service data the public sources don't hold (5.2; 7.4; 7.5).

viva_questions.q: How would P1 be tested properly?
viva_questions.model_answer: As the seventh study sets out: a deductive design in a market I didn't sample, a survey of operator pairs with the pair as the unit, each proposition set against its falsifier in Table 7.1 (7.5).
